News.title: FIFA bosses to make billions in profit as research shows World Cup 2026 to bring in nearly £4bn
News.content:
FIFA bosses to make billions in profit as research shows World Cup 2026 to bring in nearly £4bn

Brand Finance, the world’s leading brand valuation consultancy, found the tournament generated £45bn in "enterprise value". That came from £2bn in sponsorship, yielding a 22-fold return.

Spain celebrate World Cup triumph with open-top bus parade

FIFA is set to make around £3.8bn ($5.2bn) from the World Cup, according to new research.

‌



Analysis by Brand Finance, the world’s leading brand valuation consultancy, found the tournament generated £45bn in "enterprise value". That came from £2bn in sponsorship, yielding a 22-fold return.

‌



Sponsors also added an estimated £5.3bn to their combined brand value during the tournament, the longest in World Cup history held in the US, Mexico and Canada. The research combined Brand Finance's valuation model with sponsorship modelling across 21 official partners. FIFA was the 'ultimate winner' and projected to generate record revenues across the 2023-26 commercial cycle.

‌



View 2 Images England fans at the World Cup semi-final clash against Argentina (Image: World Cup 2026 News Pool (WCNP))

The people of Gaza watch the World Cup final amid the ruins of their homes READ MORE :

The "FIFA World Cup 2026 brand" was valued at £3.8bn, with sponsorship revenue accounting for £1.4bn. That was the single largest contributor to that value. FIFA's commercial success has been underpinned by expansion.

The 2026 tournament featured 48 teams and 104 matches across 16 host cities. Yet demand from sponsors continued to outpace supply.

‌



Richard Haigh, Global Managing Director at Brand Finance, said: "FIFA has built one of the strongest commercial models in sport. It secures sponsorship revenue upfront, regardless of whether an individual sponsor's campaign ultimately succeeds or falls short.

"Sponsors carry the execution risk, but our analysis suggests many are still generating significant value from the tournament. The more interesting question is what happens next.

View 2 Images Captain Harry Kane thanks the England fans at their semi-final defeat to Argentina (Image: World Cup 2026 News Pool (WCNP))

‌



"FIFA continues to expand the World Cup and its sponsorship programme, with discussions around a 64-team tournament already emerging. Historically, bigger events have risked diluting sponsor value. FIFA appears to have achieved the opposite: every expansion strengthened its commercial proposition.

"A t some point, sponsors will inevitably ask where the ceiling is. For now, however, the data suggests FIFA remains uniquely capable of monetising the world's most valuable sporting platform."

England ended their World Cup campaign in style with a thrilling 6-4 victory over France - and a touching display of sportsmanship at the end of the game. Captain Harry Kane and his side were dignified in victory, a total contrast to Argentina's disgraceful behaviour in the semi-final.

Article continues below

France's Kylian Mbappe, 27, scored twice to become the leading World Cup goalscorer in history with 22 goals. England players did not forget the loyal army of fans who had spent a fortune following the team across the United States.

Goalscorer Ezri Konsa, 28, said they reflected on the semi-final defeat, which had been 'painful'. But he added: "We have a special group with special players. We apologise that we could not go that one step further. We hope that we brought some joy back home and to the fans watching here."

News.title: 'I live off scraps from my little girl's plate - here's my message to Andy Burnham'
News.content:
'I live off scraps from my little girl's plate - here's my message to Andy Burnham'

EXCLUSIVE: As Andy Burnham promises 'breathing space' for struggling families with the scrapping of VAT on electricity bills, a single dad in fuel poverty has shared the harrowing reality of his daily life

View 6 Images Andrew Anderson describes being stuck in fuel poverty as 'a living hell' (Image: Andrew/Trussell Trust)

A father who has suffered the raw indignities of fuel poverty has spoken out following the announcement that millions of UK households will benefit from the removal of VAT on electricity bills

‌



In what marks one of his first acts at the helm of Number 10, Prime Minister Andy Burnham pledged "immediate action to cut taxes on energy bills, put more money in people's pockets and bring back hope".

‌



Intended to give households some "breathing space" amid the ongoing cost of living crisis, this measure is expected to knock £45 off the average bill.

‌



For struggling parents like Andrew Anderson, who has been forced to live off leftover scraps to cover his bills, it's a welcome move forward, but there's still a long way to go before the agonies of fuel poverty can be alleviated.

View 6 Images Downing Street has announced that the Government would remove VAT from domestic electricity bills from October 1 (Image: Fred Duval/SOPA Images/Shutterstock)

Speaking with the Mirror, Andrew, 44, says: "Change has to start somewhere, and I am happy that in his first few days the new Prime Minister is thinking of the people who have the least. To be honest, the money I save on the scrapping of VAT on my electricity for a few months won't change anything, but it starts towards helping.

‌



Unable to work because of a severe autoimmune disease, devoted dad Andrew does everything in his power to shield his young daughter, Mia, from the grinding financial instability he faces every day, exacerbated by steep energy costs. Last year, Andrew lost two stone from a lack of food, regularly skipping meals to ensure Mia didn't go hungry.

The Fife-based father routinely resorts to living off leftovers from his daughter's plate, and can't remember the last time he bought himself clothes. Back in May, it was revealed that the Ofgem price cap would skyrocket by 13 per cent to £1,862 a year for a typical dual-fuel household paying by direct debit. This marks an increase of £221, forcing families to find an extra £18 a month, and piling additional pressure onto households already on the brink.

View 6 Images Last year, Andrew lost two stone from a lack of food (Image: Andrew/Trussell Trust)

‌



Speaking with the Mirror at the time, an audibly emotional Andrew asked: "What are you supposed to do? Are you supposed to heat your home? Are you supposed to eat food?" Andrew described his current existence as "a living hell," as he fights to clothe and feed a rapidly growing child.

He shared: "I'm down to two pairs of trackie bottoms now that I have to constantly rotate. I have to watch when I put the washing machine on for my little girl's school clothes, because she's nine years old now and shooting through the roof."

To cope with the price hike, Andrew is cutting back to the bare minimum: no after-school clubs, no "doing anything nice together", and only buying the cheapest food. Andrew said, "I'm going to have to stop putting the heating on at all when my daughter's not in the house. It's going to be an awful, awful cycle."

‌



Andrew likened his situation to "banging your head off against a brick wall", questioning how people can be driven to such devastating circumstances in the UK.

When asked this week about Burnham's pledge to put the cost of living crisis at the heart of his government, the struggling dad said: "What I would say is that Andy Burham can't just try to save people money; he also has to make sure that people who have the least currently have more going forward.

6 View 6 Images Back in May, Andrew likened his situation to 'banging your head off against a brick wall' (Image: Andrew/Trussell Trust) 6 View 6 Images Struggling single dad Andrew Anderson has been forced to live off leftover scraps to cover his bills (Image: Andrew/Trussell Trust)

‌



"That's why I really want to see him bring in what the Trussell Trust is campaigning for - the rate of Universal Credit being set at what things actually cost so that when people need a bit of help, they can actually afford things like food and toiletries, which he doesn't have the power to reduce the cost of".

Given his compromised immune system, Andrew anticipates spending the winter months constantly ill, noting that "Scotland is a cold place." But his biggest fear isn't his physical health - it's what impact it will have on his daughter. "I'm having to sit in here and hide all this for my little girl, but she's going to notice this year that her dad's ill," Andrew said. "She hates it when I'm ill. It's horrible. She's already lost her mum. She is scared that something will happen to me."

On Tuesday, Downing Street announced that the Government would remove VAT from domestic electricity bills from October 1, with the next price cap announcement in late August.

‌



Small businesses that qualify for the domestic energy VAT relief, charities, and residential care homes eligible for the reduced rate will also see their bills slashed. It's understood this new measure, estimated to cost £850 million in 2026-27, will be covered by savings from the widely criticised and now-scrapped digital ID programme. There are fears, however, that this won't be enough to offer relief to the poorest households.

Helen Barnard, Director of Policy and Research at the Trussell Trust, tells the Mirror: "The proposal to cut VAT on electricity bills is a welcome sign that the Prime Minister recognises the pressures families are facing. But it will do little for people on the very lowest incomes who are being forced to turn to food banks because they can't afford the essentials.

View 6 Images The Trussell Trust has now urged the UK Government to lift the freeze on Local Housing Allowance (Stock Photo) (Image: Getty Images)

‌



"In the last year alone, 2.6 million emergency food parcels were distributed to people facing hunger and severe hardship in the UK. That’s equivalent to a parcel every 12 seconds. This is an unacceptable reality.

"We need to see more targeted support for people at the sharpest end of the cost-of-living crisis. Right now, too many families are being forced to make impossible decisions between paying the bills and putting food on the table.

"That's why we need the UK Government to lift the freeze on Local Housing Allowance, so more people are protected from rising rent costs, and take steps towards an Essentials Guarantee. This would ensure the basic rate of Universal Credit at least covers the cost of essentials – like food and toiletries.”

Article continues below

Do you have a story to share? Email me at julia.banim@reachplc.com

News.title: Is Facebook down in UK? Meta sites including Instagram face outage LIVE
News.content:
Facebook users have reported issues with the Meta app on other social media channels - thousands of reports have been logged in the UK, US and Europe

Facebook appears to be down for some people as multiple users have reported issues with the Meta app.

A number of posts have appeared on other social media channels from concerned users who have reported being logged out of Facebook, including on the app version. Others added that they are also experiencing issues with Facebook's messaging app, Facebook Messenger. Issues ahve been reported across the world including in the US, UK and Europe.

According to Down Detector, the first reports of Facebook being down were made at around 12.35pm today, with these significantly growing in volume after 1pm. There are also reports on DownDetector of issues with Instagram, which also also owned by Meta.

News.title: Ex-Southern Water CEO charged over alleged manipulation of water quality tests
News.content:
Ex-Southern Water CEO charged over alleged manipulation of water quality tests

Matthew Wright, who was chief executive of Southern Water, has been accused alongside three others of conspiring to defraud the Environment Agency and water regulator Ofwat

View Image Matthew Wright, the former chief executive of Southern Water, has been charged (stock) (Image: PA)

The former chief executive of Southern Water has been charged with conspiracy to defraud authorities over allegations he was involved in a plan to manipulate water quality tests to avoid millions of pounds in penalties, it can now be reported.

‌



Matthew Wright has been accused alongside three others of conspiring to defraud the Environment Agency (EA) and water regulator Ofwat.

‌



The EA previously asked a judge to issue a summons against Wright, as well as Philip Barker, Clive Massey and Mark Gregory, who also worked at the company, charging them with the offence.

‌



The summons was issued last year, but Wright then launched a legal challenge over the move, with his lawyers telling the High Court in June that the EA did not have the power to issue it and that it should be thrown out as a “nullity”.

On Wednesday, two senior judges dismissed Wright’s claim, and ruled that restrictions previously preventing reporting of the legal challenge should be lifted.

Separate court listings show that the case against 60-year-old Wright, of Haslemere, Surrey, Barker, 57, of Chiltington, West Sussex, 64-year-old Massey, of Brandhill, Shropshire, and 63-year-old Gregory, of Southampton, were scheduled to be heard at Medway Magistrates’ Court on July 14.

‌



The four are accused of conspiring between 2012 and 2017 to “defraud persons performing public duties in respect of environmental and financial regulation” of Southern Water, including the EA and Ofwat, by “the implementation of artificial no-flow events at waste water treatment works”.

The court listings also show that Southern Water has separately been charged with dozens of offences of failing to comply with or contravening an environmental permit condition between 2013 and 2017 at multiple wastewater treatment works.

Three individuals have also been charged with failing to comply with or contravening an environmental permit condition.

‌



Terry Stephens, 67, of Waterlooville, Hampshire, is charged with one count, alleged to have taken place in 2015.

David James, 58, of Worthing, West Sussex, is also charged with one count, alleged to have taken place in 2016.

Mark Butler, 45, of Hassocks, West Sussex, is charged with eight counts, alleged to have taken place between 2015 and 2024.

‌



Wastewater treatment works can only be run with an environmental permit issued by the EA.

Treated effluent discharge from the works is tested under an “operator self-monitoring” (OSM) scheme introduced in 2009, which sees discharges tested annually in unannounced visits.

The tests are carried out by sampling teams, which operate separately from teams that run the works.

‌



The results of the tests are shared with the EA and water regulator Ofwat, and can lead to penalties if the works do not comply with the terms of their permits.

If the discharge flow at the time of the test is insufficient to take a sample, this is not regarded as a fail, and no samples are taken for the rest of the testing period.

Rules around OSM have been tightened in the past year, including that samples must be rescheduled in the event that the flow is insufficient, with the current Labour government pledging to end the practice.

‌



In his ruling issuing the summons against the four men last year, District Judge Stephen Leake said: “The agency alleges, in the present case, that there was a deliberate plan by officers of the company to manipulate the OSM regime by contriving operational circumstances so that there was no flow through the relevant site at times when it was believed that the site would, or might, fail the OSM test, in order to avoid the consequences of the true OSM result being provided to the agency and Ofwat.”

But lawyers for Wright told the High Court that the EA only has the power to bring private prosecutions for environmental offences, not those such as fraud or conspiracy.

Barristers for the EA said that the body had a general power to bring private prosecutions, and alternatively that allegations of conspiracy to defraud were connected to its functions.

‌



Massey, Gregory and Barker did not appear at the hearing in London and were not represented.

Lord Justice Popplewell, sitting with Mr Justice Hilliard, ruled on Wednesday that the EA only being able to prosecute environmental offences would “produce unreasonable and anomalous results”.

He continued that the law “enables the EA to prosecute for any offence of any nature in circumstances in which such a prosecution is capable of being calculated to facilitate, or conducive or incidental to, the carrying out of any of its functions”.

‌



In the 48-page judgment, the senior judge continued that the charge against Wright involves “very serious allegations of criminal misconduct”.

He said: “What is alleged … involves carefully planned and extensive fraud and dishonesty at a high level within the company and on a large scale, including, for example, arranging for wastewater to be removed from facilities by tankers in order to create no flow results, with a view to covering up pollution and deceiving those whose function is to protect the public from such harm.

“The EA says that by the company’s own assessment, it avoided penalties of the order of £45 million, and on the EA’s assessment the figure is higher.”

Article continues below

Following the judgment, an EA spokesperson said: “We can confirm that we are taking criminal proceedings against Southern Water Services Limited and a number of former employees.

“We take our responsibility to protect the environment very seriously and will always pursue and prosecute those alleged to have committed serious offending against the environment. We welcome this important judgment.”

News.title: 'Ukraine needs Patriot missiles now to protect itself from Putin onslaught'
News.content:
The Kremlin's ballistic missile attacks on Ukrainian cities are on the rise as desperate Russian President Vladimir Putin smells defeat in the air and demands death and destruction.

His deluded sense of power and leverage over Kyiv is slowly dissipating as wily Ukraine is exacting punishing revenge for his murderous campaign against its citizens.

Kyiv is dismantling Putin’s oil and gas export machine with well-planned drone and missile attacks on his energy installations with deep-strike missions inside Russia - and has now targeted the logistics hub of 'Russian Amazon' - the online retailer Wildberries.

But when the former KGB officer’s back is against the wall his only instinct is to escalate the violence and intimidation-hence the increased ballistic threat.

‌



On Sunday the Kremlin’s air force launched its biggest ballistic missile attack on Kyiv since the February 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine started, in a worrying escalation.

Among the onslaught Ukraine’s intelligence officers and air force defence experts quickly calculated there were 25 ballistic missiles and ten Zircon hypersonic missiles.

President Zelensky under intense pressure in Ukraine over popular defence chief's sacking READ MORE :

View 4 Images Ukraine has launched revenge attacks on Russia (Image: east2west news)

And because these weapons descend from a steep trajectory just outside the atmosphere, or near its limits depending on its size, they are extremely hard and expensive to intercept.

‌



Without US-made Patriot missiles, which cost around £3m each, they are unlikely to be intercepted and can pile violently into civilian household causing devastation.

And Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is desperate for NATO to speed up their distribution to Kyiv as a priority to defend against the growing threat.

The problem is that America only makes as many as 650 Patriots every year and it and the Gulf States, plus Israel pressurised stocks to defend against the Iranian missile threat.

And it is possible for Russian weapons manufacturers to make 1,000 ballistic missiles every year, with production schedules accelerating at impressive speed.

‌



Olha Polishchuk, eastern Europe research manager for war monitor Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, says: “More than 1,600 days into Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Sunday night’s attack was very likely the largest ballistic missile barrage on Kyiv since the beginning of the war."

View 4 Images Cars were destroyed in Kyiv after Russian missile attack (Image: Ukrinform/Shutterstock)

“Explosions lasted for five hours in Kyiv, leading to fires and damage to civilian infrastructure across the city. At least one person was killed, 20 were wounded.

As a capital city housing the central government, Kyiv is well protected by air defence. Ukraine has mastered drone interception and successfully intercepts almost all cruise missiles. Russia therefore requires a very large number of drones and cruise missiles to overwhelm air defences for an attack to land.

‌



The situation is different, however, when it comes to ballistic missiles, which are shot down with Patriot interceptor missiles that Ukraine currently lacks.

While Sunday’s attack has not been the deadliest or the biggest in terms of the total number of missiles and drones used, it signifies Russia’s increased reliance on ballistic and Zircon missiles to exploit Ukraine’s shortage of Patriot missiles.

View 4 Images Russian President Vladimir Putin 'can smell defeat in the air' (Image: ALEXANDER KAZAKOV/SPUTNIK/KREMLIN POOL/EPA/Shutterstock)

Importantly, as Russia deploys the increasingly high concentration of ballistic missiles at a time when Ukraine’s capacity to intercept them is under increasing pressure, it chooses to hit populous residential areas and cause terror, rather than focusing strictly on militarily significant targets.

‌



Unless Ukraine can secure a steady supply of Patriot missiles, Russia may use the same vulnerability to once again disable and destroy the remaining energy infrastructure that powers and heats Ukraine ahead of the next winter season."

News.title: Cardiologist warns 'never ignore' these five symptoms of high blood pressure
News.content:
Cardiologist warns 'never ignore' these five symptoms of high blood pressure

Heart expert Dr Francesco Lo Monaco says people should be aware of red flag signs like unexplained fatigue and breathlessness

View 3 Images Anyone with concerns or questions should speak to a GP (stock image) (Image: Getty)

A cardiologist has listed five symptoms people with high blood pressure should never ignore - even if they don't realise they have the 'silent killer' condition. He has also revealed the 'silent' everyday habits that could be quietly weakening your heart.

‌



Private cardiologist consultant Dr Francesco Lo Monaco says millions of people unknowingly put extra strain on their hearts every single day through seemingly harmless habits. From uncontrolled blood pressure and untreated sleep apnoea to carrying excess weight, drinking too much alcohol and spending long periods inactive, several common lifestyle factors can force the heart to work harder over time.

‌



In some people, that can eventually contribute to weakening of the heart - a condition known medically as cardiomyopathy. Dr Francesco Lo Monaco said an enlarged heart can also develop gradually and may not cause obvious symptoms until it has become more advanced.

‌



He said: “Many people assume they would know if something was wrong with their heart, but that’s often not the case. The changes can happen slowly over many years, particularly if risk factors such as high blood pressure aren’t well controlled.”

Silent condition many people don’t know they have

One of the biggest contributors is high blood pressure, which is often described as a 'silent killer'. “When blood pressure remains elevated for months or years, the heart has to pump against greater resistance,” Dr Lo Monaco explained.

View 3 Images High blood pressure can lead to serious problems like heart attacks or strokes (stock image)

‌



“Initially the heart muscle adapts by becoming thicker, but over time these changes can affect how efficiently the heart works. If left untreated, this can contribute to enlargement and weakening of the heart and eventually increase the risk of heart failure, abnormal heart rhythms and other cardiovascular complications.”

The health expert says this is one of the reasons high blood pressure is often described as a “silent killer”. Many people have no symptoms until damage has already begun.

The NHS says: "High blood pressure significantly increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes – often described as a ‘silent killer’ as there are usually no symptoms, which makes it hard to spot. It is estimated that around 4.1 million people in England are living with it without realising."

‌



Warning signs people shouldn’t ignore

Although many people have no symptoms, Dr Lo Monaco says anyone experiencing five warning signs should seek medical assessment as soon as possible. He says these include:

breathlessness swollen ankles chest pain palpitations unexplained fatigue

“The encouraging news is that many of these risk factors are modifiable,” he said. “Keeping your blood pressure under control, treating sleep apnoea, maintaining a healthy weight, exercising regularly and limiting alcohol can all reduce the strain placed on the heart over time.”

‌



View 3 Images There are certain warning signs people should watch out for, like palpitations (stock image)

Five everyday habits that put extra strain on your heart

Poorly controlled blood pressure

“The single biggest modifiable risk factor we see is high blood pressure,” Dr Lo Monaco said. “Many people feel perfectly well, so they don’t realise the damage can be happening silently.”

Untreated sleep apnoea

Repeated drops in oxygen overnight increase stress on the cardiovascular system. “Sleep apnoea doesn’t just cause tiredness,” he said. “It is strongly associated with high blood pressure, abnormal heart rhythms and structural changes within the heart.”

Article continues below

Excess alcohol

Heavy drinking over long periods can weaken the heart muscle. “Alcohol-related heart disease often develops gradually, so people may not notice any symptoms until significant damage has occurred.”

Obesity

Carrying excess weight increases the amount of work the heart has to perform every day. Dr Lo Monaco said: “The heart has to pump blood around a larger body, meaning it works harder continuously.”

Physical inactivity

Regular movement helps maintain cardiovascular health. “A sedentary lifestyle doesn’t directly enlarge or weaken the heart on its own, but it contributes to several of the major risk factors that do, including obesity and high blood pressure.”

News.title: Cockroach infestations boom across UK thanks to summer heatwaves as locations most at risk revealed
News.content:
Cockroach infestations boom across UK thanks to summer heatwaves as locations most at risk revealed

EXCLUSIVE: Cockroach numbers pose a 'direct risk to human health', pest control experts have said after a 'significant' infestation forced an indoor market in a major UK city to close

View 3 Images Cockroach infestations are on the rise across the country (file photo) (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

Summer heatwaves have unleashed a cockroach invasion in homes and businesses across Britain, experts have warned.

‌



The household pests are notoriously difficult to get rid of but usually tend to prefer warmer climates, proving a particular problem in parts of the Mediterranean. However, a series of mild winters and warm summers have helped boost numbers in the UK, recent figures show, with more of the insects now able to survive the colder months and re-emerge in the spring.

‌



In Sheffield, the indoor Moor Market recently reopened after being closed for more than two weeks to "protect public health" amid a major infestation of German cockroaches.

‌



View 3 Images The Moor Market in Sheffield city centre was recently forced to shut over a 'significant' infestation of German cockroaches (Image: Katy Blackwood/NurPhoto/Shutterstock)

B&M hit with huge fine as mouse infestation and droppings found in UK stores READ MORE :

Ebola hope as British scientists make major vaccine breakthrough READ MORE :

Traders were dealt a blow shortly before midnight on June 25 when bosses told them the building would be closing for the "foreseeable future", with the council attributing the problem to "extreme and sustained hot weather". The market opened its doors again on July 13 after an "extensive" treatment programme, which included insecticide spray, gel treatments and replacement of monitoring equipment.

Cardiff City Council meanwhile warned in May that they were seeing a rise in pest control call-outs to deal with cockroaches, recording a 9% increase between 2024 and 2025. And an Environmental Information Regulations (EIR) request to Hull City Council earlier this year showed that one area - Beverley and Newland - had 34 call-outs alone in 2025, up from just eight the year prior.

‌



The German cockroach is the most common variety found in the UK, usually turning up in kitchens and favouring sites behind appliances with warm motors, such as ovens or fridges. Oriental cockroaches, which are much darker in appearance with longer antennae, are sometimes seen around bins.

View 3 Images German cockroaches are the type most commonly found in Britain (Image: Getty Images)

The American cockroach and Brown-banded cockroach are also known to have breeding populations in this country, though are far less common. It is thought hotter summers and milder winters mean that cockroaches are no longer dying off seasonally, with the pests thriving in conditions between 25C and 35C.

‌



Increased overseas travel, changing consumer habits and more people living in high-density blocks of flats have also seen the pests gain a foothold in the UK. Natalie Bungay, Head of Technical at the British Pest Control Association, told the Mirror: "Cockroaches pose a direct health risk to humans. T

"hey are vectors of disease, known to carry the organisms which cause food poisoning in humans and many other bacteria, such as salmonella, staphylococcus and streptococcus. An increase in cockroach activity doesn’t usually come down to one single cause. We’re seeing a combination of pressures that can make infestations more likely to take hold and spread.

"Higher-density living is a big factor. Large cities tend to have more houses of multiple occupancy, blocks of flats and shared facilities, which give cockroaches plenty of opportunities to move between properties unnoticed. Once they get established in one flat, it’s much easier for them to spread through a building.

‌



"Travel also plays a role. Cockroaches are very good hitchhikers and can be brought back in luggage, food packaging or personal belongings after holidays, short breaks or work travel. This is something we see across the UK, particularly in busy urban areas with a high turnover of people.

"Cost-of-living pressures may also be contributing. People are more likely to buy second-hand items such as microwaves, fridges or small electrical goods, which can unknowingly harbour cockroaches and introduce them into a home. Similarly, bulk food purchases and increased food storage can create better conditions for pests if hygiene or storage isn’t quite right.

"It’s also worth saying that cockroaches are under-reported. Many infestations go on for months before a professional is called, which can make it look like there’s a sudden spike when the issue has actually been building for some time."

Article continues below

She added that anyone who suspects they may have a cockroach infestation should contact a BPCA-member professional pest control company, who have "access to a range of professional use insecticides which are not available to the public". Signs of cockroach infestation include, droppings, egg (ootheca) cases, shed skins, an obnoxious ‘sour’ odour and unexplained damage to food or packaging.

News.title: Student, 19, shouted for help for 20 minutes as he drowned after night out
News.content:
Student, 19, shouted for help for 20 minutes as he drowned after night out

Evan Geoffrey d'Andilly, 19, drowned in the River Ouse in York after a night out with friends in the city on March 5 last year

View 3 Images Evan Geoffrey d'Andilly died just four days before his 20th birthday (Image: Family Handout)

A student who drowned in a river stayed afloat for 20 minutes while shouting for help that did not arrive in time, an inquest has heard.

‌



Evan Geoffrey d'Andilly, 19, entered the River Ouse from the nearby Ouse Bridge in York following a night out with friends in the city on March 5 last year.

‌



North Yorkshire Coroner's Court was shown CCTV footage of Evan, from Scunthorpe, calling for help in the freezing water as a police officer on the bank reassured him that help was on the way. He could be seen moving his arms in the water as officers shone torches towards him.

‌



Tragically, Evan disappeared beneath the surface before a rescue boat reached the scene. Evan - who was studying business management at the University of York at the time of the incident - died just four days before his 20th birthday.

View 3 Images Evan Geoffrey d'Andilly was 'full of life', his family said (Image: Family Handout)

The inquest was told that Evan entered the water at around 3.03am and that police arrived within two to three minutes. An officer threw a life ring into the water to reach Evan, who was in the middle of the 41-metre-wide river, but was unsuccessful , the court heard.

‌



Evan’s mother, Lorraine d'Andilly, told a previous inquest hearing that the available riverside rescue equipment - 18-metre reach poles and 20-metre throw lines - was unsuitable and stood no chance of reaching him, meaning "Evan lost a substantial chance of survival".

Fire crews were notified at 3.09am, with appliances from Acomb and York fire stations arriving by 3.14am and 3.18am respectively, the court was told. However, the inquest heard that North Yorkshire Fire and Rescue Service's boat was stationed in Selby and did not arrive until 3.37am - 14 minutes after the last sighting of Evan.

In a statement read to the court, a fellow student and friend of Evan said they had been drinking in the city centre and walking together when all of a sudden "Evan had gone over the bridge", adding that there was "no indication" he was going to fall.

‌



The volunteer-run York Rescue Boat, moored at King’s Staith near where Evan was in the water, was the closest vessel capable of a water rescue and could reach locations quickly. However, Ms d’Andilly said the charity boat was not called immediately.

In police bodycam footage played in court, PC Grace Sylvester, who shouted advice to Evan as he tried to stay afloat, said: "It’s a city river. Why is it taking this long [for the rescue boat to arrive]?"

Asked by Ms d'Andilly if the rescue equipment was fit for purpose, PC Sylvester said: "On occasions it’s worked. On occasions it hasn’t worked."

‌



View 3 Images North Yorkshire Coroner's Court (file) (Image: Google Maps)

Sergeant Daniel Stubbs, who was the acting police inspector on the night of Evan’s death, told the court both York Rescue Boat and the fire service’s rescue boat had been requested to attend the scene. However, he said he was unaware that the fire service’s rescue boat was not based in York.

The inquest heard that North Yorkshire Fire and Rescue Service relies on York Rescue Boat for water rescues in York, as the fire service’s nearest rescue boats are based in Selby and Malton.

‌



Ms D’Andilly questioned why York Rescue Boat was not alerted immediately by the fire service when it was told about the incident, rather than after Evan had already been in the water for 10 minutes.

She said her son had "fought for another 10 minutes" to stay afloat. "He did everything he could to survive," Ms D’Andilly said, adding: "I will never understand how a safety protocol can be so flawed."

Ben Illsley, North Yorkshire Fire and Rescue Service’s director of operational support and assurance, told the inquest that there are "no plans" to move the fire service’s rescue boat from Selby to York in the next four years.

‌



He also said that if the rescue boat was moved to York, it would take one to two years for the fire service’s staff to be trained to use it.

Ms d'Andilly described her son as "kind" with a "gentle nature" and called his death "incredibly senseless" and a "tragedy". She said: "I still struggle to believe that Evan is gone from this world - that I will never see him again. It’s hard to believe that my little water baby died from drowning."

Evan’s father, Gordon d'Andilly, described his son as someone who was "full of life" and "got on with everyone really well".

Article continues below

A North Yorkshire Police spokesperson said: "The death of Evan d'Andilly is tragic and our thoughts remain with his family and friends. North Yorkshire Police will fully support the inquest, and we will await the conclusion before commenting further." The inquest continues.

The Mirror has launched the Save Lives For Sam water safety campaign to tackle the UK's growing drowning crisis. Backed by MPs, Olympic champions, national water safety organisations and bereaved families, the campaign is calling for urgent action to make our waters safer.

That includes compulsory water safety lessons in schools, a nationwide public awareness campaign, better lifesaving equipment at high-risk waterways, the introduction of Sam's Law, and a dedicated Minister for Water Safety. Find out more about the campaign and how you can support it here.

News.title: Burnham to review early prisoner release scheme after anger over potential freeing of PC Harper's killers
News.content:
Andy Burnham has said he will review an early prisoner release policy, due to come into force this autumn, following anger that two killers of PC Andrew Harper could be freed early.

From September, thousands of offenders in England and Wales will be eligible to be released earlier under the Sentencing Act. Tens of thousands of inmates have been let out of prison to create more space in jails since 2024.

Burnham said: "I can't say that I can change the policy completely, but I will look at it in detail before we go further forward."

He acknowledged that there was "pressure on prisons places" and that a failure to invest in the prison system in the past had created "an unacceptable situation".

His comments come after the mother of police officer Andrew Harper said the potential early release of two of her son's killers felt like an "insult".

Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers were sentenced to 13 years in custody for manslaughter but could be released early under the new Sentencing Act.

The overcrowding of the prison estate has been a problem for several years and successive government have released prisoners early in a bid to free up space.

The Sentencing Act, which was passed by Sir Keir Starmer's government earlier this year, was designed to ease pressure on prisons, and will see some offenders spend less time in prison before release.

Burnham said: "I want to assure myself that everything has been looked at before this policy proceeds, and I can give that assurance that every single part of this I will look into with the justice secretary."

Concerning the case of PC Harper, he said: "I feel for the family it's an appalling crime that was committed."

He said the "main perpetrator" of his death would not be eligible for early release.

News.title: Some food prices have fallen – but inflation expected to rise from here
News.content:
Food prices are rising at their slowest rate in nearly two years, as the cost of some staples such as margarine and sugar have gone down.

Supermarket price wars have helped drive down prices in the year to June, the industry says, as retailers work to tempt customers with summer deals.

Inflation in the UK overall has fallen to 2.6% in the year to June, down from 2.8% in the year to May, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), driven largely by lower fuel and food prices.

June's figure will be welcomed by new Prime Minister Andy Burnham and his government, but analysts warn the fall is temporary, as higher energy prices in July are expected to push inflation back up.

Lower fuel costs - particularly lower diesel prices - also pushed inflation down, with prices at the pump falling for the first time since the start of the war in the Middle East.

Clothing costs fell as well due to the summer sales, with many retailers offering larger discounts than last year.

News.title: Southampton boss Eckert charged by FA over Spygate
News.content:
Southampton head coach Tonda Eckert has been charged with misconduct by the Football Association for his role in the Spygate scandal.

Saints were kicked out of the Championship play-offs in May after admitting they spied on three clubs during the campaign.

An independent disciplinary commission ruled at the time that the espionage was authorised by Eckert and was a "contrived and determined plan from the top down".

Since then the club has been the subject of an investigation by the FA, looking into who participated in the spying and assessing the culpability of those who knew it was happening.

The FA said, external Eckert "has been charged with three breaches of FA rule E3.1 in relation to misconduct between December 2025 and May 2026".

Southampton beat Middlesbrough over two legs in the play-off semi-final but, after Saints' expulsion, Boro were reinstated to the final and went on to lose to Hull City.

The English Football League (EFL) expelled Southampton from the play-offs after they admitted watching training sessions involving Oxford United and Ipswich Town, in addition to filming Middlesbrough before the semi-final.

The EFL can only take action against its member clubs but the FA can punish individuals and hand out bans.

The FA said it is "alleged that the head coach acted in an improper manner and/or brought the game into disrepute by directing and/or authorising the observation of training sessions" of these games.

Eckert has until next Tuesday to respond.

In a statement, Southampton said, external they and Eckert "acknowledge today's charges from the FA relating to a breach of rule E3.1".

The club added: "Tonda and the club will continue to co-operate fully and openly with the FA.

"Our focus remains on preparations for the 2026-27 Championship season. The club remains fully supportive of Tonda and his staff as we work towards our ambition of returning to the Premier League.

"We are unable to comment further while the process remains ongoing, but we will provide an update to supporters as soon as we are in a position to do so."

News.title: OpenAI says its AI went rogue and launched 'unprecedented' cyber-attack
News.content:
Gina Neff, head of the Minderoo Centre for Technology and Democracy at the University of Cambridge, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that the security tests - called sandboxes - are "supposed to be secure environments where you can see what the models are capable of".

"In this case, it looks like OpenAI didn't make a secure enough sandbox," she added.

Instead, the agents created their own cyber-attack against the sandbox itself, finding a vulnerability which allowed them to escape.

Once outside, the AI identified Hugging Face as a likely source of the answers they were seeking in the test, and tried to gain access.

Neil Lawrence, Professor of machine learning at Cambridge University, called it an "impressive feat", but cautioned it "falls well within the known capabilities of the current generation" of high-powered AI models.

He pointed out that OpenAI is looking to list itself on the stock market, and faces intense pressure from rival firm Anthropic, which has made headlines with its own powerful AI tool, Mythos.

"OpenAI are now playing catch-up, they are trying to demonstrate their own systems' capabilities in cyber-security."

"It shows us that OpenAI are not capable of safely deploying their own technology," he added.

In its initial disclosure of the hack on 16 July, external, Hugging Face said it was still assessing whether any customer or partner data was affected and would contact affected parties if necessary.

It said it has now closed the vulnerabilities highlighted by the incident and rebuilt the affected systems.

"Autonomous, AI-driven offensive tooling is no longer theoretical," it said.

"Defending an online platform now means treating the data and model surface as a first-class attack surface, and using AI on defence to keep pace.

"We will keep investing there, and keep sharing what we learn."

News.title: Prince George poses in suit for new photo as he becomes a teenager
News.content:
A new photograph of Prince George has been issued by Kensington Palace to mark his 13th birthday.

The photo, showing George standing with his hands in his pockets and wearing an open-necked white shirt and dark suit, was published on social media with a message which read "Happy 13th birthday, George!" alongside a party popper emoji.

The picture was taken at Kensington Palace last month straight after the Trooping the Colour ceremony, by photographer Matt Porteous.

George, the elder son of the Prince and Princess of Wales, is second in line to the throne.

This year's birthday photo is more formal than last year's, which had a rural setting and showed the prince in a countryside-style gilet and wearing a friendship bracelet in Norfolk.

The more grown-up look comes as George, now a teenager, gets ready to start secondary school in September.

News.title: Nottingham attacks NHS trust faces manslaughter probe
News.content:
The NHS trust that treated Nottingham attacks killer Valdo Calocane is being investigated for corporate manslaughter.

Calocane, who had been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020 before he fatally attacked Barnaby Webber, Grace O'Malley-Kumar and Ian Coates in June 2023, was previously sectioned by Nottinghamshire Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust.

A statutory public inquiry, which finished hearing evidence in May, was told he had been discharged in 2022 because he failed to turn up for appointments and the team had "lost" him.

The families of Calocane's victims said the NHS trust had "catastrophically failed at every level" and welcomed the investigation.

Northumbria Police confirmed it was carrying out the investigation "on behalf of Nottinghamshire Police".

A spokesperson for the Northumbria force said: "We are in contact with the victims' families and survivors and are committed to supporting them throughout this process.

"It would not be appropriate for us to comment any further."

Nottinghamshire Police has been criticised over its history of interactions with Calocane and its handling of the response and investigation into the attacks.

News.title: Military kit still failing women, troops say
News.content:
Women in the armed forces say they are still being issued kit that does not fit properly, five years after a landmark report warned they were at "greater risk of harm" from ill-fitting uniform and equipment.

The 2021 Atherton report said the Ministry of Defence should urgently roll out safer, more appropriate kit for female service personnel by the end of 2022.

Despite improvements, women have been telling the BBC some kit is still poorly fitting, with body armour failing to account for breasts, and shortages of smaller sizes resulting in "competition" among troops.

The Ministry of Defence (MOD) said it ensured everyone had access to the "best equipment they need to protect themselves in combat".

"I never felt that I was neat, tidy, presentable, or in the uniform that I was meant to be in," explains veteran Rhian Brown, who left the service in 2024.

"I never really felt that it protected me or entirely fulfilled the purpose that it was meant to."

News.title: YouTube star MrBeast marries Thea Booysen
News.content:
YouTube star MrBeast has tied the knot with his fiancee Thea Booysen.

The pair married on Richard Branson's private Necker Island in the British Virgin Islands, according to US outlets.

The 28-year-old US content creator announced he had "found MrsBeast" in a joint Instagram post, external, which featured images of them posing in white on their big day.

MrBeast, real name Jimmy Donaldson, is the biggest YouTuber in the world with more than 500m subscribers.

Donaldson popped the question to Booysen on Christmas Day 2024 while they wore matching MrBeast-branded festive jumpers.

He previously told US outlet People magazine that despite being known for huge online stunts, he wanted a "really private and intimate" proposal and small wedding.

In photos shared by the couple, Booysen can be seen wearing a floor length lace wedding dress with a floral pattern, while Donaldson opted for a white tuxedo.

Booysen also had several outfit changes throughout the day, including a white mini dress with a sparkly bodice and feathered skirt for cutting the cake, and an off-the-shoulder satin look for later in the evening.

MrBeast described it as "the best day of my life" in the post.

News.title: More young women in their 20s are getting type 2 diabetes
News.content:
England is seeing a "worrying increase" in young women in their 20s developing type 2 diabetes, experts at Imperial College London have warned.

The rise has largely occurred since the Covid pandemic and is closely linked to increasing obesity levels, according to an analysis of NHS data from 2011 to 2024, external.

Type 2 diabetes is serious, and can lead to severe complications, such as heart attacks and strokes.

When it develops at a younger age, the disease tends to be more aggressive, raising the risk of devastating complications and cutting lives short, according to Diabetes UK.

News.title: UK humanitarian worker monitored for Ebola in London hospital
News.content:
A humanitarian worker in the Democratic Republic of Congo has been medically evacuated to the UK after a potential healthcareârelated exposure to Ebola.

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said the individual, who is a UK resident and has not been named, has no symptoms, and the move is purely precautionary.

The individual remains well but is being assessed and monitored at a London hospital, the statement from UKHSA said.

The hospital has not been named but the Royal Free in north London has a high level isolation unit and is the primary national centre for high consequence infectious diseases.

The incubation period of Ebola ranges from two to 21 days and the humanitarian worker will be required to isolate throughout.

The individual had been working with a humanitarian organisation supporting the Ebola outbreak response.

Ebola is a highly dangerous pathogen. Unlike flu or Covid, it is not airborne and spreads through direct contact with bodily fluids.

Symptoms come on suddenly and start like the flu or malaria, with fever, headache and tiredness. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.

Richard Pebody, director of epidemic and emerging infections at UKHSA, said: "The risk to the general public remains low.

"This individual has been transferred out of an abundance of caution, and we're pleased they remain well."

There are currently no confirmed cases of Ebola in the UK, the agency said.

News.title: Glasgow School of Art cannot afford to restore fire-hit Mackintosh building
News.content:
Glasgow School of Art says it cannot fully restore the city's iconic Mackintosh Building to its former state without additional financial support.

The art school previously insisted it was committed to a faithful reinstatement of the building, which was designed by Charles Rennie Mackintosh but wrecked by two fires in 2014 and 2018.

However it now says "financial clarity", provided by an insurance settlement regarding the 2018 blaze, has shown it "cannot take forward the faithful reinstatement on its own."

Instead it suggests the building has potential to be an anchor for a "creative and cultural production innovation district".

But this claim that has attracted scorn from figures in the art world.

News.title: 'My sister is not just another statistic'  - Jennie's Law is signed
News.content:
Jennifer Poole, a woman murdered by her former partner, will not be "another statistic" her brother has said after a new law in her name was signed off in the Republic of Ireland.

Jason Poole's sister was unaware her partner Gavin Murphy had a history of domestic violence when he murdered her in her Dublin home in 2021.

The Domestic Violence (Judgements) Register Bill 2026, external, known as Jennie's Law, was approved by the DÃ¡il (Irish parliament) and has now been signed off by Irish President Catherine Connolly.

It will result in those convicted of domestic violence against a partner being included on a public register.

News.title: 'We just need a bed': Baby with 'days to live' can't access lifesaving treatment
News.content:
The parents of a three-month-old boy who they fear has just days to live say they're frustrated at being unable to access lifesaving treatment due to a lack of suitable hospital beds.

Dylan and Catrin Green, from Cardiff, said their "completely healthy baby" Macs started to struggle with his feeding, then caught a cold before later suffering two cardiac arrests.

He has been diagnosed with dilated cardiomyopathy, external - a condition which can lead to heart failure - and now has a "matter of days" on a machine which pumps his heart for him, Dylan said.

He urgently needs a Berlin heart , external- a device used to take over the function of a child's own heart until a donor heart becomes available.

His family said Macs has been stuck at a specialist unit in Bristol for weeks, where his condition has since deteriorated and was now in an induced coma, as the beds he needs were not available.

The two specialist hospitals in the UK where the Berlin heart can be fitted are Great Ormond Street Hospital in London and the Freeman Hospital in Newcastle.

News.title: Parts of the UK move closer to drought
News.content:
Summer so far has been exceptionally hot and dry across much of the UK, with three widespread heatwaves and the longest run of dry days in central England since 1995. England, Wales and eastern Scotland have been the driest areas over recent weeks, and this follows a very dry spring in similar regions.

England has received only 3% of its long-term average July rainfall with the south and east of England seeing no rain at all. Wisley in Surrey has seen 33 consecutive dry days.

Rainfall so far this summer has been below average across the UK as a whole, but there has been large regional contrast.

Up to the middle of summer - 15 July - parts of eastern and north-eastern England had received just 26% of their total expected summer rainfall. Areas of northern and western Scotland had more than average for the first half of the summer, though.

In Wales, where just 5% of July rainfall has fallen, Natural Resources Wales has moved the worst affected regions in the north and south-east into "prolonged dry weather status", the first step in its drought plan.

Comparisons are being made with last summer, when drought was declared across much of England, Wales and eastern Scotland. It officially ended just four months ago.

This year, drought has not developed as quickly because heavy rainfall recharged our aquifers, rivers and reservoirs during a very wet autumn and winter.

However, the UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology says flash droughts, external with a sudden transition between wet and dry conditions are "likely to happen more often, and be more intense".

As the effects of human-induced climate change continue, the Met Office expects our summers to become hotter and drier, external in the future. In fact, by 2070, our summers could be up to 60% drier and 1-6C warmer compared to 1990.

News.title: Ann Widdecombe was hit on head 21 times with hammer, prosecutors say
News.content:
Ann Widdecombe was hit on the head with a hammer 21 times at her home as she ate lunch in an attack that was caught on camera, prosecutors have told Westminster Magistrates' Court.

Prosecutor Kashif Malik said the man charged with her murder, Joshua Kerry, arrived at her house on 8 July in a red Vauxhall Corsa and entered through the front door.

Kerry, who prosecutors say was in the property for two minutes and was wearing black gloves, then allegedly hit Widdecombe repeatedly with a hammer in her kitchen, tipped her from her chair and took her wallet before driving off.

The 28-year-old from South Yorkshire later also appeared at the Old Bailey and was remanded in custody.

At the Old Bailey hearing, prosecutor Alistair Richardson said the attack on Widdecombe had been carried out with a "ferocity of violence".

Malik told the court that Widdecombe did not attend a pre-arranged online interview with Channel 5's Matt Allwright show that had been scheduled for just before 13:00 BST on 8 July.

The show's production team tried to contact Widdecombe through her personal assistant, who then asked Widdecombe's gardener to check on her, the court heard.

Prosecutors said the gardener entered the house via the open front door on 9 July and found Widdecombe lying face down on her kitchen floor with a serious head injury.

News.title: Russian warship carried out firing exercise off Plymouth coast
News.content:
The live-fire exercise took place in international waters and lasted for 30 minutes.

The Russian warship requested that the Royal Navy's HMS Tyne reposition to a safer distance, which it did.

The Russian frigate was also being monitored by a French military aircraft which made radio contact with the warship asking it to clarify its intentions, the BBC has been told.

BBC Verify has analysed flight and ship-tracking data which shows the position of HMS Tyne and several British military aircraft operating in and around the Channel near Plymouth on Monday.

Flight data on ADS-B Exchange indicates at least four Royal Air Force and Royal Navy aircraft were flying off the coast of Dorset mostly above the UK's territorial waters, including two Eurofighter Typhoons, a Voyager air refuelling tanker and a Super Lynx helicopter.

A French military H160M GuÃ©pard helicopter also flew out and over the Channel during the afternoon. It is not clear if this is the aircraft which made contact with the Russian warship.

Data on ship-tracking service MarineTraffic shows HMS Tyne began to broadcast its location about 40 miles off Plymouth at 13:57 BST on Monday. It remained in that location for around two hours before departing at 15:56 to return to Plymouth.

HMS Tyne has been tracking Neustrashimy since at least 16 July when both vessels were also captured in the North Sea about 36 miles miles from the port of Felixstowe in Suffolk on a satellite image.

The incident will be a reminder for the new prime minister of increased Russian naval activity near UK waters in recent months.

Last month, Royal Marine Commandos boarded a Russian "shadow fleet" oil tanker in the English Channel in a six-hour operation which was the first of its kind by UK armed forces.

Also in June, a British couple in international waters in the English Channel came across a Russian warship - Admiral Grigorovich - 23 miles off the Isle of Wight.

The frigate fired warning shots as Jane and Alan Kelvey sailed their yacht on what Russia's defence ministry said had been a "dangerous approach". However, the couple said they had not been on a "collision course".

Russian warships regularly pass through international waters in the Channel, which are separate from UK and French territorial waters.

News.title: Iran strikes Jordanian city near Israel as US carries out another wave of strikes
News.content:

The United States on Wednesday carried out another wave of strikes on Iran, where air defenses opened fire over the capital, Tehran. Iran launched a missile attack on a Jordanian city on Israel’s doorstep, and alerts were issued in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia.

The 11th night of American airstrikes on Iran came as diplomatic efforts have shown little public sign of progress. Officials on both sides have dug in on their dispute over the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway for global energy that remains largely closed because of Iranian attacks.

Iran has avoided striking Israel since hostilities resumed last month, apparently hoping to keep it from reentering the war. But the missile and drone attack on Jordan’s city of Aqaba, within sight of Israel’s Eilat, raised concerns over a further widening of the conflict after an agreement to halt hostilities collapsed.

The closure of the strait, through which a fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas passed during peacetime, has jolted the world economy with effects far beyond the Middle East. A new threat by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen to target Saudi shipping in the Red Sea puts another trade chokepoint at risk.

Benchmark Brent crude oil rose to around $94 a barrel in trading, and gasoline prices are once again climbing ahead of U.S. midterm elections this fall.

Attacks shake Iran and Jordan

Jordan’s military said it intercepted four Iranian missiles over Aqaba, while two others fell in “uninhabited areas.” Plumes of smoke could be seen overhead in videos filmed by people in the nearby Israeli city of Eilat. Jordan said it also intercepted four Iranian drones.

Another missile alert sounded in Bahrain, and Saudi Arabia warned residents of the Persian Gulf city of Dammam to seek shelter. Saudi authorities later said the danger had passed, without elaborating.

The U.S. military said earlier Wednesday that it had completed an 11th night of strikes on Iran, with targets including aircraft hangars and drone storage sites.

Iran's state-run IRNA news agency reported explosions across several provinces. Iran's Health Ministry says U.S. strikes over the past 11 days have killed 53 people, including six women and three children, and wounded nearly 600 people.

Iran's paramilitary Revolutionary Guard insisted its retaliatory attacks would continue.

The war has lately been focused on the Strait of Hormuz

Before the latest strikes, Iranian Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni visited Pakistan, a key mediator in the conflict, seeking to revive diplomacy. But it was unclear what new arrangement might be reached to end the war, which lately has become a battle for control over the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran's Interior Ministry spokesman Ali Zeinivand said “diplomacy isn’t called off” and that messages were still being exchanged, without elaborating, according to IRNA.

At a regional summit in the Philippines, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio denounced Iran’s actions in the strait.

“If we create a precedent in the Middle East where a nation state can decide that they are going to control an international waterway, charge a toll and if you don’t pay them, blow up your ships, we have created a very dangerous precedent which will repeat itself in other parts of the world, including in this region,” he said.

In response to Iran’s attacks, the U.S. re-imposed a blockade on Iranian ports.

Trump signals US may attack underground nuclear site

Speaking from the Oval Office on Tuesday, U.S. President Donald Trump gave a dim view on possible talks, saying the U.S. had “no interest in meeting.”

He signaled that U.S. forces could soon target an under-construction Iranian nuclear site buried deep under a mountain.

The site, known as Pickaxe Mountain, lies on the south side of Iran’s Natanz nuclear enrichment site, which was bombed by the U.S. during the 12-day war between Iran and Israel in 2025. But Pickaxe Mountain has remained untouched as Iran continues to dig at the site.

Iran has always insisted its nuclear program is peaceful, while resuming the enrichment of uranium to near weapons-grade levels since Trump scrapped a 2015 nuclear deal during his first term. The U.S. and others believe Iran had a nuclear weapons program until 2003 and may reconstitute it in the future.

___

Associated Press writers Bassem Mroue in Beirut, and Michelle L. Price and Jim Gomez in Manila, Philippines, contributed to this report.

News.title: Andy Burnham to review prisoner early release scheme after backlash over PC Harper’s killers
News.content:

We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. Your support makes all the difference. Read more

Andy Burnham will review the government’s early release scheme following backlash over the potential early release of two of police officer Andrew Harper’s killers.

The prime minister said he wants to make sure “everything has been looked at” before the policy, introduced under Sir Keir Starmer, goes ahead as planned in September.

It comes after the mother of PC Harper – who was 28 years old when he sustained fatal injuries while responding to a quad bike theft in Berkshire in August 2019 – said it was an “insult” that two of her son’s killers could be eligible to be freed from prison early.

open image in gallery Andy Burnham has said he will review a number of Keir Starmer’s policies ( PA )

PC Harper died after getting caught in a strap attached to the back of a car and dragged down a country road as three teenage suspects fled the scene of the burglary. Henry Long, then aged 19, was sentenced to 16 years while Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, both 18 at the time, were handed 13 years in custody after trial for his manslaughter in 2020.

Earlier on Wednesday, transport secretary Heidi Alexander confirmed that Long, the driver of the car, would not be eligible for automatic release, but his two passengers could be eligible to get out halfway through their sentences.

Speaking to reporters in Bath, the prime minister said: “All I can say is I will review the whole of this policy. Nobody can deny the pressure on prison places.

“We did not invest in the prison estate when we should as a country, going back a decade or so ago, when it was clear that there was going to be pressure. That has created an unacceptable situation now.

“But I want to assure myself that everything has been looked at before this policy proceeds, and I can give that assurance that every single part of this I will look into with the justice secretary.

“I can’t say that I can’t change the policy completely, but I will look at it in detail before we go further forward.”

Under the new Sentencing Act, set to come into force in September, an estimated 6,000 criminals will be eligible to be released early on good behaviour to serve the rest of their sentence on licence in the community, including a major expansion of electronic tagging.

It comes after more than 43,000 offenders were automatically released after serving 40 per cent of their sentence in 2025 in order to prevent the “collapse of a justice system” as prisons ran out of cells.

open image in gallery Pc Andrew Harper with his wife, Lissie ( Thames Valley Police )

But the prime minister’s spokesperson on Tuesday indicated that a number of key policies introduced by Sir Keir Starmer would be under review, including the prisoner early release scheme, the plan to scrap some jury trials and the deal to hand sovereignty of the Chagos Islands over to Mauritius.

“The prime minister has been in the door of No 10 just over 24 hours and he’s still making appointments to his government so we will update on policy areas in due course", his spokesperson said.

The Ministry of Justice has confirmed Cole and Bowers might be eligible to be released from prison halfway through their sentences.

Referring to concerns from the family of PC Harper about their early release, the new prime minister said: “I feel for the family, it’s an appalling crime that was committed. The main perpetrator will not be subject to any early release. Of course, others involved have potentially been identified.

“But I’ve spoken to the new justice secretary. He will review the policy together and make further statements in due course.”

open image in gallery Alex Norris has been appointed justice secretary in Andy Burnham’s Cabinet ( Getty )

Prison overcrowding has forced successive governments into making emergency releases, with the Conservative administration’s End of Custody Supervised Licence scheme, launched in 2023, releasing over 10,000 inmates between 18 and 70 days early.

This was followed by Labour’s SDS40 scheme, which has seen 56,323 offenders released after serving 40 per cent of their prison term between September 2024 and December 2025.

Reforms in the Sentencing Act came after prisons came within months of running out of space entirely last year, risking the “total breakdown of law and order” which would leave police unable to make arrests and courts unable to send offenders to custody, then justice secretary Shabana Mahmood said.

It is based a package of measures set out in David Gauke’s Independent Sentencing Review, which urged the government to take “decisive action” to ensure they are never forced to rely on the emergency release of prisoners again.

Under the new legislation, those on standard determinate sentences will only serve a third of their term in custody if they behave in prison. They would serve another third under supervision in the community and the last third on licence, facing recall if they reoffend.

Serious offenders jailed for four years or more, including some sex offenders, could be released into supervision at the half-way point.

However, under an earned progression model, inmates who break prison rules could be given extra days in custody.

The measures were broadly welcomed by prison reform experts, who say average sentence lengths have roughly doubled over the past 50 years. However there have been calls to ensure overstretched probation services are resourced to deal with the surge in offenders in the community.

open image in gallery Reforms in the Sentencing Act are based on recommendations from former Conservative justice secretary David Gauke ( PA Archive )

Earlier on Wednesday, defence secretary Wes Streeting was forced to apologise after he was caught on camera joking about the scheme.

In a video, published by the news website Guido Fawkes, new justice secretary Alex Norris can be seen walking towards Mr Streeting and Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood.

Mr Streeting can then be heard calling Mr Norris "the enemy now", adding: "He wants to let them all out”.

He later apologised, saying: "I hope everyone can see there was no ill intent behind this ribbing of the new justice secretary - it was a reference to an old May/Clarke joke.

"But I appreciate these are very serious issues and am sorry for any offence inadvertently caused by this moment of levity."

Asked if it was acceptable for members of his Cabinet to joke about early release, Mr Burnham said: “No, it’s not, and certainly that’s been acknowledged, and apologies have been made.”

A French modelling scout linked to sex offender Jeffrey Epstein has been found dead in his home on Wednesday, prosecutors said.

Daniel Siad, 69, was being investigated on allegations of supporting Epstein to traffic women but he had not been questioned before he was found dead in Colombe, a north-west suburb of Paris.

“An investigation to determine the cause of death was opened on Monday evening following the discovery,” prosecutors told the BBC. They added that an autopsy would be carried out

Siad was mentioned in over 1,000 documents in the latest tranche of documents released earlier this year.

He had denied the allegations and accused Epstein of taking “advantage of his trust”.

open image in gallery Daniel Siad has been found dead at his home near Paris ( US Department of Justice )

A close associate of Epstein he had sent photos, profiles, and travel updates of young women to Epstein, facilitating introductions under the guise of “model casting”.

Both Epstein and Siad were active in central Barcelona from 2017 onwards, with Siad stating that the city made a good base for recruitment, “much safer than Paris”, owing to the decriminalisation of sex work, the large influx of tourists and relative anonymity.

Interviewed by CNN on his connection to the disgraced financier, Siad said: “My work with him has been strictly professional.”

He claimed: “I never hard anything from anyone introduced who came back to me that they had a bad situation with him.”

Siad expressed regret over ever meeting Epstein and said the experience since had been “like a nightmare”. “I can’t believe that this person had another [side].” However, he was pushed on this as his connection with Epstein continued after the billionaire was convicted of child sex offences in 2008.

“He was such a powerful person, how can I not trust him?” he said.

open image in gallery An email sent by Siad to Epstein in the latest tranche of the Epstein files ( DOJ )

In another interview with French TV, he said: “I never introduced an underage model to him, or a model who was abused, so I have nothing to reproach myself for”.

Swedish model Ebba Karlsson recognised the model scout in pictures in the Epstein files and accused Siad of raping her in the 1990s before filing a complaint with the Paris prosecutor. In his CNN interview, Siad said: “I don’t remember at all this person. I would be very happy to confront her in the court.”

Records show Epstein paid thousands to Siad, according to the outlet. In one of the emails, Siad sent a picture of a person and Epstein replied: “too old”.

In 2022, fashion agent Jean-Luc Brunel was found dead in Paris after being accused of aiding Epstein. He was accused by Virgina Giuffre of grooming girls and sex trafficking.

He was arrested in 2020 and was charged with sexual harassment and the rape of minors. He died by suicide in February 2022 before the trial could commence.

Epstein himself died by suicide in his prison cell in New York in 2019 while awaiting trial for allegedly recruiting dozens of teen girls to engage in sexual acts with him and his friends. He was facing up to 45 years in prison if he was convicted.

The Justice Department released millions of files under the Epstein Files Transparency Act, including thousands of emails, court documents, photos and videos, many of which include images or references to high-profile figures, including the president, at the end of January earlier this year.
