It operates XP Platform, an open product platform that provides clients to access investment products in the market comprising brokerage securities, fixed income securities, mutual, hedge, and private equity funds; derivatives and synthetic instruments; credit cards; loan operations/collateralized credit…

The rivals XP must unseat

Brazil’s acquiring market is crowded with heavyweights. Stone and PagBank are strong in digital onboarding and serve millions of small businesses.

Cielo remains a legacy giant with deep ties to large retailers, while Rede is the acquiring arm linked to big-bank distribution networks.

XP’s advantage is different. It has no branch network, but it does have 4 million clients and R$1.5 trillion (US$295.9 billion) in assets on its platform.

For a business owner already investing through XP, adding a card machine from the same provider is a natural step—one that keeps more of their financial life inside XP’s ecosystem.

The competitive dynamic matters for investors because acquiring is a scale game with thin margins. Incumbents have spent years building merchant relationships and fine-tuning their technology, so XP will need to prove its integrated model can win on both price and user experience.

Unlike traditional banks that rely on physical branches, XP grew by offering a digital-first investment platform that appealed to Brazilians tired of high fees. That same playbook—lower costs, better technology, and a unified app—is now being aimed at the payments industry.

Why XP is pushing into payments now

The brokerage’s 2025 results show a company actively diversifying away from pure brokerage fees. Total client assets crossed the R$1 trillion (about US$197 billion) mark, and the firm has been explicit about growing through complementary retail products.

Cards, credit, and payments are no longer side bets—they are core growth engines.

A NeoFeed report noted XP is pushing on three fronts: stealing market share from incumbents, adding banking products like credit and cards, and expanding wholesale banking. The card-machine launch fits squarely into the second front, turning a vast investment client base into a payments and banking franchise for small businesses.

This diversification reflects a broader trend in Brazilian finance, where digital platforms are blurring the lines between brokerages, banks, and payment processors. For XP, the timing is logical: it has already built trust with millions of clients, and adding merchant services deepens those relationships while generating recurring transaction revenue.

Foreign investors who have watched XP’s stock should see the card-machine push as a signal that management is serious about becoming a full-service financial platform. The move also positions XP to capture a slice of Brazil’s enormous small-business payments flow, a market that touches nearly every corner of the economy.

What this means for expats and foreign investors

For expatriates living in Brazil, XP’s expansion could simplify financial management. A single provider handling investments, banking, and merchant payments means fewer accounts to monitor and potentially lower overall fees, especially for those running small businesses or side ventures.

Foreign portfolio investors should note that XP’s push into acquiring diversifies its revenue beyond market-sensitive brokerage fees. Payments income tends to be steadier and linked to consumer spending, which can provide a buffer during periods of stock-market volatility.

The move also highlights a wider opportunity in Latin American fintech: the bundling of financial services onto a single digital platform. As XP challenges incumbents, competition could drive down merchant fees and speed up settlement times, benefiting businesses and consumers alike.

Anyone considering opening a business in Brazil should watch how this battle unfolds. The choice of card-machine provider affects daily cash flow, and a new entrant with XP’s scale could shift the balance of pricing and service quality in the acquiring market.

What happens next

XP has not yet released a detailed public spec sheet for the new merchant terminal or acquiring contract, so pricing and feature comparisons with incumbents remain unclear. The company’s next quarterly results will likely offer the first hard data on how many merchants have adopted the new solution.

The success of this initiative will depend on execution. XP must convince small-business owners that its integrated platform is simpler and more cost-effective than sticking with established acquirers, while also ensuring its technology can handle the high-volume, low-latency demands of payment processing.

Regulatory scrutiny is another factor to monitor. Brazil’s central bank has actively promoted competition in payments through initiatives like PIX, the instant-payment system, and it generally welcomes new entrants that challenge incumbents.

Still, any misstep in settlement or fraud prevention could draw unwanted attention.

For now, the message is clear: XP is no longer just a brokerage. It is building a financial ecosystem that aims to capture every transaction in a client’s life, from the investment portfolio to the morning coffee purchase.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is card acquiring?

Card acquiring is the service that processes card payments for merchants, handling authorization, security, and settlement so funds reach the merchant’s account. In Brazil, acquirers also provide the physical card machines and often offer additional services like sales analytics and working-capital loans.

Who are XP’s main competitors in card machines?

XP is challenging Stone, Cielo, PagBank, and Rede, the dominant acquirers in Brazil’s merchant payments market. Each has a distinct strength: Stone and PagBank excel in digital onboarding for small businesses, Cielo has deep ties to large retailers, and Rede benefits from big-bank distribution networks.

Why is a brokerage entering the payments business?

XP is diversifying its revenue beyond brokerage fees by cross-selling banking, credit, and payments products to its 4 million existing clients, especially small and medium businesses. The strategy aims to deepen client relationships, capture recurring transaction income, and reduce reliance on market-sensitive brokerage revenue.

World.title: The Strokes to Play First-Ever Ecuador Show in Quito
World.content:
Ecuador · Culture

Key Facts —Band. The Strokes, the Grammy-winning indie rock band from New York City. —Date. November 24, 2026, at Quito’s Estadio Olímpico Atahualpa. —First time. This marks the band’s debut concert in Ecuador. —Support. Baltimore synth-pop group Future Islands will open the show. —Tickets. General sale starts July 28, 2026, with prices from US$ 45 to US$ 179.

The Strokes will make their long-awaited debut in Ecuador on November 24, 2026, bringing their world tour to Quito’s Estadio Olímpico Atahualpa. The concert marks a rare moment for the country, landing one of indie rock’s most influential acts as a headline stop rather than an afterthought.

Who Are The Strokes

Formed in New York City in 1998, The Strokes reshaped rock music at the turn of the millennium with their razor-sharp guitar lines and effortless cool. Their 2001 debut, “Is This It,” is widely considered one of the greatest albums of the 21st century.

The band—Julian Casablancas, Nick Valensi, Albert Hammond Jr., Nikolai Fraiture, and Fabrizio Moretti—has won a Grammy and headlined festivals worldwide. For Ecuadorian fans who have waited decades, this show is a landmark cultural event.

The Quito Concert: Date, Venue, and Support

The show takes place on November 24 at the Estadio Olímpico Atahualpa, Quito’s largest multi-purpose venue with a capacity exceeding 35,000 people. The stadium sits in the heart of the capital and has hosted everything from World Cup qualifiers to major concerts.

Baltimore’s Future Islands, known for their emotive synth-pop and frontman Samuel T. Herring’s unforgettable stage presence, will open the evening.

Their inclusion adds a rich layer to a bill that bridges guitar-driven anthems and electronic heart.

Why a Quito Stop Matters for Ecuador

Major international tours often skip Ecuador, favoring larger markets like Brazil, Argentina, or Colombia. Landing a direct, headlining date from The Strokes signals a shift in how global promoters view the country.

This booking builds confidence among regional promoters and venues. It proves Ecuador can sustain high-demand, top-tier events, which could unlock more visits from arena-level acts in the coming years.

Tickets and the South American Tour

A presale runs from July 24 to July 27 for Banco Guayaquil cardholders and PeiGo users via the Feel The Tickets platform. General sales open on July 28 at 10:00 AM, with face values ranging from US$ 45 to US$ 179 before taxes and service charges.

The Quito date sits inside a robust South American leg. The Strokes will also perform in Lima on November 20, Santiago on November 27, Buenos Aires on November 29, Bogotá on December 2, and São Paulo on December 5.

What This Means for Expats and Investors

For the growing expat community in Ecuador, a concert of this caliber adds to the country’s quality-of-life appeal, blending rich local culture with global entertainment. It signals that life in Quito can include the same world-class events found in larger Latin American capitals.

Investors in Ecuador’s tourism and hospitality sectors may see this as a bellwether. A successful, sold-out show could encourage further investment in entertainment infrastructure, hotels, and services that cater to high-spending international visitors.

A Look at Ecuador’s Growing Live Music Scene

Ecuador has long nurtured vibrant local music scenes, from Andean folk to Quito’s indie rock underground, but it has historically been overlooked by the biggest global touring circuits. The country’s geography and smaller market size often meant fans had to travel to Bogotá or Lima for stadium-level international shows.

In recent years, however, Quito and Guayaquil have slowly begun attracting more prominent names, laying the groundwork for a moment like this. The Strokes’ decision to include Ecuador as a primary tour stop reflects years of growing local demand and improved production capabilities.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is this really The Strokes’ first concert in Ecuador?

Yes — despite a career spanning more than two decades, the band has never performed in Ecuador. The November 24 show at Estadio Olímpico Atahualpa is their official debut, a historic night for local rock fans.

How can I buy tickets for The Strokes in Quito?

General ticket sales begin July 28, 2026, at 10:00 AM through the Feel The Tickets platform. A presale for Banco Guayaquil cardholders and PeiGo users runs from July 24 to July 27, offering early access before the public on-sale date.

What other South American cities are on the tour?

The tour includes Lima, Santiago, Buenos Aires, Bogotá, and São Paulo. Mexico City also appears on the broader Latin American schedule, making this one of the band’s most extensive regional runs in years and giving fans across the continent multiple chances to see them live.

World.title: Hay Festival Querétaro Faces 64% Municipal Cut
World.content:
Mexico · Culture

Key Facts —Municipal reduction. Querétaro cut its Hay Festival contribution from 11.18 million pesos (about US$643,000) (US$604,000) to 4 million pesos (about US$230,000) (US$216,000). —Percentage drop. The 7.18-million-peso cut represents a 64.22% reduction in municipal support. —Total public funds lost. Combined public support fell from 13 million pesos (US$702,000) to 4.6 million pesos (US$248,000). —Federal offset. The festival obtained 600,000 pesos (about US$34,500) (US$32,400) from the Profest 2026 federal program. —2026 dates. The Querétaro edition runs from 4 to 6 September 2026.

The Hay Festival in Querétaro, the Mexican edition of the globe-trotting literary gathering born in Wales, is proceeding with its 2026 program after its host municipality slashed direct funding by 64.22 percent.

What the Hay Festival brings to Querétaro

The Hay Festival is an international cultural and literary organization that began in Hay-on-Wye, Wales, in 1987. It now runs festivals and cultural projects in Colombia, Peru, Spain, the United States, and Mexico.

The Querétaro edition brings together writers, thinkers, and artists for public conversations in the historic center of the colonial city, drawing an international audience of expats, tourists, and Mexican readers alike.

For a foreign visitor or resident, the festival transforms Querétaro’s UNESCO-listed streets into a walkable hub of ideas, with talks often held in English and Spanish. It has become a signature event that puts the city on the global cultural map alongside better-known destinations like Cartagena and Arequipa, where the festival also has a strong presence.

Beyond the main stage, the gathering typically includes workshops, book signings, and youth programs that ripple out into local schools and cafes. This blend of high-profile international authors and accessible community events has made it a rare point of connection between Mexico’s literary scene and the wider world.

The numbers behind the cut

Querétaro’s municipal government reduced its contribution from 11,180,000 pesos (US$604,000) to 4,000,000 pesos (US$216,000). That 7,180,000-peso (US$388,000) drop is a 64.22 percent reduction, according to reporting by Milenio.

Combined public support from municipal and other government sources fell from roughly 13,000,000 pesos (US$702,000) to 4,600,000 pesos (about US$34,500) (US$248,000), a total decline of 8,400,000 pesos (US$454,000) or 64.61 percent.

To put these figures in perspective, the original municipal contribution of 11.18 million pesos (about US$643,000) represented a significant bet on soft power and cultural tourism for a mid-sized Mexican city. The new figure of 4 million pesos (about US$230,000) is closer to what a single large corporate sponsor might contribute, leaving a gap that cannot easily be filled by ticket sales alone.

The combined public-funding drop of 8.4 million pesos (about US$483,000) (about US$230,000) means the festival’s operating budget for 2026 will likely be leaner, potentially affecting the number of invited authors, the scale of free public programming, or the marketing reach that draws international attendees.

The municipality’s reasoning

City officials said they are prioritizing infrastructure and cultural spaces that leave a permanent mark on the community. The budget was distributed “parejo” — evenly — across projects, they argued, and must build lasting cultural infrastructure.

Funds are being directed to the renovation of the Teatro Hércules, the Teatro en la Ciudad, and several cultural centers. The municipality framed the shift as a long-term investment in brick-and-mortar venues rather than a transient festival.

The Teatro Hércules, a historic venue in the city center, and the Teatro en la Ciudad are both well-known to locals but have long needed upgrades to host modern productions. For city planners, fixing roofs, improving acoustics, and updating seating creates a year-round asset that can serve school plays, concerts, and conferences long after the festival crowds have gone home.

This tension between funding ephemeral events and building permanent infrastructure is not unique to Querétaro. Municipalities across Latin America often face the same dilemma, especially when budgets tighten and officials must show voters tangible, lasting results from public spending.

How the Hay Festival is responding

The festival moved to seek federal support through Profest 2026, a Mexican government program that backs professional arts festivals. It secured 600,000 pesos (about US$34,500) (US$32,400) from the program to partially offset the municipal cut.

Organizers have not issued a direct public rebuttal beyond that financing response. The 2026 edition remains scheduled for 4 to 6 September 2026 in the city of Querétaro, a UNESCO World Heritage site in central Mexico.

Profest is a competitive federal fund administered by the Ministry of Culture, designed to strengthen Mexico’s festival ecosystem. The 600,000 pesos (about US$34,500) awarded is a modest sum compared to the 7.18-million-peso (about US$413,000) hole, suggesting the festival will need to lean more heavily on private sponsors, ticket revenue, and perhaps international grants to maintain its usual caliber.

By quietly securing federal money and confirming the dates, the festival signals resilience rather than retreat. For the international literary community that follows the Hay Festival circuit, the message is clear: the show will go on, even if the stage feels a little smaller.

What it means for expats, investors, and cultural tourists

For the expat community and foreign investors who call Querétaro home, the funding cut is a signal that the city is rethinking how it spends its cultural budget. A leaner festival could mean fewer English-language sessions or a reduced international lineup, which might affect the event’s draw for non-Spanish-speaking attendees.

Cultural tourists who plan trips around events like the Hay Festival should monitor the program announcements closely. A scaled-back edition may still offer rich conversations, but the intimate, high-wattage encounters that defined past years could be harder to stage without full municipal backing.

On the investment side, the redirection of funds toward permanent venues like the Teatro Hércules could eventually benefit the city’s cultural infrastructure, making Querétaro a more attractive long-term destination for arts-related businesses and real estate. However, the immediate loss of a marquee international event’s full luster may dampen the city’s short-term appeal as a cultural hub.

Ultimately, the situation highlights a broader question facing many Latin American cities: how to balance the glamour of global events with the grind of fixing local infrastructure. For now, Querétaro has chosen bricks over books, and the Hay Festival must adapt.

What happens next for the Hay Festival in Mexico

With the 2026 dates locked in, attention now turns to the program announcement and whether the festival can attract enough private sponsorship to close the funding gap. The federal Profest grant is helpful but not a long-term solution, as such programs are subject to annual budget cycles and political shifts.

If the municipality’s infrastructure bet pays off, the renovated theaters could one day host festival events, creating a symbiotic relationship between the permanent spaces and the temporary gathering. In the meantime, the festival’s ability to deliver a world-class experience on a tighter budget will be closely watched by other host cities across Latin America.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Hay Festival?

The Hay Festival is an international literary and cultural organization founded in Hay-on-Wye, Wales, in 1987. It stages public conversations with writers and thinkers in several countries, including Mexico, Colombia, and Peru, and has grown into one of the world’s most respected platforms for the exchange of ideas.

How much did Querétaro cut from the Hay Festival?

The municipality cut its contribution by 7,180,000 pesos (US$388,000), from 11,180,000 pesos (US$604,000) to 4,000,000 pesos (US$216,000), a reduction of 64.22 percent. Combined public support fell by 8,400,000 pesos (US$454,000) or 64.61 percent.

Will the Hay Festival Querétaro 2026 still happen?

Yes — the festival is set for 4 to 6 September 2026 and has secured 600,000 pesos (US$32,400) in federal Profest funding to help offset the municipal cut. Organizers are expected to announce the program in the months before the event.

World.title: Nutresa Buys Venezuela’s Tío Rico Ice Cream for US$30M
World.content:
Colombia · Business

Key Facts —Buyer. Grupo Nutresa, the Colombian food conglomerate controlled by the Gilinski family and IHC. —Target. Industrias Tío Rico C.A., Venezuela’s leading ice-cream company with over seven decades of history. —Price. Around US$30 million, according to a Bloomberg source familiar with the terms. —Assets. A 210,000 m² plant in Guacara, five distribution centers, and a portfolio of eight brands. —Market share. Tío Rico holds more than 55% of Venezuela’s ice-cream market.

Nutresa, Colombia’s largest processed-food company, announced on July 21, 2026, that it had agreed to buy 100% of Industrias Tío Rico C.A., the iconic Venezuelan ice-cream maker, for around US$30 million.

Two Companies, One Sweet Deal

Grupo Nutresa is a Colombian powerhouse with leading brands in cold cuts, biscuits, chocolates, coffee, pasta, and ice cream. Controlled by banker Jaime Gilinski and the Abu Dhabi-based International Holding Company (IHC), it has been pushing aggressively into international markets.

Tío Rico is a household name in Venezuela. Founded in Caracas in 1952 as Helados Club, it was later owned by Grupo Cisneros and then Unilever before landing with Mack de Venezuela C.A., the seller in this deal.

What Nutresa Gets

The transaction hands Nutresa a 210,000-square-meter industrial complex in Guacara, Carabobo state, along with five distribution centers that give it nationwide reach. The deal also includes the full brand portfolio: Tío Rico, Bati Bati, Crema Real, Chocolito, Merengada, Rico Gol, Chocomalta, and Tío Rico Trisabor.

Those brands command more than 55% of Venezuela’s ice-cream market. That kind of dominance is rare in any consumer category and gives Nutresa an immediate leadership position.

Why Venezuela, and Why Now

Nutresa had already flagged Venezuela and the United States as its two priority growth markets for 2026. The company described the acquisition as a continuation of its expansion strategy in Venezuela, where a gradual economic reopening has drawn fresh interest from regional players.

The Guacara plant is not just for Venezuelan sales. According to Colombian magazine Semana, Nutresa envisions the facility as an export platform serving Colombia, the Caribbean, and the United States.

The Gilinski Factor Behind Nutresa’s Move

Jaime Gilinski, the Colombian financier who now controls Nutresa alongside IHC, is the driving force behind the company’s Venezuelan push. Bloomberg identified him as the architect of the Tío Rico acquisition.

Under Gilinski’s leadership, Nutresa has accelerated deal-making across the region. The Tío Rico purchase fits a pattern of buying established local brands that already own deep consumer trust.

A Brand With Deep Venezuelan Roots

Tío Rico’s story began in 1952 when it was founded in Caracas under the name Helados Club. It became a cultural staple, surviving decades of economic ups and downs while remaining a fixture in corner shops and supermarkets nationwide.

The brand changed hands several times before this deal. It was acquired by the powerful Venezuelan media and business group Grupo Cisneros in 1978 and rebranded as Tío Rico, then sold to Anglo-Dutch consumer giant Unilever in 1994.

What It Means for Expats and Investors

For foreign readers watching Latin America, this deal is a concrete signal that large, sophisticated companies are willing to commit real capital to Venezuela’s consumer sector again. It suggests a calculated bet that demand for everyday treats like ice cream will keep growing as the economy stabilizes.

The acquisition also highlights a broader trend of Colombian multinationals expanding across borders. For investors, it reinforces that regional champions like Nutresa are using their balance sheets to snap up dominant local brands at prices that may look attractive compared to building from scratch.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who owned Tío Rico before Nutresa?

The seller was Mack de Venezuela C.A. Before that, the brand passed through the hands of Grupo Cisneros and Unilever over its seven-decade history.

What does the deal mean for Venezuela’s consumer market?

It signals that large regional players see enough stability and demand to invest real money in Venezuelan consumer brands, betting on a recovery. The move may encourage other multinationals to re-evaluate opportunities in the country.

Will Tío Rico products change?

Nutresa has not announced any immediate changes to recipes or branding. The company typically preserves local brand identities that already enjoy strong loyalty, so consumers can expect the same ice cream they have known for decades.

World.title: Grupo Bimbo Bets US$101 Million on New Puebla Plant
World.content:
Mexico · Business

Key Facts —Total Mexico investment. Grupo Bimbo will invest US$2 billion in Mexico between 2025 and 2028. —Puebla plant cost. The new Puebla facility requires an investment of more than MX$1,760 million (US$101.2 million). —Plant modernization. More than 30 existing plants across Mexico will be modernized under the plan. —Job creation. The national program will generate 2,000 direct jobs and over 1,800 indirect positions. —Fleet upgrade. The company will expand its low-emissions vehicle fleet as part of the investment cycle.

Grupo Bimbo, the Mexican multinational that ranks as the world’s largest bakery company, is building a second plant in the central state of Puebla with an investment of more than MX$1,760 million (US$101.2 million). The project anchors a far larger capital expenditure cycle that signals robust confidence in Mexican household consumption.

A US$2 Billion Bet on Mexico

The Puebla facility is just one piece of a national expansion plan valued at US$2 billion, running from 2025 through 2028. Grupo Bimbo will modernize more than 30 plants, expand its low-emissions delivery fleet, and create 2,000 direct jobs plus over 1,800 indirect positions.

For a company that operates in 34 countries across the Americas, Europe, Asia, and Africa, the decision to concentrate this much fresh capital in its home market is a deliberate signal. It tells investors and competitors that Mexican demand for packaged bread, snacks, and tortillas still has room to grow.

The scale of the commitment places Grupo Bimbo among the most aggressive consumer-goods investors in Latin America right now. While many multinationals spread capital thinly across regions, this plan doubles down on a single country, betting that proximity to consumers and deep distribution networks will yield better returns than chasing riskier frontier markets.

What Grupo Bimbo Is Building in Puebla

Puebla, an industrial hub east of Mexico City with strong highway and rail links, is already home to one Grupo Bimbo plant. The new facility doubles the company’s manufacturing footprint in a state that serves as a logistics gateway to southern and southeastern Mexico.

While the company has not disclosed the exact product lines or capacity figures for the second plant, the scale of the check speaks for itself. A MX$1,760 million (US$101.2 million) single-site investment in baking infrastructure typically covers automated production halls, high-speed packaging lines, and cold-chain distribution bays.

For foreign readers unfamiliar with Mexican geography, Puebla sits on the corridor connecting Mexico City to the port of Veracruz on the Gulf coast. That location lets Grupo Bimbo move fresh baked goods rapidly to millions of consumers in the densely populated central highlands while also pushing product toward the faster-growing Yucatán Peninsula.

A Track Record of Plant Investment

The Puebla move follows a pattern Grupo Bimbo established in 2023, when it deployed roughly US$50 million at its Azcapotzalco plant in Mexico City. That project added a new production line, created 80 temporary construction jobs, and brought 50 permanent positions to a factory that already employed 950 workers.

Those incremental upgrades are now giving way to greenfield construction. The shift from modernizing existing lines to building entire plants suggests the company sees demand growth that cannot be met by simply squeezing more output from older factories.

Investors familiar with the company will recognize this rhythm. Grupo Bimbo has historically alternated between upgrading legacy bakeries and breaking ground on new ones, a strategy that keeps its asset base fresh without abandoning markets where it already holds dominant shelf space.

What This Says About Mexican Consumption

Grupo Bimbo’s capex cycle arrives as Mexico benefits from nearshoring trends and rising real wages. Packaged food is a volume business, and a US$2 billion commitment implies a conviction that Mexican households will keep buying more sliced bread, buns, and wrapped snacks.

The investment also creates a durable local supply chain. Modern bakeries need flour millers, packaging suppliers, and logistics providers, many of which will expand alongside Bimbo.

That multiplier effect embeds the company even deeper in the domestic economy.

For expats and tourists, the expansion means the familiar Bimbo-branded products found on every Mexican corner store will remain reliably available, and the company’s push into low-emissions delivery vehicles may gradually improve urban air quality in cities where its distinctive white trucks are a constant presence.

What Happens Next for Investors and Job Seekers

The national program’s promise of 2,000 direct jobs and more than 1,800 indirect positions makes Grupo Bimbo a significant employment engine in a country where formal manufacturing work remains highly prized. Engineers, production supervisors, and logistics planners will be in particular demand as the new Puebla plant takes shape.

For portfolio investors, the spending cycle is a double-edged signal. On one hand, it shows management’s bullish read on Mexican consumer health; on the other, a US$2 billion outlay over three years will pressure free cash flow, and markets will watch closely to see how quickly the new capacity translates into revenue growth.

The company has not published a precise timeline for the Puebla plant’s groundbreaking or inauguration. However, given the 2025–2028 window, site preparation and early construction are likely already underway or imminent, with production ramp-up expected before the end of the decade.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is Grupo Bimbo investing in its new Puebla plant?

Grupo Bimbo is investing more than MX$1,760 million, which equals approximately US$101.2 million, in a second manufacturing plant in Puebla, Mexico. The facility will double the company’s production footprint in a state that serves as a key logistics corridor for central and southern Mexico.

What is Grupo Bimbo’s total investment plan for Mexico?

The company has announced a US$2 billion investment program for Mexico spanning 2025 to 2028. The plan covers modernization of more than 30 existing plants, construction of new facilities including the Puebla plant, expansion of a low-emissions delivery fleet, and the creation of 2,000 direct jobs plus over 1,800 indirect positions.

Why is Grupo Bimbo expanding in Mexico right now?

The expansion reflects strong confidence in Mexican household consumption, supported by nearshoring trends that bring manufacturing jobs closer to North American markets, rising real wages that boost purchasing power, and growing demand for packaged baked goods across the country. For a company operating in 34 nations, concentrating this much capital at home signals that management sees Mexico as its highest-return market.

World.title: Ecuador’s 2040 Plan Gets $7.5 Billion Development Bank Boost
World.content:
Ecuador · Business

Key Facts —Plan name. Agenda de Crecimiento Ecuador 2040, a 15-year policy roadmap. —IDB pledge. US$7.5 billion over five years, potentially rising to US$10.5 billion. —Initial loan. A US$200 million policy-based loan was approved for tax and energy reforms. —Four pillars. Institutional strength, fiscal stability, competitiveness, and financial depth. —Priority sectors. Mining, energy, agribusiness, manufacturing, and tourism for private investment.

Ecuador formally presented its Agenda de Crecimiento Ecuador 2040 on July 21, 2026, a 15-year policy roadmap designed to lift employment, attract investment, and reshape the business climate with technical backing from the Inter-American Development Bank.

What the 2040 Agenda Promises

The plan was drafted by the ministries of Economy and Finance, Production, Foreign Trade and Investments, and the Public Administration Secretariat, with the IDB providing technical accompaniment throughout the process.

It sets out a coordinated reform path built on four pillars: institutional strength and legal certainty, fiscal stability, competitiveness and productive investment, and strengthening dollarization and financial depth.

For a country that adopted the US dollar as its official currency in 2000, that last pillar is especially critical—it means keeping the banking system liquid and credible so that dollars stay inside the economy rather than fleeing abroad.

Priority public sectors include security, education, health, employment, and housing, reflecting an attempt to tackle the social deficits that have historically undermined political stability.

For private capital, the government and the IDB have flagged mining, energy, agribusiness, manufacturing, and tourism as target industries where foreign and local investors can expect clearer rules and active promotion.

Who Is the IDB and Why It Matters

The Inter-American Development Bank, known as the IDB, is a multilateral lender owned by 48 member countries, including the United States, major European economies, and Latin American nations.

It provides loans, grants, and technical expertise to governments and businesses across Latin America and the Caribbean, often acting as a policy anchor that other investors watch closely.

For a plan of this scale, the IDB’s involvement signals more than a seal of approval—it brings the financial firepower and policy know-how that can turn a printed agenda into paved roads, upgraded ports, and reformed tax offices.

When the IDB attaches its name and balance sheet to a long-term roadmap, it also creates a form of external discipline: future governments may find it harder to rip up the plan without losing access to billions in committed financing.

The Money Behind Ecuador’s Ambitions

IDB President Ilan Goldfajn announced that the bank group would provide US$7.5 billion for Ecuador over the next five years, a figure that could climb to US$10.5 billion if the country successfully mobilizes additional resources and maintains investment-friendly conditions.

To put that in perspective, the IDB’s previous 2022–2025 country strategy for Ecuador had anticipated roughly US$1.4 billion in approvals, making the new envelope a dramatic scaling-up of the lender’s engagement.

An immediate US$200 million policy-based loan has already been approved, targeting reforms to the tax system, public spending quality, strategic planning, and private investment in energy and tourism.

Policy-based loans are a tool the IDB uses to reward governments for enacting specific legal and regulatory changes, meaning this first tranche is not just a cash transfer but a down payment on concrete reform milestones.

A Plan Is a Plan Until It Is Financed

The IDB is also launching a dedicated support program called “Ecuador Crece” to accompany implementation, combining financing, non-reimbursable resources, knowledge transfers, and investments across both the public and private sectors.

Sober observers note that roadmaps in Latin America often age gracefully on shelves, but the difference here is the scale of committed money and the short-term reform triggers attached to the initial loans.

The agenda’s horizon stretches to 2040, yet its first test will arrive quickly: disbursements depend on measurable progress in tax reform, spending quality, and opening energy and tourism to private capital.

For a country that has cycled through periods of boom, bust, and political turmoil, the question is whether this time the institutional scaffolding—and the IDB’s leverage—can keep the reform train on the tracks.

What It Means for Expats and Investors

For foreign residents and anyone considering moving money into Ecuador, the plan’s emphasis on legal certainty and financial depth is a direct response to long-standing complaints about unpredictable courts and a shallow banking sector.

The explicit focus on dollarization means there is no hidden agenda to de-dollarize, a fear that has periodically spooked expat retirees and business owners who hold assets in the country.

Investors eyeing the flagged priority sectors—mining, energy, agribusiness, manufacturing, and tourism—should watch for follow-up regulations that translate the roadmap’s broad promises into specific tax incentives, licensing shortcuts, or public-private partnership frameworks.

The IDB’s “Ecuador Crece” program also opens a channel for private-sector co-financing, which could create opportunities for smaller foreign firms to partner with multilateral-backed projects and reduce their political risk exposure.

What Happens Next

The immediate next step is the rollout of the tax and energy reforms tied to the US$200 million policy-based loan, which will serve as an early signal of the government’s ability to deliver.

Over the coming months, the IDB and Ecuadorian authorities are expected to detail the disbursement schedule for the broader US$7.5 billion envelope, linking each tranche to verifiable reform benchmarks.

The plan’s 2040 endpoint is deliberately distant, but the five-year financing window means the international community will have a clear report card on Ecuador’s progress by 2031.

For now, the announcement has given the country something it has often lacked: a multi-year, externally validated script that both public officials and private actors can use to make long-term decisions.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Ecuador’s Agenda de Crecimiento 2040?

It is a 15-year national policy roadmap designed to boost growth, create jobs, attract investment, and improve the business environment through coordinated public-sector reforms. Drafted with technical support from the Inter-American Development Bank, it rests on four pillars: institutional strength, fiscal stability, competitiveness, and financial depth.

How much money did the IDB pledge to Ecuador?

The IDB committed US$7.5 billion over five years, with the potential to reach US$10.5 billion if additional financing is mobilized and reform conditions are met. An initial US$200 million policy-based loan has already been approved to support tax and energy reforms.

Which sectors will the plan prioritize for private investment?

The government and the IDB identified mining, energy, agribusiness, manufacturing, and tourism as key sectors to stimulate private capital. These industries are expected to benefit from clearer regulations and targeted incentives as the roadmap is implemented.

World.title: Despertares 2026 Brings Star Ballet Gala to Mexico City
World.content:
Mexico · Culture

Key Facts —Date and time. August 29, 2026 at 8:30 p.m., single performance. —Venue. Auditorio Nacional in Mexico City, a 10,000-seat arena. —Tickets. From MX$800 (US$46) to MX$4,600 (US$265) on Ticketmaster. —Creator. Mexican dancer Isaac Hernández, a principal at English National Ballet. —Notable guests. Roberto Bolle, Maria Khoreva, and Kristián Mensa debut.

Despertares, the ambitious dance gala that transforms a massive Mexico City arena into an intimate celebration of movement, returns for its twelfth edition on August 29, 2026. Creator Isaac Hernández has again assembled a cast of international stars for a single night at the Auditorio Nacional.

What is Despertares?

Despertares is not a typical ballet evening in a hushed opera house. It is a gala conceived by Mexican dancer Isaac Hernández that fills the 10,000-seat Auditorio Nacional with ballet, contemporary dance, tap, and acrobatic theatre.

The format is rare. Most ballet galas play to small theatres, but Hernández built this event to be accessible and spectacular, drawing thousands of people who might never buy a ticket to a traditional dance programme.

The name “Despertares” means “awakenings” in Spanish, a fitting title for a show designed to jolt audiences into a new appreciation for dance. Since its debut, the gala has grown into one of Latin America’s most anticipated cultural events, blending high art with the energy of a rock concert.

For foreign residents and visitors, the event offers a unique window into Mexico City’s vibrant arts scene. It is a place where a principal dancer from London shares a stage with a tap artist from New Zealand, all before a crowd that cheers like it is at a football match.

Who is Isaac Hernández?

Isaac Hernández is one of Mexico’s most celebrated cultural exports. He is a principal dancer with the English National Ballet in London and a global figure who has won the prestigious Benois de la Danse award.

Born in Guadalajara, Hernández trained in the United States and built his career in Europe. He created Despertares to bring world-class dance home and to show Mexican audiences the breadth of what the art form can be.

His journey from a young student in Mexico to the top of the international ballet world is a source of national pride. Hernández has used his platform not just to perform, but to open doors for other artists and to challenge ideas about who ballet is for.

He runs the production company Soul Arts Productions alongside his brother Esteban Hernández, who is also a professional dancer. Together, they have turned Despertares into a brand that signals quality and surprise.

The 2026 Despertares lineup

Hernández himself will perform “Sinatra Suite” by the legendary American choreographer Twyla Tharp, marking his first time dancing the piece at this gala. Italian star Roberto Bolle, a household name in Europe, returns to the event after a celebrated previous appearance.

Maria Khoreva, a principal dancer from Russia’s historic Mariinsky Theatre, makes her Mexican debut. Czech movement artist Kristián Mensa, known as Mr. Kriss, also debuts, alongside New Zealand tap dancer Bayley Graham.

The programme also features the Yoann Bourgeois Art Company performing a piece titled “Approach 17. Opening.

The unreachable suspension point.” This French troupe is known for blending acrobatics, theatre, and dance in ways that defy easy categorisation.

While the full cast may still expand, the confirmed names already span classical ballet, contemporary dance, tap, and physical theatre. That mix is the signature of Despertares: a deliberate collision of styles that keeps the audience guessing.

Tickets and practical details

Tickets are on sale now through Ticketmaster and at the Auditorio Nacional box office. Prices range from MX$800 (US$46) for the second level to MX$4,600 (US$265) for VIP seating near the stage.

The performance starts at 8:30 p.m. on Saturday, August 29. The Auditorio Nacional sits on Paseo de la Reforma, Mexico City’s grand boulevard, and is easily reached by taxi or the city’s Metrobús system.

For international buyers, Ticketmaster Mexico accepts most foreign credit cards. Selecting the “Will Call” option allows you to pick up physical tickets at the venue on the day of the show, avoiding shipping complications.

Given the single-performance format, tickets tend to sell quickly once the full lineup is widely publicised. Early booking is advisable, especially for the mid-range and premium sections that offer the best sightlines.

What Despertares means for expats and investors

For expats living in Mexico, Despertares is a cultural anchor that signals the capital’s global ambitions. Attending the gala is a way to connect with a local success story while enjoying a world-class show that requires no fluency in Spanish.

Investors and business travellers should see events like this as indicators of Mexico City‘s soft infrastructure. A city that can fill a 10,000-seat arena for a dance gala is a city with a deep, diverse consumer market and a robust cultural economy.

The gala also highlights the growing role of private cultural entrepreneurship in Mexico. Soul Arts Productions, the company behind Despertares, represents a model where artists become producers, creating high-value cultural products that attract sponsorship and tourism.

For the tourism sector, Despertares adds a compelling reason to visit Mexico City in late August. It sits alongside the capital’s museums, gastronomy, and architecture as a draw for high-spending cultural travellers.

What happens next

With the 2026 edition still months away, Hernández and his team may announce additional guest artists in the coming weeks. Past editions have often added surprise names close to the performance date.

Beyond the gala itself, Despertares has sparked conversations about dance education and accessibility in Mexico. Hernández has used the event’s profile to advocate for arts funding and to inspire young dancers across the country.

For readers planning ahead, the gala’s consistent late-August slot makes it a predictable fixture on the cultural calendar. Those who miss this year’s tickets can already pencil in a potential thirteenth edition for 2027.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Despertares suitable for people who do not watch ballet?

Absolutely — the gala mixes styles and keeps a fast pace, a welcoming introduction for newcomers to dance. Short pieces, varied music, and a lively crowd create an atmosphere closer to a variety show than a formal ballet evening.

How do I buy tickets from outside Mexico?

Ticketmaster Mexico accepts international credit cards; choose the “Will Call” option to collect tickets at the venue on show day. Bring the card used for purchase and a photo ID.

Who produces Despertares?

The gala is produced by Soul Arts Productions, the company founded by Isaac Hernández and his brother Esteban, also a professional dancer. The brothers oversee everything from artist selection to staging, ensuring the event reflects their vision of accessible, high-quality dance.

World.title: Mexican Giant Alpek to Shut Argentina Recycling Plant in 2026
World.content:
Argentina · Business

Key Facts —Plant. Ecopek in General Pacheco, Buenos Aires province, producing rPET resin. —Closure date. Operations cease on 31 March 2026. —Jobs. About 40 workers face dismissal or possible redeployment. —Stated reasons. Weak demand, no recycled-content rules, and pressure from imports. —Parent scale. Alpek has 31 plants in nine countries and nearly US$500 million in annual EBITDA.

Alpek Polyester Argentina is shutting its Ecopek PET recycling plant in General Pacheco, Buenos Aires province, with operations set to end on 31 March 2026.

What PET Recycling Means

PET, short for polyethylene terephthalate, is the clear, lightweight plastic used in billions of beverage bottles and food containers worldwide. Recycling it mechanically turns used bottles into rPET, a resin that packaging makers can melt and shape again.

The Ecopek plant took post-consumer bottles and produced rPET feedstock for the beverage and packaging industries. Without such plants, more plastic flows to landfills or incinerators, and manufacturers rely on virgin fossil-fuel-based resin instead.

Why Alpek Is Pulling the Plug

The company said the decision followed a careful evaluation of structural conditions in Argentina and the region. It pointed to persistent demand weakness, a lack of regulations that reward recycled content, and growing pressure from imported products, especially from China.

In its first-quarter 2026 report, Alpek framed the shutdown as part of a footprint-optimization strategy. The group is redirecting assets toward more competitive and scalable operations, noting that demand for virgin PET is actually rising.

The Human Cost in General Pacheco

About 40 workers are tied to the Ecopek site. Their status was still under review at the time of reporting, with the company weighing dismissals against possible redeployment within its Argentine operations.

For a multinational of Alpek’s size, 40 jobs is a modest number. But in the industrial corridor of Buenos Aires province, each position anchors a household, and manufacturing employment has been thinning for years.

Argentina’s Industrial Climate in Focus

The closure does not happen in a vacuum. Industry reports contrast Argentina with Brazil and Uruguay, where stricter recycling rules and mandatory recycled-content requirements support a steadier market for rPET.

Argentina’s absence of such incentives leaves recyclers exposed to cheaper virgin plastic and imports. Even a large multinational with nearly US$500 million in annual EBITDA and 31 plants across nine countries concluded the local math no longer works.

Alpek still keeps a PET resin manufacturing site in Zárate and a corporate office in Vicente López. But the Pacheco shutdown signals that, without policy change, circular-economy investments will struggle to hold ground in the country.

What It Means for Expats, Investors, and the Circular Economy

For foreign investors watching Argentina, the Ecopek closure is a real-world signal about the cost of policy gaps. When a global player with deep pockets retreats from recycling, it often means the regulatory framework does not offset the higher cost of collecting, sorting, and reprocessing used plastic.

Expats and environmentally conscious consumers may notice fewer locally recycled packaging options on supermarket shelves. Brands that want to meet their own global sustainability pledges could find it harder to source Argentine-made rPET, potentially pushing them toward imported recycled resin or back to virgin plastic.

The move also highlights a broader tension in emerging markets: governments often speak favorably about the green economy, but without concrete mandates or tax incentives, recycling plants can become financially unviable overnight. Investors eyeing sustainability-linked ventures in Latin America may now look more closely at Brazil or Uruguay, where rules create a more predictable floor under demand.

What Happens Next

Alpek says it will continue optimizing its footprint, which suggests more asset shifts are possible if conditions do not improve. The company’s Zárate virgin-PET plant remains active, so its Argentine story is not over, but its focus is clearly narrowing to the most profitable units.

For the 40 affected workers, the coming weeks will be decisive as the company finalizes whether to offer redeployment or proceed with layoffs. Local officials and industry groups may use the closure to press for recycled-content legislation, though Argentina’s political calendar makes rapid reform uncertain.

In the meantime, the empty Ecopek facility will stand as a case study of how quickly a circular-economy project can unwind when market signals and policy support point in opposite directions.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is rPET and why does it matter?

rPET is recycled PET resin made from used bottles that cuts fossil-fuel use and waste, but needs steady demand and supportive rules to compete with cheap virgin plastic. Without plants like Ecopek, more bottles end up in landfills and manufacturers lean harder on new petroleum-based resin.

Will Alpek leave Argentina entirely?

No — Alpek keeps a virgin PET plant in Zárate and a corporate office in Vicente López. The closure affects only the recycling arm, not the broader polyester business.

How many people lose their jobs?

About 40 workers are affected, and the company is still reviewing whether they will be dismissed or moved to other Argentine operations. A final decision is expected closer to the 31 March 2026 shutdown date.

World.title: Flooding Shuts Route 32 and Cuts Route 4 in Costa Rica’s Caribbean
World.content:
If you are driving to the Caribbean coast or the Northern Zone today, plan for trouble. The main highway between San José and Limón, Route 32, closed overnight after mud and rock slid onto the road, and there is no guarantee it will stay open once you set out. Days of rain from tropical wave 24 have soaked the region, and officials have placed the entire Caribbean slope, the Northern Zone, and the canton of Turrialba under a yellow alert.

Here is why the closures keep happening. After days of rain, the steep ground above Route 32 is 80 to 95 percent saturated, which means it cannot soak up any more water. Every new downpour sends loose soil, rock, and whole trees sliding onto the highway, and crews have to shut the road to clear it. When more rain falls before they finish, the material comes down again. That cycle is why a road can reopen in the morning and close by afternoon, so the status you saw last night tells you almost nothing about the status right now.

As of early Tuesday, Route 32 was closed and had not reopened. Your most reliable alternative for any vehicle is Route 10, which runs through Turrialba between Siquirres and Turrialba; crews cleared a landslide there and reopened it. The Vara Blanca route (Route 126) is open only to light vehicles. Route 4 was cut entirely at the El Tigre straightaway, where water ran across the road. Check conditions right before you leave rather than the night before, because the picture changes by the hour.

The worst damage so far is in Guácimo, in Limón province, where the Parismina River overflowed into several communities. A washed-out crossing at La Perla is closed, and a landslide has weakened the Guacimito bridge. In Sarapiquí, the Tigre, Sarapiquí, Puerto Viejo and Sucio rivers all climbed, forcing preventive evacuations from Naranjal 1, Álamo, Oropel, Carretones and El Tigre, and crews were still moving families out of Los Ángeles de Nogal and Pénjamo.

By Monday night, five shelters were housing evacuated residents; the National Emergency Commission counted 220 people, while later reporting put the figure closer to 254 as more communities were cleared. Officials expect the number to rise. A temporary shelter has opened in Santa Rosa.

More rain is coming. Forecasters expect another 60 to 80 millimeters (2.4 to 3.1 inches) across Limón and the Northern Zone through Tuesday, with some areas nearing 100 millimeters (3.9 inches), and the heaviest bursts arriving in the afternoon, at night, and again before dawn. The unsettled pattern holds through Wednesday. Strong trade winds are a second hazard, with gusts capable of bringing down branches, signs and power lines.

If you can postpone a trip to the Caribbean or the Northern Zone, do it. If you have to go, take Route 10, carry enough fuel and water to wait out a long closure, and never drive through water sitting on the road. You cannot see whether the surface beneath it has washed away, and moving water hides how deep it really is. Stay well back from swollen rivers and quebradas, and if you live near one, decide now where you would go if the water rises. The emergency line is 9-1-1.

World.title: Historic UCR Music School Faces Possible Closure
World.content:
The historic building that houses the University of Costa Rica’s School of Musical Arts could lose its operating permit after health inspectors found infrastructure and sanitation problems, including openings that allow raccoons to enter the facility. The Ministry of Health gave the university until Monday, July 20, to comply with a sanitary order issued after an inspection in April. The order requires the university to address the building’s structural problems, eliminate areas where animals can shelter and improve waste-management practices.

Failure to comply could lead to penalties ranging from a temporary closure to the cancellation of the school’s sanitary operating permit. One of the most visible problems involves raccoons entering through openings near the building’s roof and exterior eaves. The animals have reportedly gained access to classrooms, offices and other interior spaces.

The School of Musical Arts has responded with cleaning and disinfection, more frequent garbage collection and efforts to seal entry points. However, administrators say those measures have reduced the problem without providing a permanent solution. University officials say the aging building requires broader structural work that the music school cannot complete with its own budget. The UCR rector’s office submitted a corrective plan to health authorities in June and requested additional time to carry out the repairs.

The university has said that concerns about the building’s condition were raised internally as early as 2023. Since then, the school has sought technical support and funding for repairs. The building contains classrooms, rehearsal rooms, administrative offices, a music library and spaces used for concerts and academic research. A closure would disrupt lessons, rehearsals and other activities while the university looks for temporary locations or completes the required work.

The School of Musical Arts is now waiting for the Ministry of Health to decide whether to approve the corrective plan and extend the deadline. No closure had been officially announced as of Monday morning.

World.title: Hattieville man fined $305 for $50 sledgehammer from employer who would not give him payment in advance
World.content:
Hattieville man fined $305 for $50 sledgehammer from employer who would not give him payment in advance

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Hattieville construction worker has been fined more than six times the value of a sledgehammer he admitted stealing from a man who hired him for a day’s work after he would not give him an advance in payment.

Forty-two-year-old Felix Larance Petillo appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Tuesday and was charged with stealing a red Truper-brand sledgehammer, valued at $50, from a construction worker who had hired him.

Petillo initially pleaded not guilty and was offered bail of $1,000. However, while waiting to secure bail, he returned to court and changed his plea to guilty.

Senior Magistrate Mannon Dennison fined him $300, along with $5 in court costs. He was given until August 31, 2026, to pay or serve two weeks in prison.

According to the allegations, the construction worker hired Petillo on July 19 to assist with removing cement material from a demolished house on Locario Street in Hattieville.

Later that evening, Petillo reportedly asked for an advance payment for work scheduled for the following day. When the construction worker refused, Petillo allegedly threatened to take some of his tools.

The following morning, the construction worker discovered that his sledgehammer was missing and reported the matter to police.

Police later detained Petillo, who reportedly admitted placing the tool inside a mechanic’s vehicle. The mechanic subsequently handed the sledgehammer over to police and was not charged.

World.title: Businessman Miguel Guerra shot during armed robbery at Hand Money Loans; $80 stolen
World.content:
Businessman Miguel Guerra shot during armed robbery at Hand Money Loans; $80 stolen

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating an armed robbery in Belize City that left a 67-year-old businessman injured on Tuesday morning.

The incident occurred at approximately 11:15 a.m. at Handy Money Loans on Handyside Street.

Police said the suspect entered the establishment under the pretense of pawning a cellphone before producing a firearm and demanding money.

The robber reportedly fled with approximately $80 in cash after firing a single shot at the businessman, Miguel Angel Guerra.

Guerra was transported to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where he is receiving medical treatment.

Police investigations continue.

World.title: Joseph Vaccaro receives disclosure in Gaston Barrow murder case
World.content:
Joseph Vaccaro receives disclosure in Gaston Barrow murder case

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Thirty-year-old taxi operator Joseph Gabourel Vaccaro has received disclosure in the murder case stemming from the September 2025 shooting death of Gaston Barrow at Old Belize.

Vaccaro, a resident of Cumberbatch Street, appeared unrepresented before the Chief Magistrate in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Tuesday.

He was provided with 154 pages of disclosure, five compact discs and photographs forming part of the prosecution’s evidence. The matter was adjourned until September 7, 2026, when a preliminary inquiry is scheduled to begin.

Vaccaro was first arraigned for Barrow’s murder on October 6, 2025, and was remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

Police said Barrow and another man, Hank Carr, were shot at the Old Belize compound on the night of September 28, 2025. Barrow was pronounced dead on arrival at the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, while Carr was treated and later released.

Investigators allege Carr was driving a vehicle with Barrow in the front passenger seat when a gunman near a taxi opened fire. The shooter reportedly entered the taxi and escaped towards the nearby police checkpoint.

Police later reviewed surveillance footage from the area, which reportedly led to Vaccaro’s detention and subsequent charge.
