World.title: Video: PM Magyar spat on at Budapest railway station before major rail announcement
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar was spat on by a man at Budapest’s Nyugati railway station on Wednesday morning, shortly before unveiling the government’s new railway development strategy alongside Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy.

The incident, which was captured on video, occurred as the two politicians were at Nyugati railway station ahead of a press conference presenting the Baross Gábor Railway Development Plan at Rákospalota-Újpest railway station.

Man confronts prime minister

According to footage published by Hungarian media, a man approached Magyar and Vitézy at Nyugati station.

The man reportedly shouted: “How could you? You dared to come here?!” When he received no response, he spat at the prime minister from behind.

Magyar reacted calmly, wishing the man “good health” before commenting:

“This is what remains of the faces of Fidesz.”

He then added that perhaps this was why former Transport Minister János Lázár had not travelled by train.

Political tensions still high

It is not the first time a politician from the governing Tisza Party has reported being spat on in public. In November 2025, MP Kriszta Bódis said she had been spat on in the street.

Commenting on this new incident on Wednesday, Bódis wrote that those serving in public life must sometimes endure unfair treatment, adding that she believed years of political hate campaigns had contributed to such behaviour and expressing hope that public discourse would improve.

World.title: ‘They knelt on my head’: New witness testimonies reveal alleged abuse in Hungary’s ‘gold convoy’ scandal
World.content:
Newly obtained witness testimonies have shed light on one of the biggest political and diplomatic scandals of the final weeks of Viktor Orbán’s government, with Ukrainian cash couriers alleging they were subjected to physical abuse and unlawful detention after a dramatic counter-terrorism raid in Hungary in what has since been called the “gold convoy” scandal.

The testimonies, published by Hungarian investigative outlet 444.hu, were given by the seven Ukrainian couriers between 27 May and 10 July via video link as part of an investigation into suspected unlawful detention. The witnesses describe what they say happened after Hungary’s Counter Terrorism Centre (TEK) stopped their convoy carrying more than HUF 27 billion (EUR 74 million) worth of gold and foreign currency on 5 March.

The allegations are the couriers’ account of events and have not been proven in court. However, 444 reports that the testimonies are largely consistent with one another and do not contradict internal documents or previous witness statements from Hungarian authorities that have emerged during the investigation.

‘Someone knelt on my head’

According to the testimonies, the convoy had collected the shipment from a Raiffeisen Bank branch in Vienna before obtaining the necessary customs documentation at Vienna Airport. After crossing into Hungary, police reportedly inspected the documents at the Austrian-Hungarian border and allowed the vehicles to continue.

The situation changed after the convoy passed Budapest. Witnesses say police directed the vehicles into a MOL petrol station near Vecsés, where heavily armed TEK officers surrounded them. The couriers allege they were forced onto the ground, handcuffed, blindfolded with masks placed over their eyes, searched, and separated.

One courier recalled:

“When they removed my bulletproof vest, they stepped on my head. Then someone crouched beside me and knelt on my head.”

According to the testimonies, officers repeatedly demanded to know where weapons were hidden, despite no firearms reportedly being found during the operation.

The confiscated assets. Photo: MTI/Magyarország Kormánya

Convoy leader alleges beating while in custody

The most serious allegations concern convoy leader Hennadiy Ivanovych Kuznetsov, a retired Ukrainian intelligence officer.

He told investigators that he was questioned extensively about his previous military and intelligence service before his health deteriorated while in custody. Kuznetsov claimed that instead of receiving his medication, several officers forcibly attempted to move him into a wheelchair.

He alleged that during the incident he was repeatedly struck in the face and kicked in an injured leg.

“I screamed incoherently,” he reportedly told investigators, adding that he could not identify those involved because several officers wore masks.

Kuznetsov also claimed he was injected with an unknown substance before later being taken to hospital. According to previous testimony from former TEK director János Hajdu, the convoy leader was treated at two Budapest hospitals while remaining in TEK custody.

Viktor Orbán and János Hajdu. Photo: Facebook/Orbán Viktor

Other witnesses report hearing screams

Several other couriers said they heard shouting during the interrogations. One witness said that while being questioned, he heard “terrible screaming” coming from another room that lasted for about a minute and sounded as though someone was in severe pain.

According to earlier evidence cited by 444, a senior official at Hungary’s National Tax and Customs Administration (NAV) was also informed by colleagues that shouting could be heard during the questioning, although the official said they did not know what had caused it.

Background: Hungary’s ‘gold convoy’ affair

The case became one of the most controversial episodes before Hungary’s April general election.

The convoy was transporting cash and gold belonging to Ukraine’s state-owned Oschadbank from Austria to Ukraine. Lawyers representing both the Ukrainian bank and Austria’s Raiffeisen Bank have consistently maintained that the shipment was fully documented and legally transported with the required permits.

Despite this, the previous Orbán government suggested the shipment could be linked to money laundering and, without presenting public evidence, hinted at possible connections to financing the opposition Tisza Party.

Subsequent investigations took a different turn. The confiscated assets have since been returned to the Ukrainian bank, while Hungarian prosecutors are reportedly preparing to close the money laundering investigation against the couriers due to a lack of evidence of any crime.

Meanwhile, the investigation into the conduct of Hungarian authorities has continued.

On 29 June, former TEK director János Hajdu was formally named as a suspect on suspicion of unlawful detention involving the mistreatment of detainees.

Earlier reporting by Hungarian media also suggested that prosecutors have examined the role of several former senior officials involved in authorising the operation, while previous reports claimed the raid itself had been ordered at the highest political level.

World.title: Hungary submits landmark bill to open Communist-era secret service files
World.content:
The Hungarian government has submitted a new bill to Parliament that would pave the way for the most comprehensive disclosure yet of Communist-era state security files, fulfilling what it describes as a promise left unfulfilled since the country’s democratic transition more than three decades ago.

According to the government’s statement, the legislation was finalised after a public consultation and seeks to replace previous piecemeal measures with an entirely new legal framework governing the disclosure of documents created by the Communist dictatorship’s secret services.

Government aims for greater transparency with opening Communist-era files

The cabinet argues that previous governments have repeatedly attempted to uncover the activities of the Communist-era state security apparatus since the regime change, but none of those initiatives proved either comprehensive or successful.

It said the continued secrecy surrounding the identities and activities of informants who monitored innocent citizens has undermined public trust in state institutions and politicians. The government maintains that confronting the country’s past and ensuring the transparency of public institutions are essential pillars of a democratic state governed by the rule of law.

According to the proposal, the legislation is intended to restore public confidence, provide moral redress for victims of the Communist regime and deepen historical understanding by making agent files available to the public as extensively as possible.

Historical archives to make records widely accessible

A key element of the bill is the expanded role of the Historical Archives of the State Security Services. The institution would be tasked with making previously classified documents available in the simplest and broadest possible way.

To facilitate public access, the government plans to launch a dedicated online platform where documents can be searched and viewed digitally.

Parliament has already approved preparatory measures for the disclosure process through earlier legislation. The newly submitted bill is designed to regulate the entire process from publication to data protection.

Disclosure to happen in several stages

The government also outlined a timetable for releasing the records. The first documents expected to become publicly available will be the so-called “six cards” (hatos kartonok) and the notorious magnetic tape archives, shortly before the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Hungarian Revolution.

The six cards contain information relating to the recruitment of informants into the Communist-era surveillance network. Meanwhile, the magnetic tapes are digital copies created in January 1990 containing several state security databases:

the G database, covering operational records;

the H database, containing the network register of informants; and

the K database, the Central Counterintelligence Registry.

According to the government, these databases were copied onto magnetic tapes without systematic organisation at the time.

Throughout the remainder of the year, authorities plan to gradually publish the surviving B dossiers, which include recruitment files, evaluations of recruited individuals, the identities of people connected to the network and records indicating from whom informants gathered intelligence.

Privacy safeguards remain part of the process

Before any material is published, officials will review the documents to determine whether disclosure would infringe the fundamental rights, privacy or human dignity of individuals mentioned in the files. Particularly sensitive personal information—including details concerning an individual’s health, pathological addictions or sexual orientation—will only be made accessible under strict legal conditions.

The government says the legislation seeks to strike a balance between the public interest in understanding the past, academic freedom, individuals’ rights to informational self-determination and the protection of national security interests that remain relevant today.

Stay up-to-date: Péter Magyar’s first major misstep? What the presidential nomination really revealed

A promise dating back to the democratic transition

The government says the legislation represents a significant step towards historical accountability and will help both researchers and the wider public better understand Hungary’s Communist past.

By opening the archives, the cabinet argues it is delivering on a commitment first made during the democratic transition more than 30 years ago, while creating a legal framework intended to reconcile transparency with privacy protections and national security considerations.

World.title: Fidesz: From now on, our mission is “to restore the democratic rule of law”
World.content:
The national executive committee and parliamentary group of opposition Fidesz have issued a “declaration of resistance”, in which they called “the new political regime” illegitimate, saying it was established “in gross violation of the Fundamental Law and because its goal is the exclusive exercise of power”.

Fidesz issued a “declaration of resistance”

In a statement on Tuesday, Fidesz said it “rejects the new authoritarian regime”, will not participate in the election of replacements for the ousted officials, and will review its decisions only once “the democratic rule of law has been restored”.

Fidesz said that following the 2026 elections, the Tisza Party had altered Hungary’s constitutional system. “After the 17th amendment to the Fundamental Law, Hungary is no longer a democratic state governed by the rule of law, and an era of autocracy has once again dawned in Hungary,” it said.

They complain that the rule of law has officially ended

“By restricting the right to vote, political competition has ceased, and with it, democracy has come to an end. The President of the Republic and the President of the Constitutional Court have been removed, thereby abolishing the separation of powers; checks and balances have been eliminated, and the rule of law has been dismantled,” they added.

The statement said that every citizen had the right to take a stand against “autocracy”, and as a result, Fidesz would “oppose not only the government but also the new political regime”. They emphasised that, starting today, their mission was “to restore the democratic rule of law”.

Stay up-to-date: Fidesz’s parliamentary group elected new leader after previous one stepping down

“We will help the victims”

“We will help the victims of the authoritarian regime. We are documenting the violations of the law committed by the Tisza government,” the statement said. “Once the democratic rule of law is restored, we will provide the victims and those who have suffered harm with the redress they are entitled to.”

World.title: Two trams collide in Budapest: two people injured, major route disrupted
World.content:
Two trams collided on Hűvösvölgyi Road in Budapest’s 2nd district on Tuesday, leaving two people with minor injuries and temporarily disrupting public transport in the area.

Tram collision in Budapest, again

According to Hungary’s disaster management authority, professional firefighters from the capital, assisted by volunteer firefighters from Rózsadomb, carried out technical rescue operations at the scene. Ambulance crews also attended the incident, and the two injured people were treated for minor injuries.

Tram services temporarily suspended

The collision affected tram services on two key routes. Following the accident, trams 56A and 61 were suspended between Budagyöngye and Hűvösvölgy, with replacement buses introduced to transport passengers. Travellers were also advised to use bus routes 29 and 129 while emergency crews worked to clear the scene.

By around 7:15 PM, Budapest’s public transport operator, BKK, confirmed that both tram lines had resumed normal operations along their full routes after the affected section had been reopened.

Second tram collision in Budapest within days

The latest incident comes just days after another tram collision in the Hungarian capital. In the early hours of Sunday, two trams travelling to a depot collided near the Mester Street stop on Könyves Kálmán Boulevard in Budapest’s 9th district. In that accident, one of the tram drivers sustained minor injuries.

The two incidents in quick succession have drawn attention to tram safety, although authorities have not yet disclosed the cause of Tuesday’s collision.

World.title: Romanian prime minister Ilie Bolojan congratulates new Moldovan PM Vasile Tofan
World.content:
Romania’s acting prime minister Ilie Bolojan sent congratulations to Vasile Tofan, who was confirmed as the Republic of Moldova’s new prime minister on Tuesday, July 21.

"I assure him of the full support and cooperation of the government of Romania. It is important that we continue to move forward with the projects on our bilateral agenda, from transportation and energy interconnection projects to those in the fields of culture and education," acting prime minister Ilie Bolojan wrote on X.

He also praised "Chișinău's progress in the EU accession process: As I have said on other occasions, Romania remains its most active and dedicated supporter."

Vasile Tofan’s cabinet was approved by the Moldovan Parliament on July 21, receiving the votes of the 53 deputies of the governing PAS party out of 101.

Asked where he would like to make his first foreign trip during an interview, Vasile Tofan indicated Romania, mentioning the strategic partnership linking the two countries. "We have not yet agreed on the first visit. I believe we have a strategic partnership with Romania. I would like it to be Romania," replied the new prime minister.

"Now I understand that the political situation in Romania is a little more complicated than ours, but if you ask me where I would like to go on my first visit, I would like to go to Romania," Vasile Tofan added during the program "În PROfunzime" on ProTV Chișinău, in reference to Romania’s ongoing political crisis.

He also said that a second important destination would be Brussels. As PM-designate, Tofan said he would accelerate Moldova’s accession to the EU.

In the same interview, Tofan said he has two citizenships, "like all well-intentioned Moldovans" (with dual citizenship), those of the Republic of Moldova and Romania. He added that around a third of all Moldovans are in the same situation.

Tofan, 44, studied at Erasmus University Rotterdam and Harvard Business School, and speaks fluent English, French, Dutch, Ukrainian, and Russian.

He worked as an investor through Horizon Capital, a fund with approximately USD 1.6 billion in assets under management, focused on Ukraine and the Republic of Moldova. He led investments in the companies Purcari, Glass Container Company, and Maib. He was a member of the boards of directors of AmCham Moldova, Startup Moldova, and Media Alternativa (TV8/1TV).

Earlier this month, the previous Moldovan PM, Alexandru Munteanu, announced his resignation amid an investigation by Ziarul de Gardă into the state-owned enterprise MoldATSA, the body charged with air traffic safety in the Republic of Moldova.

World.title: Romania’s weather agency issues red alert for Tulcea county amid widespread storm warnings
World.content:
The National Meteorological Administration (ANM) issued a red weather warning for Tulcea county as heavy rain, strong winds, and severe thunderstorms are expected to affect parts of Romania through Thursday morning, July 23. Yellow and orange alerts have also been issued for several other regions, with forecasters warning of torrential rain, hail, and damaging wind gusts.

The red alert for Tulcea is in effect from 6:00 p.m. on Wednesday until 6:00 a.m. on Thursday. Forecasters expect exceptionally severe weather, including torrential rainfall, frequent lightning, wind gusts exceeding 80-90 km/h, and storms. Rainfall totals are forecast to reach 90-110 liters per square meter, with isolated areas receiving more than 120 l/sqm.

An orange warning covering the same period has been issued for Galați, Brăila, and Constanța counties, as well as the eastern parts of Ialomița and Călărași counties. These areas are expected to experience heavy downpours, thunderstorms, and wind gusts of 70-90 km/h, with rainfall amounts of 30-50 l/sqm and isolated totals of up to 90 l/sqm.

A yellow alert is in place overnight for eastern Muntenia, southwestern Moldova, and parts of the Eastern Carpathians, where thunderstorms, heavy rain, hail, and wind gusts of 50-70 km/h are forecast.

Earlier on Wednesday, ANM issued yellow and orange warnings for large parts of the country, including Oltenia, Muntenia, Dobrogea, southern Moldova, southern Transylvania, and mountain areas, as storms moved eastward during the day.

After the red warning expires, Tulcea county will remain under an orange alert from 6:00 a.m. until noon on Thursday, with additional heavy rainfall, thunderstorms, and wind gusts of 70-90 km/h expected.

ANM said it will update its forecasts depending on the evolution and intensity of the weather system.

World.title: Four Romanian female tennis players included in 2026 US Open main draw
World.content:
Four Romanian players have been accepted directly into the women's singles main draw of the 2026 US Open, according to the entry lists published on Wednesday, July 22, by the United States Tennis Association (USTA).

Sorana Cîrstea, ranked 17th in the WTA rankings, is the highest-ranked Romanian representative on the US Open entry list. She is followed by Jaqueline Cristian (WTA No. 41), Elena-Gabriela Ruse (WTA No. 73), and Irina-Camelia Begu, who will compete using a protected ranking, reserved for players who have been absent from the tour for an extended period due to injuries, according to Mediafax.

The 2026 US Open will take place from August 23 to September 13, with the main draw singles matches beginning on August 30.

The entry lists were compiled based on the ATP and WTA rankings of July 20. The last woman accepted directly into the main draw is Anastasia Zakharova, ranked world No. 102, while in the men's draw the last direct entrant is Filip Misolic, who entered using a protected ranking.

In the women's competition, world No. 1 Aryna Sabalenka will attempt to win her third consecutive US Open title. Other leading favorites include Elena Rybakina, this year's Australian Open champion, Jessica Pegula, Coco Gauff, Mirra Andreeva, and Iga Swiatek.

In the men's competition, world No. 1 Jannik Sinner will attempt to reclaim the trophy he lost last year to Carlos Alcaraz. The former recently defeated Alexander Zverev in the Wimbledon final to win his fifth Grand Slam title. Alcaraz, who missed the last two major tournaments due to a wrist injury, is on the entry list and hopes to return to the tour during the North American hard-court season.

The US Open initial field includes 17 former Grand Slam singles champions (11 women, six men), including 10 former US Open champions.

Among the countries represented at the US Grand Slam, the United States has the largest delegation, with 28 players accepted directly into the main draws, 14 women and 14 men.

The 128 places in each main draw will be completed by players receiving wild cards from the organizers and by athletes who qualify through the preliminary tournaments scheduled during the week preceding the start of the main draws.

World.title: Air traffic at Bucharest airports reaches record 8.45 mln in first half of 2026
World.content:
Bucharest’s two airports, the Henri Coandă International Airport and the Băneasa "Aurel Vlaicu" International Airport, welcomed 8.45 million passengers in the first half of 2026, according to the National Company Bucharest Airports.

Traffic data for the first six months of this year indicate a significant 5.08% growth from the same period in 2025.

Air traffic growth was also reflected in the number of aircraft movements. During the first half of the year, 68,367 landings and take-offs were recorded, 3.37% more than in the January–June 2025 period.

"The results we have achieved are the effects of the new management strategy, focused on attracting new airlines, expanding the number of routes operated from Bucharest, increasing operating frequencies on existing routes, and, last but not least, optimizing the quality and safety of airport infrastructure," said Bogdan Mîndrescu, General Director of the National Company Bucharest Airports, cited by Economedia.

Henri Coandă Airport exceeded the threshold of 7.7 million passengers, but the absolute record belongs to Băneasa Airport, which reached 745,674 passengers in the first half of the year, 50,956 more than the total number of passengers recorded at this airport throughout the entire year of 2025.

"The National Company Bucharest Airports recorded solid and sustainable growth, with the priority of CNAB's management being to ensure optimal conditions for this development, with major concern for maintaining the strictest standards of safety and security for passengers and air operations at the Capital's airports," Bogdan Mîndrescu said.

Last year, the Social Democratic-led Ministry of Transport blocked a key procedural step required for the listing of Bucharest Airports Company on the Stock Exchange (BVB), then valued at around EUR 1 billion. The ministry owns roughly 80% of the company’s stocks.

World.title: CoE Commissioner for Human Rights expresses concern over illegal care homes case in Romania
World.content:
The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights, Michael O'Flaherty, addressed an open letter to Romanian acting prime minister Ilie Bolojan on Tuesday, July 21, expressing concern over the issue of the unauthorized care homes operating in Bihor County, western Romania.

The letter follows a visit to Romania that O’Flaherty conducted in May of this year, during which he gained “deep insights into the human rights situation of older persons in residential care.” The CoE official noted that Romania achieved progress in reforming social services in recent years.

“I was encouraged by the commitment demonstrated by many of those working in care homes,” he said.

The visit also revealed problems. “Older people and others in care institutions continue to be regarded as beneficiaries of services rather than fully-fledged rights holders, a perspective that warrants reconsideration across the social care system. The ongoing shortage of care services makes access difficult, particularly as Romania’s population ages and care needs are growing,” the official noted in the letter.

Similarly, some of the most vulnerable, including those living in poverty or with disabilities or mental health issues, struggle to obtain proper care.

Bihor illegal care homes

The letter, however, centered on the issue of unlicensed care homes operating illegally in various forms in Romania, particularly the ones in Bihor County, where Ilie Bolojan served as mayor of Oradea and then County Council president.

“For many years, this institution operated unlawfully, reportedly hosting thousands of vulnerable people under abusive conditions, with over a thousand deaths recorded. I welcome the recent intervention of the Directorate for Investigating Organised Crime and Terrorism and the transfer of residents to hospitals and licensed care facilities. However, I am concerned by how long this situation persisted, despite repeated alerts from civil society and journalists,” the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights said.

The CoE official argued it would be useful to review and adopt legal provisions to combat the operation of illegal care homes and to strengthen independent monitoring mechanisms. He said Romania should establish clear procedures for reporting and investigating deaths occurring in homes for elderly people.

Michael O'Flaherty also said that care home residents should have access to mechanisms through which they can report problems and request their resolution. At the same time, the role of non-governmental organizations in promoting respect for human rights and the dignity of residents should be recognized and supported.

Care homes owner’s response

The owner of the illegal care homes in Bihor, Viorel Paşca, responded to O’Flaherty’s letter, rejecting his criticism. Paşca disputed the CoE official’s information and said that his establishment, Dumbrava, never operated as a center or a care home.

“All the locations were actually residential homes where Romanian citizens lived and had their official residence. None of them lived there illegally, were held against their will, abused, or tortured, as was claimed in the media,” he said in a post on Facebook.

Finally, Viorel Paşca criticized O’Flaherty’s appreciation for DIICOT prosecutors and the way they acted in the Dumbrava case.

The Bihor illegal care homes case broke at the end of last month, uncovering similarities with another, more serious case from 2023. Prosecutors claim that hundreds of elderly individuals, people with severe mental disabilities, and homeless people were turned into simple “sources of income” under the guise of charitable activity. According to DIICOT, over 2,200 vulnerable persons passed through centers controlled by the group in the last 6 years.

Unlike the 2023 case, however, the situation of the care homes in Bihor is not as clear, leading many to argue that Viorel Pașca and his association were doing their best with the available resources, taking care of patients who had been abandoned by state institutions.

(Photo source: Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights on Facebook)

World.title: German company DEHN starts production at first Romanian factory in Pitești
World.content:
German electrical technology company DEHN has started production at its first manufacturing facility in Romania, located in Pitești. The new plant will supply surge protection devices for European markets and is expected to employ up to 150 people.

The facility, which began operations in July, is part of DEHN's global manufacturing network and complements the company's existing production sites in Neumarkt and Mühlhausen, Germany. While the German factories focus on high-volume, highly automated production, the Romanian site specializes in smaller production runs that require a higher degree of manual assembly, the company said.

The 9,500 sqm built-to-suit factory was developed by industrial real estate company CTP at CTPark Pitești and marks DEHN's first manufacturing investment in Romania.

“We are proud to have partnered with DEHN on its first manufacturing investment in Romania and to contribute to strengthening the country’s position as a destination for high-value industrial production. This project also reflects the growing demand we see from international manufacturers looking for flexible, future-ready facilities in strategically located industrial parks,” said Tatiana Axinte, CTP Romania Business Developer.

According to the company, Romania was selected after evaluating several locations across Europe, with factors including transport infrastructure, access to skilled workers, and proximity to technical universities contributing to the decision.

In addition to manufacturing and logistics, the Pitești site will also host support functions such as human resources, IT, marketing, and other shared services.

The factory is part of DEHN's broader strategy to expand production capacity closer to key markets. The German family-owned company, which specializes in lightning protection, surge protection, and electrical safety equipment, also opened a manufacturing facility in Mooresville, North Carolina, last year to serve customers in the United States.

Located near the A1 motorway, CTPark Pitești now comprises around 80,000 sqm of industrial space and provides direct road connections to Bucharest, Western Europe, and the Port of Constanța.

World.title: Romania's acting defense minister warns Black Sea attack shows war threat is real
World.content:
Romania’s acting defense minister, Radu Miruță, said on Wednesday, July 22, that the incident involving the vessel Gas Lisbon, which was attacked and set on fire outside Romanian territorial waters, is yet another reminder that the country must be prepared for worst-case scenarios.

He argued that Romania cannot be defended through slogans and conspiracy theories, a veiled criticism of the popular far-right, pro-Russian Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR) party.

"In such a context, investments in equipping and organizing the Romanian Army are not a luxury and not an option, but an obligation towards the safety of our citizens," Miruță wrote on Facebook.

The official also condemned "increasingly frequent disinformation and fake news campaigns that try to convince people that there is no danger, that the war does not concern us, or even that Russia is not the aggressor state in this conflict."

"Just a few dozen kilometers from our borders, for more than four years, a war triggered by Russia's military aggression against Ukraine has been taking place. Romania cannot afford to build its security policies on illusions or on the propaganda of those trying to downplay this threat," the minister also wrote.

Miruță then gave further details of the rescue operation for the 17 crew members of the gas tanker Gas Lisbon. Three sailors were injured and were transported to Tulcea County Hospital but are in stable condition.

The ship, an LPG tanker flying the Liberian flag, had departed from the port of Alexandria (Egypt) and was heading to Reni (Ukraine), transiting Romania's Exclusive Economic Zone. It was approximately 20 nautical miles southeast of the town of Sfântu Gheorghe when it suffered major damage and a fire broke out on board.

Sources from the Lower Danube River Administration in Galati told Digi24 the ship was attacked by a naval drone. The sailors said they were woken up by powerful explosions. “When I woke up, I heard those explosions. It was like a bomb, like a missile,” one of the crew members recounted, according to TVRInfo. Several sailors stated that the vessel had allegedly been hit by three drones.

The investigation is ongoing. The vessel is currently anchored, and a warning has been issued for other ships to avoid the incident perimeter.

Also on Wednesday, representatives of the Romanian Naval Authority (ANR) announced that the fire aboard the Gas Lisbon decreased in intensity and that it represents no risk to the population. “The fire aboard the Gas Lisbon vessel has decreased in intensity, and the evolution of the situation is closely monitored by the competent authorities. Given the vessel’s position, approximately 14 nautical miles from the shore, there is no risk to the population, tourists or activities carried out on the Romanian coast,” ANR representatives said.

World.title: Timișoara joins Romania's Literary Map network
World.content:
Timișoara will officially join the Literary Map network on August 2, becoming the fourth city featured on Romania’s first interactive digital platform dedicated to places connected with literature. The launch will coincide with Timișoara Day celebrations and include guided literary tours and public events.

Launched in 2025, the Literary Map (Harta Literară) is an interactive platform that maps locations featured in books, sites of literary significance, and cultural landmarks such as bookstores, libraries, and cafés. Following Bucharest, Iași, and Brașov, Timișoara is the latest city to be added to the national network.

The launch program, running on August 2-3, includes the official presentation of the Timișoara module and two literary walking tours led by local writers Tudor Crețu and Robert Șerban, each offering a different perspective on the city's literary heritage.

“We are pleased to complement Timișoara's literary, emotional, and ysymbolic map with a technological component by placing on the interactive platform the places described and imagined by the city's writers. We hope both residents and visitors will have an easy-to-use tool […] that helps them discover how the city's geography is reflected in literature," said Cristina Foarfă, manager of the Literary Map project.

The official launch event will take place on August 2 at FABER and will include a presentation of the project, its methodology, and a discussion on Timișoara's literary identity with local authors. Admission is free, subject to available seating.

Participation in the two literary tours is also free but requires prior registration due to limited capacity. Registration for the tour led by Tudor Crețu is available here, while for the tour led by Robert Șerban here.

The Literary Map project is developed by the NGO Tech and Tonic and aims to encourage readers to explore cities through literature by combining digital technology with cultural heritage. According to the organizers, the platform has attracted more than 30,000 active users since its launch and reached over one million people through its communication channels.

World.title: North Macedonia’s Access-to-Information Agency Accused of Hindering Appeals
World.content:
North Macedonia’s Agency for the Protection of the Right to Free Access to Public Information. Photo: BIRN.

Legal experts and transparency advocates have criticised North Macedonia’s Agency for the Protection of the Right to Free Access to Public Information after it began requiring electronic signatures on email appeals, arguing that this unlawfully restricts access to public information.

The Agency is the only institution responsible for deciding appeals when public bodies refuse or fail to provide information requested under the country’s freedom of information law.

Until recently, appeals could be submitted by email without additional formalities. However, the Agency has started rejecting emailed appeals unless they are certified with an electronic signature, which costs 2,000 to 4,000 denars (30 to 65 euros) annually.

Critics say the changes create an unnecessary financial and administrative obstacle to exercising a constitutionally guaranteed right.

“I believe they obstruct free access to public information in this country,” German Filkov, one of the authors of the Law on Free Access to Public Information and president of the Centre for Civil Communications, an anti-corruption and transparency watchdog, told BIRN.

Instead of creating new barriers, Filkov said, the Agency should focus on the growing number of state institutions that fail to respond to freedom of information requests.

The Agency has defended the new requirement by citing the 2015 Law on General Administrative Procedure, which it says obliges anyone communicating electronically with state institutions to use an electronic signature.

However, the State Administrative Inspectorate, which the Agency initially cited as the source of the guidance, told BIRN it had issued no written decision or instruction requiring such a practice.

One of the authors of the Law on General Administrative Procedure, which the Agency cites as the legal basis for its new practice, Skopje university law professor Borce Davitkovski, also questioned the Agency’s interpretation.

“They are not allowed to reject an appeal because it lacks an electronic signature,” Davitkovski told BIRN, noting that the law was designed to protect citizens rather than burden them with unnecessary bureaucracy.

Konstantin Bitrakov, an assistant professor at Skopje’s State Faculty of Law, argued that the Agency was misapplying the legislation and “setting a negative example for public institutions that hold information, whose decisions it is supposed to review on appeal”.

He said the legal provisions on electronic signatures apply to officials issuing administrative decisions, not to citizens filing appeals.

Lawyers told BIRN that citizens and organisations whose appeals have been rejected for lacking an electronic signature should challenge the Agency before the Administrative Court within 30 days.

The dispute comes amid concerns over access to public information.

A BIRN analysis found that the number of appeals filed with the Agency over administrative silence or incomplete responses had doubled last year, from over 300 filed in 2024 to over 600 in 2025.

The European Commission’s latest Rule of Law Report warned that some public institutions continue to reject information requests on arbitrary grounds or with significant delays.

In April, the new head of the Agency, Petar Gajdov, told BIRN in an interview: “As institutions, we are service-oriented towards citizens.”

World.title: Who Really Benefits from ‘Strategic Investor’ Status in Albania?
World.content:
A company granted a stretch of Albania’s Adriatic coastline lists its official address as the 12th floor of the European Trade Centre in Tirana, where, according to a BIRN investigation, “there was no company sign, and building staff said they were unaware of any company by that name”.

A public asset belonging to all citizens is now registered under the name of a company that cannot even be found at its own listed address – because its ownership has been ‘constructed’ as a chain of corporate shells, one nested inside another, with the final shell empty. In that vacuum is where the problem begins.

Attempts to frame the public debate over luxury tourist developments in Zvernec, on the Albanian coast, and nearby Sazan island as a choice between environmental protection and economic development are, at best, unhelpful. At worst, they are misleading.

World.title: EU’s Failure to Address Balkan Disputes Undermines Its Credibility
World.content:
It also underlines the consequences of the EU’s failure to put forward an overall strategy to address the many bilateral disputes in the Western Balkans.

North Macedonia’s current centre-right government led by Hristijan Mickovski, elected in 2024, has insisted that before it amends the constitution, Bulgaria should guarantee it will make no new demands that could further block negotiations down the road.

The background to this request relates to the long list of obstacles placed on the country’s aspirations to join the European Union ever since it applied for membership in 2004, and successive governments’ efforts to address them with varying degrees of success.

In her response, however, Commissioner Kos underlined that “EU enlargement is not built on guarantees given in advance. It is built on trust, commitments, dedication in fulfilling these commitments and hard work”.

A week later, she repeated the same call on the government to build trust with all the EU member states.

In doing so, she seemed to forget the number of times North Macedonia’s citizens were let down by promises made by the EU which were not kept. She should acknowledge that trust can only succeed if it exists on both sides and is based on solid foundations.

Under the so-called Prespa Agreement, signed with Greece in June 2018, the country agreed to replace its constitutional name with “Republic of North Macedonia”, to be applied erga omnes. The agreement also included recognition of the Macedonian language.

In return the EU assured the country that this agreement would open the door to EU and NATO membership, only to be confronted with a French government veto in 2019, calling for a pause on EU enlargement.

This was resolved the following year with the adoption of a revised methodology for accession negotiations, and the European Council recommendation that negotiations should start with both Albania and North Macedonia.

However, Bulgaria then decided to impose its own veto against the latter, which was transformed into an EU veto in 2022, with the adoption of the French proposal. Under this proposal, formal negotiations with both countries were launched in July 2022. But until parliament in North Macedonia adopts the constitutional amendment, its accession negotiations remain blocked.

Renewed momentum flawed by unanimity rule

World.title: ‘Nobody Mentions Us’: Silence Surrounds Wartime Rape of Kosovo’s Ethnic Minorities
World.content:
Those who fled and never returned often have no means of applying for recognition as survivors of wartime sexual violence.

That includes a fourth woman interviewed by BIRN, who was 29 years old when she was raped twice by uniformed men in the police headquarters in Gjakova/Djakovica in March and April 1999. A cleaner in the building, she fled when the war ended out of fear of being targeted for revenge as a former employee of the Serbian state.

The woman now lives in the Montenegrin capital, Podgorica, but does not possess Kosovo documents.

“Living in a refugee camp for a long time, we didn’t have food, let alone a psychologist,” she told BIRN. “Sometimes I bought sedatives when I had a few dinars.”

When the war ended, ethnic minorities were targeted for revenge by Kosovo Albanian guerrillas and civilians.

Speaking to BIRN, an Egyptian woman from a village near Peja/Pec recalled five armed men entering her house on July 27, 1999, one of them in a T-shirt featuring the symbol of the guerrilla Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA. Her husband was beaten and she was dragged into the woods. “One of them raped me, and my husband was unable to help.”

The men later went next door, where they raped the woman’s neighbour.

Three days later, the family left Kosovo. Her case was documented in a 1999 report by the Belgrade-based Humanitarian Law Centre. In the report, she says: “When they came, they asked me to find two other women and go with them. I told them I could not find any and begged them to let me go because I was a mother with small children. One of them threatened to kill my husband if I did not comply. Crying, I went there. They left me there, crying and dishonoured.”

However, Kosovo’s Law on the Status and Rights of Martyrs, Invalids, Veterans, Civilian Victims, and Victims of Sexual Violence only provides for recognition of survivors of wartime sexual violence between February 1998 and June 20, 1999, i.e. roughly a week after Serbian forces pulled out of Kosovo and the war ended.

The woman said she doesn’t “need” recognition. “But I am frustrated that nobody mentions us,” she said. “Egyptian Roma women have also been raped here.”

Agushi, the Roma rights activist, said rape survivors from minority communities barely feature in public discourse surrounding the war and wartime sexual violence; those raped after the official cessation of hostilities are doubly discriminated against.

“They are even more marginalised, and those who were victims of sexual violence after June 20, 1999, are particularly discriminated against because they are not legally recognised and remain in the shadows.”

Campaign of terror

World.title: Land Registry Cyberattack Exposes Holes in Romania’s Digital Defences
World.content:
Photo illustration: EPA/SASCHA STEINBACH

This summer was supposed to mark an important milestone for Stefania Guga. By the end of July, the 32-year-old had hoped to buy a two-room apartment in a newly built complex on the outskirts of Bucharest, fulfilling her ambition of becoming a homeowner, Guga told BIRN.

“I wanted to finalise the transaction before August 1 to avoid paying the higher VAT rate. But for more than a week now, everything has been at a standstill, and I still don’t know whether I’ll make the deadline. It’s no longer up to me – the problem lies with Romanian state institutions,” she said.

Guga’s plans have been disrupted by a cyberattack on July 14 targeting the IT infrastructure of Romania’s National Agency for Cadastre and Land Registration, ANCPI, effectively freezing property registration services and real estate transactions.

For Guga, the timing could hardly be worse. Under the government’s latest fiscal package, the VAT rate for newly built homes will rise from 9 to 21 per cent on August 1.

If she misses the deadline, it will significantly raise the overall cost of her apartment, adding thousands of euros to the price.

The ANCPI has described the cyberattack as “the most serious technical incident in the institution’s history”.

It crippled the agency’s digital systems, disrupting online land registry services, official email communications and apps used daily by notaries, lawyers, cadastral surveyors and ANCPI staff.

Authorities were left unable to register new property transactions, process pending requests, or issue essential land registry documents, bringing much of Romania’s real estate market to a standstill.

Just one day after the agency’s systems were compromised, some of the stolen data appeared for sale on a well-known hacking forum.

The leaked files included employee login credentials, internal documents and technical information about the agency’s IT infrastructure, raising concerns that the attackers had gained deep access to critical systems.

Experts say that, although the attack did not look particularly sophisticated from a technical standpoint, its consequences are serious.

“This is arguably the most severe cybersecurity incident in Romania’s relatively short history of the digitalisation of public administration,” said cybersecurity expert Andrei Avadanei.

“It affects data belonging to infrastructure classified as critical national infrastructure, including records covering every property in the country.

“It has disrupted essential public services and directly affects hundreds of thousands of citizens whose property transactions and administrative procedures are now vulnerable,” he added.

Avadanei also said the incident could likely have been prevented if the ANCPI had invested more consistently in cybersecurity and implemented stronger preventive measures.

The agency’s spending priorities appear to reinforce that criticism.

According to media reports, ANCPI has invested around 710 million lei, or about 135 million euros, in digitalisation over the past two decades. But only about 0.2 per cent of that, roughly 305,000 euros, was allocated to cybersecurity.

Experts say that figure is woefully inadequate given the sensitivity of the data the agency manages and its role in operating one of the country’s most critical public databases.

Officials have sought to reassure the public and limit the fallout from the cyberattack. In a statement, ANCPI said the incident “did not compromise the agency’s technical or legal databases” and stressed that core land registry records were neither altered nor destroyed.

The agency also said it has begun migrating its applications to the Romanian Government Cloud, a process expected to be completed on Wednesday. Once the migration is finished, specialists will carry out comprehensive integrity checks before services are gradually restored.

At the same time, the incident has exposed the fragility of Romania’s public digital infrastructure at a time when the country is facing a sustained wave of cyber threats linked to the broader security environment created by Russia’s invasion of neighbouring Ukraine.

Romanian authorities and cybersecurity experts have repeatedly warned that government institutions, critical infrastructure and public databases have become attractive targets for hostile cyber actors.

“This incident should serve as a wake-up call for the entire public administration,” interim Digitalisation Minister Irineu Darau said in a televised interview.

Darau acknowledged that the digitalisation of Romania’s public institutions has been carried out in a fragmented way, without a coherent national strategy or common security standards.

“It is time to make digital transformation and cybersecurity genuine national priorities,” he said.

“That also means offering better salaries to cybersecurity professionals working in the public sector so that state institutions can attract and retain the expertise needed to protect critical systems,” he concluded.

World.title: Tests Show Faeces Contaminated North Macedonia Town’s Water Supply
World.content:
The centre of Gostivar, North Macedonia. Photo: Fazlijah/Wikimedia Commons.

Lab tests have confirmed the presence of faecal contamination in the drinking water supplied to the western North Macedonian town of Gostivar, local prosecutors announced on Tuesday.

The findings, disclosed by the Gostivar Basic Prosecutor’s Office, appear to prove that the town’s water supply is linked to an epidemic of gastrointestinal illness that has overwhelmed local health services since last week.

On Monday, police detained the head of the local public water utility, Artana Asani, and two other managers over the outbreak that has made more than 3,000 people sick so far.

The Gostivar Prosecutor’s Office said three officials are suspected of committing “serious crimes against the environment and nature through the pollution of drinking water.

“The suspects, acting together in their official capacities … made the drinking water in the overflow chamber of the system supplying Gostivar municipality and several surrounding villages unusable by introducing a harmful substance into it,” the Prosecution said.

The probe suspects the water supply became contaminated when the water company, in a presumed attempt to increase the water supply last month, connected additional pumps to the existing system that drew in water from an unhealthy surface-level source.

According to the prosecution, laboratory tests conducted by the Institute of Public Health detected faecal contamination in the water supply, including extremely high concentrations of coliform bacteria and the presence of Escherichia coli (E. coli), indicating contamination with human or animal faecal matter and rendering the water unsafe to drink.

Before her arrest, water utility head Asani last week insisted the outbreak of illness in the town was not caused by water but food poisoning. But authorities pinpointed drinking water as the most likely culprit, given the sheer scale of the outbreak.

The outbreak has sent more than 3,000 people to hospitals and clinics with symptoms including severe stomach pain, diarrhoea, vomiting and nausea, making it one of the largest recorded waterborne health incidents in North Macedonia in decades.

The Health Ministry has warned that the flow of new patients is not subsiding yet and is running at about 200 to 300 new patients per day.

Meanwhile, tap water in the town of roughly 80,000 people, some 65 kilometres west of the capital, Skopje, is unusable, and the municipal and state authorities have sent trucks with bottled water for residents’ use.

The Health Ministry on Monday said some of the contaminants found in the system are not easy to deal with, so the ban on drinking tap water will likely stay in place for some time.

The incident has triggered widespread public anger, with residents questioning how contamination on this scale could have gone undetected until thousands of people had already become ill.

Gostivar Mayor Valbon Limani on Monday denied any responsibility for the crisis himself, saying he had no role in the water company.

“I do not feel any moral responsibility because the public utility company Komunalec is a separate legal entity that manages and operates the water supply system. Otherwise, the citizens who know me are aware that, had the situation been different, I would certainly have been the first to resign,” Limani said.

World.title: Hungarian PM’s Presidential Gambit Fails as Polgar Declines Nomination
World.content:
“The responsibility is entirely mine,” Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar admitted on Monday night, after he had failed to convince the world’s greatest female chess player of all time, Judit Polgar, to accept the nomination to be the country’s next president.

“I don’t feel the strength to take on the historic responsibility, therefore I am unable to accept the invitation,” Polgar, 49, posted last night, ending a day of intense speculation in Hungary and abroad.

Nominating a grandmaster as Hungary’s next president was just the latest in a series of unconventional moves by the government headed by Magyar’s Tisza party. It was a hasty decision by a government that seems to be under constant time pressure to deliver on the numerous promises it made during the campaign for the April 12 election, which it won by a landslide.

“The selection of Hungary’s next president should not be rushed, Peter Magyar is acting as if there were no time for a meaningful public debate about the country’s next head of state,” the human rights watchdog Amnesty International said in a statement.

Tamas Sulyok was regarded as an ideological presidential appointee of former prime minister Viktor Orban. According to Sulyok’s critics, he stood by as the previous government weakened democratic institutions and undermined the rule of law. As a result, voters had lost confidence in him, Magyar argued during the campaign, and his removal would be an essential step in rebuilding democracy and the system of checks of balances in Hungary.

Sulyok refused to budge for weeks until a constitutional amendment was passed on July 13 by the Tisza-dominated parliament which, among other measures, term-limited MPs to 12 years, pensioned off constitutional court judges at 70 and, in a single sentence, terminated the president’s mandate with immediate effect. Sulyok announced on Saturday he would sign the constitutional amendment, “fulfilling my obligation under the Fundamental Law [Hungary’s constitution] after carefully weighing my legal options and my conscience”.

In a lengthy video posted on Facebook, the outgoing president lamented the “end of constitutionalism” and warned that the Tisza government posed a threat to Hungarian democracy. The president has a largely ceremonial role but can block some legislation and delay appointments.

Hungary’s parliament now has 30 days to elect a new head of state, who will be in office until a new constitution is drawn up and adopted, but no longer than five years.

Magyar had promised broad public consultation in choosing the next president, saying he wanted a person capable of uniting Hungary’s deeply polarised society and representing the country abroad. But on Sunday, only hours after Sulyok had stepped down, a group of Hungarian intellectuals, athletes and public figures – mainly critics of the former Fidesz government but also some more aligned with it – published an open letter on Facebook endorsing Polgar for the presidency.

Magyar replied in a Facebook post that he would discuss the matter on Monday with Polgar, who he saw as the most suitable candidate. Tisza’s parliamentary group leader Andrea Bujdoso also described Polgar as the party’s preferred candidate for the presidency.

Some sensed a stitch-up after evidence emerged showing Magyar meeting with Polgar two weeks earlier at the US embassy’s Fourth of July reception in Budapest, where she quickly defeated the prime minister in a chess match. It remains unclear whether they discussed a possible political role before or after the event.

Polgar and her two older sisters were born into a Hungarian Jewish family and educated by their father, Laszlo Polgar, who developed an unconventional method aimed at proving that geniuses are made rather than born. The sisters did not attend school in Communist Hungary but instead spent eight to ten hours a day playing chess. The family travelled extensively around the world at a time when few Hungarians enjoyed such opportunities.

Polgar won her first championship at the age of nine and became the world’s highest-ranked female player at just 12. Throughout her career she played in the men’s league, and defeated several world champions, including Garry Kasparov and Anatoly Karpov. “They thought I was this little girl with a cute ponytail, but I wasn’t that cute when I played,” she once said in an interview.

At the age of 15, she became the youngest grandmaster in history at the time, breaking Bobby Fischer’s longstanding record. A documentary of her life, Queen of Chess, was released earlier this year and became an instant hit on Netflix. Since retiring from competitive chess in 2014, Polgar has focused on educational initiatives and promoting chess among children. She is married to a veterinarian, has two children, and lives in Budapest.

Her potential nomination prompted a variety of reactions. Critics argued that Polgar has never shown any interest in politics and was never publicly critical of Orban’s government. Supporters argued it is an advantage that she has never been affiliated with any political party or movement, but is admired across the political spectrum as one of Hungary’s most accomplished and internationally respected public figures.

But most criticism was focused on the speed with which Tisza tried to rush through the nomination process, arguing that there had been little genuine public consultation despite the lack of urgency.

Fidesz politicians maintain that whoever is elected under the current circumstances will lack democratic legitimacy because of the manner in which the previous president was removed.

World.title: It’s Time NATO Stopped Ignoring Bosnia’s Ammunition Industry
World.content:
When NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte warned Allied defense ministers that Russia produces in three months what the entire Alliance produces in a year, Europe quickly moved.

Germany’s Rheinmetall accelerated artillery production across two countries. The US Army drove toward 100,000 155mm shells per month. Billions of euros poured into the EU’s Act in Support of Ammunition Production. Summits convened. A strategy for Industry-NATO Cooperation was adopted. Commitments were signed.

What largely escaped notice in all those urgent conversations was a pair of factories in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the only country currently in NATO’s Membership Action Plan.

Pretis d.d., located in Vogosca, near Sarajevo, and Binas d.d., in Bugojno, have operated quietly for decades, largely overlooked by NATO. Pretis is among the few facilities in Europe producing 155mm artillery shells to full NATO standards – the exact caliber at the center of the Alliance’s ammunition crisis.

World.title: Will Smith Visits Rimac Campus Near Zagreb
World.content:
July the 22nd, 2026 – Hollywood star Will Smith paid a visit to Rimac Campus near Zagreb this week, where he was treated to something special indeed.

The well known actor was given a behind-the-scenes look at one of Croatia’s most celebrated technology companies, and judging by his reaction, he was thoroughly impressed! Poslovni reports that the Oscar-winning actor toured the state-of-the-art headquarters of Rimac Technology, meeting founder and CEO Mate Rimac while exploring the cutting-edge engineering and production facilities that have helped place Croatia firmly on the global automotive map.

During the visit, Smith experienced several of Rimac’s innovations firsthand, including the company’s world-renowned electric hypercars. Videos shared from the visit captured the actor reacting with visible excitement, laughing, shouting in amazement and expressing disbelief at the performance and technology on display. According to those present, Smith was particularly impressed by the speed, engineering and innovation that have become synonymous with the Rimac name.

putting croatian innovation on stage

Founded by Mate Rimac back in 2009, the company has grown from a small garage startup into one of the world’s leading developers of high-performance electric vehicle technology. Today, Rimac supplies advanced battery systems, electric powertrains and software to some of the biggest names in the automotive industry, while its Nevera hypercar has repeatedly broken global performance records. The Rimac Campus, located in Kerestinec on the outskirts of Zagreb, has become a symbol of Croatia’s growing reputation as a centre for advanced engineering and innovation.

Smith’s visit shines another international spotlight on one of Croatia’s biggest business success stories. Over the past few years, the company has welcomed politicians, investors, automotive executives and celebrities eager to see firsthand how a Croatian startup evolved into a global technology powerhouse. The visit also serves as another reminder that Croatia’s international reputation is increasingly being shaped not only by tourism, but also by world-class innovation and high-tech manufacturing.

more than just fast cars…

While Rimac’s electric hypercars often capture the headlines, the company has become equally important as a technology partner for the wider automotive industry. Its expertise in battery systems, electric drivetrains and vehicle software is helping shape the next generation of electric mobility, with technologies developed in Croatia finding their way into vehicles produced around the world. For Will Smith, the visit offered a glimpse into the future of transportation. For Croatia, it was another high-profile endorsement of a company that continues to demonstrate the country’s ability to compete at the highest possible levels of global technology.

World.title: Largest Croatian Cave System Was Discovered by Chance
World.content:
July the 22nd, 2026 – The largest Croatian cave system was discovered entirely by chance, and it revealed fascinating evidence of a 20,000 year old hunter…

The largest Croatian cave, located in beautiful Ogulin, is widely considered to be the country’s most remarkable archaeological and natural treasure. More interestingly still, it owes its entire discovery to pure chance.

The Đula-Medvedica Cave System, the largest cave complex in all of Croatia, was uncovered unexpectedly during railway construction back during the early 20th century. Putni kofer writes that what initially began as an ambitious but otherwise normal engineering project soon turned into one of the country’s most significant archaeological discoveries in history, revealing evidence of human life dating back tens of thousands of years.

the best discoveries usually happen by accident…

What eventually turned out to be the largest Croatian cave system ever discovered came to light while workers were building the railway through Ogulin, exposing a vast underground network hidden deep beneath the landscape. Subsequent exploration revealed kilometres upon kilometres of interconnected passages, underground chambers and various waterways, making it the largest known cave complex in Croatia and an important site for both speleologists and scientists.

a present-day window into prehistoric croatia

Among the cave’s most extraordinary discoveries was the bone of a prehistoric hunter estimated to be around 20,000 years old. Archaeologists also uncovered numerous traces of Ice Age human activity, confirming that the cave provided shelter to people living in the region during the last Ice Age. The finds have helped researchers better understand how prehistoric communities survived in what is now Croatia during one of Europe’s harshest climatic periods.

Beyond its archaeological importance, the deep Đula-Medvedica Cave System is renowned for its geological features. The labyrinth of passages includes underground rivers, enormous chambers, dramatic rock formations and unique ecosystems that support species specially adapted to life in complete darkness. Because of its scientific value and fragile environment, much of the cave remains protected and is accessible only to researchers and experienced cavers.

ogulin’s subterranean attraction

While many visitors know Ogulin as the hometown of Croatian fairy-tale writer Ivana Brlić-Mažuranić, this picturesque but often bypassed area is also home to one of Croatia’s most fascinating karst landscapes. The rich cave system lies beneath a region shaped by many sinking rivers and limestone formations that have been carved over millions of years, creating an extraordinary underground world hidden in depths, far beneath the town.

the discovery was a turning point for croatian archaeology

Over a century has now passed since its accidental discovery, and yet the Đula-Medvedica Cave System continues to provide valuable insights into Croatia’s natural and human history. From prehistoric hunter-gatherer human remains to utterly spectacular geological formations, this incredible cave stands as an eternal reminder that some of the country’s greatest discoveries have happened entirely by accident, lying patiently in wait, deep beneath the surface, until the right moment revealed them to the world.

World.title: Croatian Retailers Push Back Against Night-Time Alcohol Sales Ban
World.content:
July the 22nd, 2026 – Croatian retailers are strongly pushing back against the recently introduced night-time alcohol sales ban which they claim makes them feel invisible.

As Index reports, Croatian retailers are loudly voicing growing concerns over new local restrictions banning night-time alcohol sales shops between 21:00 and 06:00. They are arguing that this recently introduced measure unfairly targets their businesses only, all while leaving bars, restaurants and nightclubs totally unaffected.

The debate follows Makarska’s decision to become the first Croatian city to prohibit alcohol sales in retail stores between 21:00 and 06:00. The measure was introduced to tackle late-night noise, public disorder and anti-social behaviour during the busy summer season, with other coastal cities, including Split, actively considering similar rules.

“why is it all on us?” ask shop owners and managers

The Association of Small Retailers operating within the boundaries of Split-Dalmatia County are claiming that the new restrictions place neighbourhood shops, kiosks and convenience stores at a significant disadvantage. Its secretary, Boris Listeš, argues that small retailers weren’t even consulted before these decisions were made and that they will suffer the greatest financial impact because many rely heavily on evening sales during the tourist season. He says larger supermarkets, which generally close their doors at around 21:00 or 22:00, will barely notice the change, while cafés, restaurants and clubs will continue serving alcohol without any of these restrictions.

“these rules should apply to everyone”

Retailers insist that if authorities believe limiting alcohol availability will improve public order, the restrictions should apply equally across all businesses selling alcohol. They argue that tourists determined to drink late into the night will simply buy alcohol before the ban begins or continue consuming it in hospitality venues, meaning the new rules are unlikely to achieve their intended effect while disproportionately hurting small family-run businesses.

Rather than introducing ill-thought-out blanket bans, retailers say authorities should focus on enforcing existing public order regulations. They argue that police and municipal wardens already know the locations where disturbances regularly occur and that stronger enforcement against disruptive behaviour would be more effective than restricting legal businesses throughout an entire city. According to the association, the new measures risk penalising responsible retailers instead of addressing the individuals causing problems.

other cities are watching how the situation unfolds in makarska…

Makarska may have been the first to adopt the night-time retail alcohol ban, but it’s highly unlikely to be the last. Split is currently considering introducing similar rules, while other coastal cities are weighing whether such restrictions are necessary in their own communities. At the same time, some destinations, including Supetar and Trogir, have indicated they do not currently plan to follow Makarska’s example. As this heated debate continues, Croatia faces a broader question: how to balance the needs of residents seeking quieter summer nights with those of small businesses that depend on the tourism season for a large share of their annual income.

World.title: Domestic Flights Return to Osijek, Reconnecting Eastern Croatia With the Coast
World.content:
July the 22nd, 2026 – Domestic flights have returned to Osijek, connecting eastern Croatia with the coast once again with Trade Air.

The return of these routes strengthens domestic connectivity during the busy main summer season and provides a faster alternative for both tourists and business travellers heading to Croatia’s most popular coastal destinations.

bridging the gap between eastern croatia and the coast

As Dalmatinski portal reports, these seasonal domestic flights once again link Osijek Airport with several destinations on the Adriatic, significantly reducing travel times between Croatia’s eastern and southern regions. For many travellers, the flights offer an attractive alternative to driving for several hours or making multiple transfers by rail or bus, particularly during the height of the summer holiday season.

Although Croatia is remarkably well connected internationally during the summer months, domestic air links have traditionally been more limited. The renewed services aim to improve connections between Slavonia and the coast, making it easier for residents, tourists and business travellers to move around the country while supporting regional tourism and economic activity. Officials have long argued that stronger domestic transport links are essential for balancing tourism development and improving accessibility across Croatia’s regions.

The flights are expected to benefit not only holidaymakers but also local businesses, allowing visitors to combine different parts of Croatia within a single trip. Instead of entering the country through Zagreb, international visitors can more easily explore both Slavonia and Dalmatia, helping spread tourism beyond the traditional coastal hotspots. The renewed connections also provide residents of eastern Croatia with quicker access to the Adriatic during the peak holiday season.

strengthening croatia’s domestic air network

As Croatia continues investing in transport infrastructure, from new rail projects to airport upgrades, the return of seasonal domestic flights represents another step towards improving nationwide connectivity. For travellers looking to swap a lengthy drive for a short flight, the renewed Osijek routes offer a convenient way to travel between the country’s eastern plains and its Adriatic coastline, reinforcing links between two of Croatia’s most distinctive regions.

World.title: Croatian Clubs Discover Potential European Draws
World.content:
Croatia’s European hopefuls found out their possible third qualifying round opponents on Monday, with draws confirmed across the Europa League, Champions League, and Conference League paths.

Hajduk could face Salzburg

Should Hajduk get past Cypriot side Pafos in the second qualifying round of the Europa League, their reward will be a third-round clash with Austria’s Salzburg. Hajduk host Pafos in the first leg on Thursday in Split, with the return fixture in Cyprus the following Thursday. Should they progress, Hajduk would again have home advantage in the first leg of the third round, with the second leg to follow in Salzburg. Third qualifying round ties are scheduled for August 6 and 13.

Should Hajduk instead lose against Pafos, they would drop into the Conference League third qualifying round, where they’d face the winner of the tie between Georgia’s Dinamo Tbilisi and Lithuania’s Žalgiris, with the first leg played away from home.

Dinamo await Vikingur or Hapoel

Champions Dinamo Zagreb have also learned their potential path forward. Should they be eliminated by Switzerland’s Thun in the Champions League second qualifying round, Dinamo would drop into the Europa League third qualifying round to face either Iceland’s Vikingur or Israel’s Hapoel Beer Sheva.

Should Dinamo instead get past Thun and reach the Champions League third qualifying round itself, Mario Kovačević’s side would face the winner of the tie between Faroese side Klaksvik and Lithuania’s Kauno Žalgiris, coached by Željko Sopić. First legs in that round are set for August 4/5, with second legs on August 11.

UEFA has scrapped the previous system of forming subgroups ahead of the “champions’ path” draw this season, meaning Dinamo faced a considerably wider pool of possible opponents than in previous years.

Before turning their attention to the third qualifying round, Dinamo first face Thun in the first leg of the second qualifying round on Tuesday in Switzerland, kicking off at 8 pm, with the return leg set for Tuesday, July 28.

Rijeka and Varaždin could head to Iceland

Rijeka and Varaždin also discovered their potential third qualifying round opponents in the Conference League on Monday. Rijeka, if they eliminate Ireland’s Derry City in the second round, would face the winner of the tie between Iceland’s Stjarnan and Finland’s Ilves. Varaždin, if they see off Czech side Jablonec, would take on the winner between Latvia’s RFS and Iceland’s Vestri.

Third qualifying round fixtures in the Conference League are scheduled for August 6 and 13.
