World.content:
Tourist arrivals in Armenia reach record high

Armenia‘s tourism sector has reported a new record. The country welcomed 1.042 million tourists in the first half of 2026. According to Sona Hovhannisyan, head of the International Cooperation Department, the number of tourists who visited Armenia between January and June was 14.8% higher than during the same period last year.

Although this is the highest figure on record, the Tourism Committee expects to break the record again by the end of the year. Officials expect the number of tourists to surpass last year’s total of 2.2 million visitors.

Main sources of tourist arrivals

According to the Tourism Committee, visitors from Russia, Georgia and Iran have made up the largest share of tourists travelling to Armenia for many years. As of June this year, that pattern had not changed. The figures are as follows:

Around 40% of all visitors came from Russia,

15% from Georgia,

8% from Iran.

Compared with the three leading source markets, visitor numbers from other countries remain relatively low. According to Sona Hovhannisyan, head of the International Cooperation Department, several factors explain why tourists from these countries account for the largest share of arrivals:

“Iran and Georgia are Armenia’s closest neighbours, while Armenia has historical ties with Russia. It is also important that people can travel to Armenia from these countries relatively quickly. The presence of Armenian diaspora communities in these countries also plays a role.”

Hovhannisyan said countries with direct flights to Armenia, as well as those whose citizens benefit from simplified visa rules, have seen growing numbers of visitors. She cited China as an example, saying the sharp increase in Chinese tourists followed the launch of direct flights between Urumqi and Yerevan, along with the introduction of a visa-free regime.

Hovhannisyan also explained what has driven growth from other countries:

“The significant increase in the number of tourists from Italy is due to the expansion of flights between our countries. The same factor has influenced arrivals from Germany, where visitor numbers had previously declined. The launch of a direct flight from Kazakhstan has also boosted tourist flows.”

Armenia has also recently become a more popular destination for tourists from Spain, the Czech Republic, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom.

Hovhannisyan said visitor numbers from those countries remain well below the figures for Russia. However, she added that the recent launch of direct flights between London and Yerevan gives reason for optimism.

“The peak tourism season is gradually getting longer”

Armenia usually sees the highest number of tourist arrivals during the summer and in September and October. Activity typically begins to slow towards the end of November. According to Hovhannisyan, however, the peak season is gradually becoming longer. She said more tourists are now choosing to visit the country during the winter months.

“It is encouraging to see growing activity during the winter as well. The government is taking steps to support this trend. If this January’s record figures are sustained and become the norm, we can expect strong tourism for almost the entire year.”

Trade fairs and other PR efforts to attract tourists

The Tourism Committee is running a number of programmes to make Armenia a more attractive destination on the international tourism market.

According to Diana Karapetyan, head of the Marketing Department, Armenia showcased national pavilions at major tourism fairs in Spain, Germany, Romania and Russia this year.

“By the end of the year, we plan to take part in several more international events. Armenian tourism companies attending these exhibitions present highly attractive offers. They promote our country’s cultural events, cuisine and tourist attractions. They also offer tastings, distribute brochures and show promotional videos.”

The committee also works with international media outlets, PR agencies, well-known bloggers and influencers. It organises familiarisation trips to Armenia and runs promotional campaigns. Karapetyan said these efforts have led to more frequent coverage of Armenia in the international media, with growing attention to its tourism appeal and potential.

“Armenia has established itself on the global tourism market as a safe and reliable destination,” she said.

Tourist arrivals in Armenia reach record high

World.title: Aleksandre Kartozia to receive accreditation as Georgia’s ambassador to Germany
World.content:
Accreditation of Georgia’s ambassador to Germany

Aleksandre Kartozia, who was appointed Georgia‘s ambassador to Germany in September last year, is set to present his credentials to German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier on 23 July.

The information was published on the official website of the German president.

The website lists the ambassadorial accreditation ceremonies scheduled for 23 July. Seven ambassadors are due to present their credentials, with Kartozia first on the programme. According to the schedule, his accreditation ceremony is set to begin at 10:30.

Ambassadors from Chile, Honduras, Nigeria, Mauritania, Madagascar and the Vatican’s Apostolic Nuncio are also scheduled to be accredited on the same day.

Why is the accreditation important?

Aleksandre Kartozia was appointed Georgia’s ambassador to Germany in September last year, succeeding Levan Izoria, who had served in the post since 2020.

Before an ambassador can officially take up their duties in Germany, they must present their credentials to the country’s president. Only after this ceremony are they formally accredited and able to carry out the full responsibilities of the role. Until now, Kartozia had been awaiting an invitation to present his credentials.

Letters of credence are official documents by which one head of state appoints a diplomat as their representative to another country.

The documents identify the appointed diplomat and their diplomatic rank. They also contain a formal request from the sending head of state to the receiving head of state to “give credence” to everything the diplomat says or does on behalf of their country.

The accreditation also carries added political significance given the strained relationship between Georgia and Germany.

Relations between Tbilisi and Berlin have been tense over the past two years. Senior Georgian officials have repeatedly criticised Germany’s ambassador to Georgia, Peter Fischer, while Germany has voiced concern over developments in Georgia.

There have also been several occasions when the German ambassador was summoned by the Georgian authorities.

On 31 December 2024, Germany imposed entry bans on nine people it said were responsible for violence against protesters and opposition figures in Georgia.

Who is Aleksandre Kartozia?

Aleksandre Kartozia served as Georgia’s education minister from 1998 to 2004 under President Eduard Shevardnadze.

He has worked as a researcher and taught courses and seminars at leading universities in Berlin, Frankfurt and Bremen. In 2022, he was awarded the Order of Merit of the Federal Republic of Germany.

During his tenure as education minister, Kartozia faced corruption allegations. In 2002, Givi Targamadze, a member of Georgia’s Anti-Corruption Council, publicly accused him of corruption. In 2004, prosecutors charged Kartozia and his deputy, Vladimir Sanadze, with abuse of office and the embezzlement of public funds.

Accreditation of Georgia’s ambassador to Germany

World.title: China demands Australia stop 'inciting confrontation' over South China Sea
World.content:
China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs has demanded Australia stop "exaggerating tensions and inciting confrontation" over the South China Sea after Penny Wong warned Beijing against "destabilising" conduct in the region.

The comments came after China and the Philippines blamed one another for a physical confrontation between the China Coast Guard and the Philippine Navy in the South China Sea on Monday.

On Wednesday Senator Wong said Australia was concerned about "aggression" and "destabilising conduct" and that countries had a "choice to make" about how to respond.

When asked about Senator Wong's comments, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said that "whenever there is the slightest disturbance at sea … the same small handful of countries rush to the forefront to oppose China without regard for the facts".

"China urges the relevant countries to stop exaggerating tensions and inciting confrontation, and to genuinely respect the efforts made by regional countries to maintain peace and stability in the South China Sea," Mr Lin said.

China says Australia is inciting confrontation amid tension over the launching of a missile that landed in the intended area. (CCTV)

The spat comes against the backdrop of an intense bout of regional diplomacy in the Philippines, which is hosting dozens of foreign ministers and senior officials for the annual ASEAN meeting in Manila.

The issue of China's behaviour loomed large ahead of the meeting, and ASEAN foreign ministers are eager to make progress on a South China Sea code of conduct that they hope will be finalised by the end of the year.

But the physical confrontation, in which a Filipino sailor was struck on the head with a baton, threw the issue back into the spotlight.

At a press conference, local journalists asked Senator Wong about the incident, as well as a Chinese missile test and rising tensions in the region.

"We are concerned about some of the aggression we are seeing, we are concerned about some of the destabilising conduct we are seeing," the foreign minister said.

"The countries of the region have a choice to make about how we all respond to that and Australia believes we should respond to that by working for peace and stability … [and] by continuing to call for and encouraging compliance with observation of international law and of safe and professional conduct at sea and in the air."

Senator Wong met with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi on Tuesday night and raised Australia's concerns over China's missile test earlier this month.

China fired a dummy warhead from a nuclear-powered submarine. It landed in the Pacific, around the exclusive economic zone of Tuvalu.

Minister to use ASEAN as platform

The verbal stoush comes as the foreign minister prepares to deliver a sometimes-grim speech on the sidelines of the ASEAN Foreign Ministers' Meeting on Thursday, where she will urge for freedom of navigation to be protected and warn the region that no "single power" should be able to "set the terms of our future".

Senator Wong is expected to use the address to make it clear that critical waterways like the Strait of Hormuz must remain toll-free.

"The Strait of Hormuz shows what we in this region have always understood … that people suffer when a strait is weaponised," she will say.

She will once again take aim at China over its recent ballistic missile test, saying it "came with too little information and notification, particularly to the Philippines — which the missile flew over — and Pacific nations, near where the missile landed".

"It comes in the context of China's rapid military build-up, including of its nuclear arsenal, without the transparency or reassurance the region expects," she will say.

"Which is why Australia has described the test as provocative and destabilising."

She is also set to urge other countries in the region to "resist the urge to turn inwards" and "the trend away from rules to use of power" in the face of global strategic ruptures and China's growing might.

"It demands we invest in our region, in our relationships, in the rules — in our collective resilience — before it is too late," she will warn.

"Before the rules are so diminished that they are no longer recognisable.

"Before crisis closes the door on cooperation."

While she does not mention the most recent South China Sea confrontation in her speech, she will also vow to continue "registering our concerns about China's vessels engaging in destabilising and dangerous conduct".

Philippines says navy personnel injured

China's Foreign Ministry has again blamed the Philippines for the physical altercation, in which the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) said one of its navy personnel was injured.

Loading...

Footage of the incident shows the China Coast Guard and Philippine Navy briefly engaging each other from inflatable boats.

The incident took place at the Second Thomas Shoal, where the Philippines has a military outpost on a grounded ship.

"China has already made clear its solemn position regarding the malicious attacks by Philippine personnel against Chinese law enforcement officers," Mr Lin said.

For its part, AFP said China's Coast Guard "reacted violently and aggressively".

The Second Thomas Shoal is within the Philippines' exclusive economic zone, which China claims as its own, along with much of the South China Sea.

China's nine-dash line claim was rejected by a tribunal at The Hague a decade ago, but China disputes the ruling.

Philippine Foreign Minister Theresa Lazaro raised the incident during talks with Mr Wang on Wednesday.

China reminds world of growing military power This latest military test demonstrates China's growing willingness to use its military strength to send a warning to the Pacific: that Beijing now has the military and nuclear means to assert its dominance in the region.

"I reiterated our strong protest over the unacceptable actions against Filipino personnel near Ayungin Shoal," Ms Lazaro said on social media.

The US State Department in a statement said it condemned "China's dangerous and aggressive actions against Philippine navy personnel".

"China's troubling pattern of provocation against lawful Philippine maritime operations undermines regional peace and stability and directly contradicts China's repeated commitments to resolve disputes peacefully," the statement said.

In a statement, the European Union delegation to the Philippines expressed "its deep concern over the steady increase of tensions and dangerous incidents in the South China Sea".

World.title: Government reveals proposed plans for new aquatic centre for 2032 Games
World.content:
The state government has unveiled fresh renders of the new National Aquatic Centre in Brisbane as it locks in a trio of architectural firms to design the marquee 2032 Olympics venue.

The Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority (GIICA) will take over Centenary Pool at Spring Hill on September 1, when early works will begin on site.

The state has chosen three firms to design the centre: ARM Architecture, NH Architecture and Queensland-based Arkhefield.

The proposed design features a wave-shaped roof.

The Centenary Pool at Spring Hill is set to close on August 31. (ABC News)

Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie will make the announcement tomorrow, six years out from the start of the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games in Brisbane.

"This design trio will develop an iconic new home for high-performance aquatic athletes, as well as a legacy for community sport," Mr Bleijie said.

Five years since Brisbane secured the Olympics Broken promises and scarcely broken ground. Five years since Brisbane secured the 2032 Olympic Games, this is the state of play.

"This isn't just a venue for a few weeks in 2032.

"It's a lasting investment in Queensland's future that will support community sport, high-performance athletes and keeping us cool for generations to come."

NH Architecture played a role in the redevelopment of Melbourne Park, while ARM Architecture delivered the RAC Arena in Perth.

The centre is expected to have up to 25,000 seats during the Games, with a legacy capacity of 8,000 seats.

Mr Bleijie was asked today whether the capacity could be scaled back to save costs, but he did not directly answer the question.

He insisted, though, the $7.1 billion funding envelope for Games infrastructure would not change.

Kids lining up to leap off a high dive platform at Brisbane's Centenary Pool in 1966. (Supplied: Brisbane City Council)

"GIICA is leading the charge with respect to the delivery of those venues," Mr Bleijie said.

"What we said we were going to deliver was a National Aquatic Centre that will be the envy of the world.

"The best aquatic centre in the world at the moment is in Budapest, and they delivered an aquatic centre, and ours wants to be absolutely better than that."

Mr Bleijie also noted the government was going through a process with GIICA for all the venues.

"We did ask them to look at the costings, because when you appoint architects and designers, they have to do it within budget," the deputy premier added.

"Obviously GIICA has not released the results of the design phase and so forth … and we look forward to being briefed on that."

World.title: Details of allegations against Alan Jones emerge after judge decision
World.content:
Details of veteran broadcaster Alan Jones's alleged offending against six men can now be reported after a non-publication order was lifted by a judge.

Mr Jones, 85, is due to stand trial next month on 22 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching of six complainants, between 2003 and 2020.

He has pleaded not guilty to all charges.

Some detail of the allegations, revealed in pre-trial hearings in the Downing Centre Local Court in Sydney, had been subject to interim non-publication orders sought by Mr Jones's defence team.

Lawyers for Mr Jones argued media coverage of the high-profile case could sway complainants and witnesses, and even the judge himself, just weeks before the trial.

But Judge Glenn Walsh on Wednesday dismissed a request for a formal suppression order over the crown case statement and other pre-trial argument, declaring because it was a judge-only trial, the risk of media reporting was lower.

"There is no jury panel to be prejudiced," Judge Walsh declared.

It means some details of Mr Jones's alleged offences against six men, who cannot be identified, can be revealed.

The evidence expected to be considered at trial was outlined by the prosecution during arguments about whether to admit tendency and coincidence evidence, which is evidence used to suggest a person has tendency to act on a particular state of mind.

Judge Walsh ruled on Monday that tendency and coincidence evidence could be admitted in the trial, meaning the prosecution can argue Mr Jones displayed a pattern of behaviour in his alleged offending.

Details of the allegations were heard in pre-trial hearings in the Downing Centre Local Court. (ABC News: Jak Rowland)

"I am not persuaded I will use the evidence in a prejudicial way," he told the court on Monday.

The court heard the prosecution will argue Mr Jones has a "sexual interest in men particularly younger than himself" and a "tendency to act upon that interest".

During argument about tendency evidence, prosecutors outlined details of allegations which can now be reported with the dismissal of an application for a non-publication order.

Jones's alleged acts of indecent assault

One man, Complainant C, made allegations that Mr Jones kissed and touched him several times, including in the lift at Mr Jones's Macquarie Street apartment.

The court heard the prosecution will allege Mr Jones put his hand over the man's crotch while he was driving Mr Jones, and then approached and kissed him in the lift.

Prosecutors allege the man told Mr Jones "no, no" and moved his head to the side, while on other occasions, he allegedly told Mr Jones he had a throat or mouth illness to stop a kiss.

On another occasion, the man is expected to allege he felt Mr Jones's hand on his upper thigh and crotch area at a lunch in Sydney.

Mr Jones faces eight charges in relation to Complainant C.

Another nine charges relate to another man, Complainant J, who the court heard was a young man when Mr Jones first met him.

Mr Jones allegedly gave him a mobile phone, and asked him to come visit him at his apartment.

During the young man's first visit to the apartment, Mr Jones allegedly put his arms around him, gave him a "squeeze" and a "peck" on the mouth, and told him, "I love you mate".

Mr Jones's alleged offences were against six younger men. (ABC News: Ethan Rix)

Other charges relate to incidents in the following year, where Mr Jones allegedly touched Complainant J's penis under his clothes while he was in a car with Mr Jones, driving to his second residence at Fitzroy Falls, in the NSW Southern Highlands.

It is alleged while at the house, Mr Jones committed other acts of indecent assault, including masturbating his own penis while touching the complainant and kissing him.

It is alleged Mr Jones kissed another man, Complainant I, on the corner of the mouth at a public event, and then texted him, saying something to the effect of "I want to be kissing you all night long".

That man further alleges that sometime between 2018 and 2020, he was in Mr Jones's home, when Mr Jones allegedly kissed him, pushing his genitalia into the complainant's body.

Complainant A is alleged to have been touched on the backside and kissed by Mr Jones at the broadcaster's Fitzroy Falls home.

Prosecutors will tell the court the man recalled being shocked by the alleged incident.

Another man, Complainant H, has alleged Mr Jones sexually touched him without consent on the backside and back at an event.

Non-publication order dismissed

Mr Jones's defence lawyers argued against the tendency evidence being admitted, saying it did not have significant probative value.

In deciding to dismiss the application for a non-publication order, Judge Walsh said he was not convinced reporting of pre-trial arguments would impede the course of justice.

"No material presented show that any media reporting to date has not been fair and accurate," he said.

The former 2GB and 2UE breakfast radio host is alleged to have committed the offences against the men during the time he worked in radio.

An investigation into the alleged offending, and his subsequent arrest in 2024, happened following a series of stories published in the Sydney Morning Herald, which made allegations against Mr Jones.

Mr Jones has always maintained his innocence.

He has not appeared in court for pre-trial hearings.

World.title: Doctor reveals injuries of woman allegedly sexually assaulted by Yung Filly
World.content:
WARNING: This story contains details some readers may find distressing, including descriptions of alleged sexual assault.

Graphic photographs of injuries allegedly inflicted by an internationally renowned YouTube star on an infatuated fan in his hotel room after a concert have been shown to a jury at his sexual assault trial in a Perth court.

Andres Felipe Valencia Barrientos, known to his millions of fans as Yung Filly, is on trial in the Perth District Court, accused of the brutal rape and assault of a 20-year-old woman at the Intercontinental Hotel in Perth's CBD in September 2024.

The 30-year-old rapper had been in Perth performing at Bar1, a waterfront venue in Perth's northern suburbs, and after the show had taken the young woman back to his hotel.

The pair had consensual sex in his room at the Intercontinental, before he allegedly violently raped her and repeatedly assaulted her, including biting and slapping her on the face, neck and breasts, strangling her, spitting in her mouth and forcing her to perform oral sex.

Andres Felipe Valencia Barrientos's social media profiles have garnered millions of followers. (ABC News: David Weber)

Mr Barrientos denies all the charges against him, which include sexual penetration without consent, impeding a person's breathing and assault.

Today the court heard evidence from sexual assault specialist Geraldine Hoy, who examined the young woman at the Sexual Assault Resource Centre two days after her alleged ordeal.

Multiple bruises

Dr Hoy took a series of close-up photographs of the 20-year-old's face, neck and breasts that were shown to the jury, depicting multiple large bruises and swellings.

The 21 photos included what Dr Hoy described as a "green purply" bruise on her neck, a linear bruise on her neck and a "large … yellow bruise just above the right areola area of the breast".

Court hears Yung Filly choked, sexually assaulted young fan A Perth court hears disturbing details of the YouTube personality's alleged sexual assault of a young woman who had a "celebrity crush" on him.

Nearby on the same breast was another bruise measuring 4 centimetres x 8 centimetres, as well as a bruise that Dr Hoy described as yellow in colour.

Describing the photos in detail as they were displayed in court, Dr Hoy said the bruises on her face included two linear red swollen bruises on her right cheek, and bruising on the left side of her face that extended to her neck.

Dr Hoy said some of the bruising and swelling on the left side of the 20-year-old's neck could have been caused by obstructing the jugular vein, a form of strangulation.

Earlier the trial heard the 20-year-old woman had a "celebrity crush" on Mr Barrientos and had spoken of him as "her future husband".

She had worn her "lucky" white top to the gig in the hope of gaining access to the VIP area of the venue to get close to him, the court heard, which she was ultimately able to do late in the evening, before leaving with the rapper and his entourage in a van, back to his hotel.

The trial continues.

World.title: Jail for acccountant who gambled away $878,000 stolen from IGA
World.content:
An accountant for a network of IGA supermarkets in New South Wales has been jailed for defrauding $878,000.

Narelle Labuts, 61, worked with the Singh Group, which owns 10 IGA stores in the Hunter Valley.

She was sacked in 2021 after a bank flagged an unusual transaction.

Labuts stole the company's money by using white font on 522 transactions to hide her misconduct over a four-year period, the Newcastle District Court heard.

In October 2024, police charged her with obtaining financial advantage by deception and making a false document to obtain a financial advantage.

Labuts pleaded guilty at the end of last year.

Today she was sentenced to three and a half years in prison with a two-year non-parole period.

Judge Tim Gartelmann SC said what began as an opportunistic crime spiralled into something "that required significant planning and organising".

"The sentences for fraud offences must deter others to commit them," he said.

" They are easy to commit and hard to detect. "

Narelle Labuts was sacked after an irregular transaction was flagged. (Facebook)

The court heard Labuts had only returned a fraction of the stolen money, repaying $3,500 while the IGA network clawed back a further $9,000 by refusing to pay her entitlements.

At the sentencing hearing Labuts said she was addicted to gambling and that 90 per cent of the embezzled funds had gone into poker machines.

When the Crown asked her what happened to the remaining $80,000 that had not been gambled, she said "to be honest, I couldn't tell you".

Labuts said she knew that what she was doing was wrong thing but was "praying for a big win to return it all back".

"The house always wins, so it never eventuated," she said tearfully.

Labuts said she was "so incredibly sorry" and acknowledged she had "destroyed the trust [her employer] put in me".

Narelle Labuts said she gambled most of the money. (ABC Newcastle: Alex Turner-Cohen)

The court heard she has since worked as a bookkeeper at a transport and a concreting company, but did not disclose why her employment at the IGA network came to an abrupt end.

She said she would "probably" tell future employers about the conviction because it was now common knowledge.

Defence barrister Stephen Hopper emphasised that Labuts was addressing her gambling addiction and had been getting counselling since June 2022.

Labuts disagreed with a suggestion from the Crown that she only sought help for her gambling problem because she had been caught.

She will be eligible for parole in July 2028.

World.title: Meet the Australian multi-millionaire pardoned by Trump
World.content:
Chris Wade has been unsuccessfully sued by Apple, arrested by the Secret Service and summoned to the White House to troubleshoot with Elon Musk and Donald Trump.

He is probably the most successful Australian entrepreneur you've never heard of, and is certainly the only Australian tech executive to be pardoned by the current US president.

Despite decades spent in the US that took him from convicted hacker to the White House, he is back in his home town of Murwillumbah on the NSW north coast.

Last year, the cybersecurity startup Mr Wade co-founded, Corellium, was bought by tech firm Cellebrite for $285 million.

Soon after the sale of his business, one company executive called him to ask him which supercar he bought.

He responded: "I didn't buy a supercar, I bought a pub." Wade paid $17.8 million for Murwillumbah's Riverview Hotel in December last year.

Chris bought Murwillumbah's Riverview Hotel for $17.8 million. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

His American colleague was stunned.

"He said, 'Only an Australian would buy a pub instead of a Ferrari or a Lamborghini or something'," Wade said.

"But I tell you what, I get way more value out of the pub, and it gives back a lot more. I get to meet a lot of new people and I get to share in experiences."

Wade's current project is teaching a 3-tonne welding robot to shake a cocktail. That passion for tech started when he was a child, when his father Peter says Chris was always tinkering with electronics.

As well as working at the pub, Chris Wade has a keen interest in robotics. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

"We used to go to the local dump and he'd bring home all the electronic stuff he could find," Peter Wade said.

"This is when he was four or five and he'd pull it all apart and make things work and play around with stuff. And he was into high voltage before he was even 10. That's what worried me — but yeah, he managed to survive."

As a child, Chris would work on his own DIY projects. (Supplied)

Having learned to code on a Commodore 64, by the time Wade was a teenager he was assembling computers, selling them to friends and teachers.

Spams, scams and the Secret Service

At age 21, in the early 2000s, Wade moved to the United States, where he got himself into trouble while awaiting his working visa.

"A guy that I knew approached me and said, 'Could you write a piece of software that allows me to proxy through other computers?' I said, 'Yeah, easy. No problems. A couple of thousand dollars, I'll do it.' And he took the software and plugged it into a spamming engine."

Chris Wade moved to the States at the age of 21. (Supplied)

The spams promoted financial scams, and because the emails crossed state borders, they were investigated by a federal authority — the US Secret Service.

In 2005, armed agents raided Wade's home in Dallas, Texas. Wade was arrested at gunpoint, handcuffed and charged with federal crimes.

Foreign citizens convicted of crimes in the US are usually deported once they have served their sentence.

But the authorities realised that Wade was no hardened criminal, and had some very useful skills.

He was given a choice.

"I could help them with cases that they struggled with, where they didn't have the technical know-how to solve the cases, and in exchange, my time would be cut down," Wade said.

He was fined approximately $US70,000 ($99,800) and sentenced to two years' probation.

Cracking passwords for the FBI

In that time he began working with Chris Tarbell, an FBI Special Agent who specialised in cyber crimes.

"When I first met Chris, man, I under-utilised him," Tarbell told 7.30.

"I didn't realise how smart he was.

"If some technical question came up in some sort of strange investigation, he would be my go-to. I'd ask him, and everything I'd ask him to do seemed kind of stupid to him."

Chris's technical skills became an asset to US authorities.

Wade worked with authorities for more than 10 years and helped on some of Tarbell's biggest cases, including investigations into the Silk Road drugs marketplace and the Anonymous hacking group.

"I would do my piece of it," Wade said.

" Which was to solve a puzzle or understand the data that they couldn't figure out … or crack some passwords or things like that. "

In return, Wade got to stay in the US.

Chris Wade went on to build his career in the US and eventually created a cybersecurity company. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

He developed software that allowed app developers to emulate Androids and iPhones inside a computer.

His startup, Corellium, was feted by software engineers but targeted by Apple, which sued Corellium for infringing its copyright in 2019.

Despite his business success and work with the FBI, Wade's felony convictions remained a problem when his probation finished. He would be questioned, extensively, every time he entered or left the United States.

"It certainly made it uncomfortable to travel internationally," Wade said.

"It always weighed on me knowing that at some point the immigration and customs could show up at my door and escort me to the border and put me on a plane and I'd never be allowed to come back to the US, which is where my business was."

A sick fish and a Marvel-lous pardon

One way around the problem would be executive clemency — a presidential pardon.

"You need a sponsor, someone to advocate for you. And that could be a senator, someone famous, one of the Kardashians. And I didn't have anyone," Wade told 7.30.

That was until Gemmy, Wade's tropical Gem Tang, fell ill.

Wade collected coral and saltwater fish.

Chris Wade's aquarium at home. (Supplied)

"I got really into it," he said.

"I think at one point I had nine or 10 fish tanks in the house and eventually I reduced that to one big one."

A specialist went to his Florida home to treat Gemmy.

Gemmy is a tropical Gem Tang, a highly prized specimen known for its rarity. (Supplied)

"The fish doctor came over and saw all the fish tanks I had and said, 'There's only one other person in the world that I know that's as crazy about fish as you are,' and he introduced us, and that was 'Ike'," Wade said.

"Ike" turned out to be Isaac Perlmutter, the publicity-shy chairman of Marvel Entertainment.

The pair met outside Miami Seaquarium. At the time, neither man had any idea what the other did for a living.

"We hit it off," Wade said.

Chris Wade and Isaac "Ike" Perlmutter developed a close bond. (Supplied)

After their first lunch, Perlmutter came back into the restaurant and said his car was showing a flat tyre alert.

"It was pouring rain outside … I remember going out and getting a tyre pump out of the back of my car and standing in the rain pumping his tyre up. And I think from that point on, he would always be there if I needed it," Wade said.

The pair became friends and Perlmutter, a member of Trump's Mar-a-Lago club, advised Wade to seek a presidential pardon.

Ike Perlmutter was a member of the Mar-a-Lago club and had connections to Donald Trump. (Supplied)

"Ike definitely put in a word for me," Wade said.

"And I think they looked at my file. Others like Chris Tarbell … they wrote letters for me. And I think that made an impact."

Tarbell confirmed his contribution.

"I more than happily wrote a letter to President Trump telling him how great Chris had been," the former FBI agent told 7.30.

Chris Tarbell's letter to the president described Chris Wade's "positive conduct and stellar reputation". (Supplied)

'World's greatest hacker' and Elon Musk

Perlmutter soon invited Wade to Mar-a-Lago.

Eventually, Wade met Jared Kushner, Ivanka Trump and even Donald Trump himself. Trump, in turn, introduced Wade to Elon Musk as "the world's greatest hacker".

Chris would go on to meet Jared Kushner, Ivanka Trump and Donald Trump at Mar-a-Lago. (Reuters: Kevin Lamarque)

Musk called Wade after the meeting, beginning a relationship that is still in place today.

Wade says he has been called to the White House for late-night meetings with Musk.

"It's just like anything, he runs into issues and he has a lot of smart people … and sometimes they bring me in on things to help," Wade said.

Chris was introduced to Elon Musk through the president. (Reuters: Chip Somodevilla)

In December 2020, Kushner called Wade with some good news.

The Australian had been granted a presidential pardon.

"I'd met maybe once in passing to shake their hand or something, both Ivanka and Jared, but I'd never spent any time with them," Wade said.

"It always struck me how amazing it was that Jared took an interest because I have no value to him, but they treated me unbelievably and I really appreciate that they did that for me because it changed my life."

In December 2020, the same week he received the pardon, there were two more pieces of good news.

Forbes magazine said Wade's company, Corellium, had created the cybersecurity product of the year; then a US court dismissed Apple's lawsuit against the company.

The president's man

Since then, Wade has become a US citizen and continues to help both Musk and Trump.

"[Donald Trump] has called me before, but normally there's a PA, or someone will call me, or Ike will call me and say, 'I just talked to the president. He needs your help with this'," he said.

He says the White House is on his list of allowed callers, "so that they wake me up even if I have 'do not disturb' on," he told 7.30.

Chris Wade has become a US citizen and continues to help Donald Trump when called. (Supplied)

" I always told the president that he literally saved my life and if there was anything I could ever do to help … I would show up and help him out. "

As part of the sale of his business, Wade was required to stay on to work for new owner Cellebrite, something he wanted to do.

"I believe in the company … and I wanted to make sure they didn't screw up my technology," Wade said.

Cellebrite is one of the world's biggest "mobile forensics" companies, with more than 1,000 employees.

Its products are used by law enforcement in both the US and Australia to unlock and extract information from suspects' devices, once court approval has been granted.

"Cell phones have become like the storage locker of our lives," Wade said.

"So … if you have criminal investigations and you can't get into the phones, it hinders them immensely."

The technology is used to unlock phones on major investigations, like the attempted assassination of Trump.

"The FBI and Secret Service will bring the phone in and they will plug it into a Cellebrite machine, which will extract all the data from the phone and it unlocks the phone as well if there's a password on it so that they can do the criminal investigation," Wade explained.

As Cellebrite's chief technology officer, Wade is focused on the tech staying ahead of criminals.

Now free to travel to and from the US, Chris Wade has returned to the Northern Rivers. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

"I'm heavily focused on what's next. How do we stay ahead of the criminals? How do we get better at solving cases?" Wade said.

"So my focus is on the next three to five years of where a criminal's going, what technologies they're using, how do we keep up with them, and how do we take all that information and give it to AI in such a way that cold cases can be solved or even new cases are solved faster."

And while International time zones make his working day quite tricky, he is still making time for the pub and his hobbies.

"I work from 10 o'clock at night until five o'clock in the morning. And then, not every day, but some days, I'll be at the pub from about 9am til about 3pm.

" I do sleep in there a little bit, which leaves some time for robots and trains. "

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: Eels defend Luai's 2027 signing ahead of Chiefs move
World.content:
Parramatta coach Jason Ryles says he is unapologetic about agreeing to Jarome Luai's one-season stopover at the Eels.

Luai, who is the PNG Chiefs' marquee recruit for 2028, last week signed with the Eels for next season.

A four-time premiership winner with the Panthers, Luai was released by Wests Tigers, which want to give their younger halves opportunities in first grade.

Ryles said he had no concerns Luai's arrival would discourage Parramatta's halves prospects.

Luai joins Parramatta, Marshall slams relationship breakdown rumours Benji Marshall has slammed "bull**** rumours" claiming a fractured relationship with Jarome Luai contributed to the star five-eighth's early exit from Wests Tigers.

He said signing Luai was a win for the 15th-placed Eels' stable of younger halves options, which includes Joash Papalii, Lincoln Fletcher and Lorenzo Talataina.

"We're sitting in a spot on the ladder that we don't want to be," Ryles said.

"It's no-one's fault directly but we need more experienced players. Jarome fits that bill at the moment.

"We have got younger players that are coming through our pathways and our system that may be ready in 12 months.

"But this gives them an extra bit of time to … learn off a true pro that's won a lot of premierships."

Amid a season of injury concerns for the Eels, centre Will Penisini could return from osteitis pubis via reserve grade this weekend.

Ryles said he was hopeful veteran prop Junior Paulo and outside back Bailey Simonsson would be back from their long-term injuries in "the next one or two weeks".

AAP

World.title: Private 'space port' to test guided weapons in Queensland outback
World.content:
A small outback town will host a private weapons and aerospace testing facility in its backyard as part of the Queensland government's efforts to bolster local industry.

The 1.2 million-hectare MaxQ range will test horizontal-launch equipment and guided weapons on leased grazing land near Thargomindah, 11 hours west of Brisbane.

Due to enter operation in mid-2028, phase one of the project will be available to "domestic and allied" users, according to the state government.

The new launch infrastructure, explosives storage and a 2.5-kilometre runway are expected to create 60 construction and operational jobs.

The range, operated by Black Sky Aerospace, has been known as the Outback Space Port and used for sub-orbital rocket launches.

State push for sovereign defence capability

Loading...

Attending a missile launch at the range, Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie said the government would be funding half of the $15 million project.

"This is going to go 'boom' for the Queensland economy in the defence space, literally," Mr Bleijie said.

He said weapons manufacturers currently had to look interstate or overseas for testing sites.

"This is the sort of facility you can't do in South East Queensland," he said.

"I don't think Brisbane would be particularly happy with rockets being launched and missiles being launched from their backyards."

Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie says the outback is better suited for defence testing than the city. (Supplied: 9News)

The state's contribution is drawn from its $180 million Sovereign Industry Development Fund launched last year to invest in defence, biomedical and biofuel capabilities.

"It is so uncertain in the world at the moment, and the dynamics the world has at the moment in defence and security," Mr Bleijie said.

" We've got to look at sovereign capability, we've got to look at national security. "

Queensland sets sights on space industry with outback rocket launch A rocket carrying Australia's first commercial payload is launched skyward in the state's southern outback.

Expanded industry an 'oil boom' for community

Bulloo Shire Mayor John 'Tractor' Ferguson said he welcomed the employment the project would bring to the region.

"I'm over the moon with it," Cr Ferguson said.

"Most people in Thargo are pretty positive about new industries coming to town because, you know, most of these little towns are crying out for other industries other than council work."

Bulloo Shire mayor John 'Tractor' Ferguson is welcoming the announcement of a weapons testing facility near his town of Thargomindah. (ABC News: Laura Lavelle)

The outback mayor compared the expansion of defence industries to the oil boom decades prior.

"I remember when they first [established] Jackson's oil fields back in the 80s. Straight away there was a new motel built in Thargomindah used to accommodate the throughput of traffic," Cr Ferguson said.

" That's more people in the town, that's more families, that's more kids at the school. It's all good stuff. "

Cr Ferguson said Black Sky had been "mucking about" at the site for several years.

"I don't know where else they've looked in Queensland but this seems to be the [one]. They're very excited about this site," he said.

Black Sky offers its outback launch range for sub-orbital missions. (Supplied: 9News)

Queensland-based Black Sky Aerospace was founded in 2018 and develops propulsion technology including rocket motors and fuels.

Headquartered in Logan it also operates a launch and production facility near Goondiwindi.

The federal government has previously invested in the company's manufacturing capability.

World.title: We feel your pain: PM sets election battle lines with One Nation, pledges cost of living relief
World.content:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will set up his bid for a third term with a promise of further expensive cost of living measures to address financial stress fuelling One Nation’s ascension as he expands a program to pay health workers as they study. However, Labor ministers are downplaying the prospect of a tax on gas exports before a fight at its national conference on the popular proposal, signifying tension in Labor ranks over how aggressively Albanese is pursuing populist causes. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese addresses the national Labor conference in 2023. Alex Ellinghausen In a speech to Labor faithful on Thursday that Albanese will use to frame the election’s battle lines, the prime minister will invoke 135 years of Labor tradition on practical responses to boost workers’ living standards rather than “raging against a system … without a plan to fix it”. Albanese will say that “people have been given every reason to feel like the economy is simply not working for them” as he seeks to boost the government’s political fortunes and meet pessimistic voters where they are.



“That goes deeper than sentiment – it’s a reality people are up against,” he will say, according to an advance copy of his speech, noting he was riding “rough seas” after a series of economic shocks and an oil crisis sparked by the Middle East war. Related Article Political leadership Albanese once took on his own frontbench. Now he’s in charge, that would never happen “It’s how we prove that the status quo is not set in stone. How we demonstrate to Australians that their hard work will pay off, that their effort is worth it. That faults in the system can be fixed [and] that Labor is delivering the real change Australians deserve.” His emphasis on helping voters pay their bills, and stating this was a fundamental contrast with his opponents, suggests that Labor will test the fiscal boundaries and focus on cost of living relief in its next two pre-election budgets after spending political capital on revenue-raising tax concession changes this year. Albanese does not mention One Nation by name but his exhortations to reject populist politics underline the upended political dynamic two years out from the next election. Just over a year after his historic win, Albanese’s party has dropped 6.5 percentage points on first-preference vote, according to Poll Bludger’s average of major polls, and is only narrowly ahead of Pauline Hanson’s party, with the Coalition languishing in third.



Albanese will take a veiled swipe at Hanson’s recent controversies on race relations by suggesting the surging populist leader was “blaming people who cannot defend themselves” and championing a form of politics that “doesn’t build anything”. In the face of criticism from Opposition Leader Angus Taylor about an expanding and unproductive care sector, Albanese will on Thursday announce Labor is extending financial support to health students while they undertake training as part of their degrees. Labor did not provide the cost of the policy. Related Article University University in 2027: see how much your degree will cost This will offer a weekly stipend to thousands of students in physio and occupational therapy, clinical psychology, pharmacy and podiatry, speech pathology, audiology, radiography, rehab therapies and paramedics. The government first announced in its 2024 budget that it would give weekly payments to students undertaking practical placements for their teaching, nursing, midwifery and social work qualifications – one of its cost of living pitches to young Australians before the 2025 election. The indexed subsidy is almost $340 a week.



But allied health groups and young students in health professions wanted the prac payments extended to them. The issue has been taken up in parliament by independents Helen Haines and David Pocock. Photo: Matt Golding Parliamentary Budget Office modelling commissioned by Haines found that extending the payments to health and medical students – including psychologists, paramedics and physiotherapists – would cost $290.4 million through to the 2028-29 financial year, on top of $505.3 million budgeted for the current scheme over the same period. Albanese said the program had changed the lives of students who were struggling to make ends meet during university, moving in with their parents or juggling part-time work with their placements to pay rent. Causing headaches for Albanese has been a campaign from MPs including Labor’s Ed Husic, unions, the left-wing Australia Institute think tank, and online content creators to levy gas firms with a 25 per cent export tax.



The issue caught on in the public discourse right at the same time as Albanese was trying to secure fuel from Asian neighbours at the start of the US and Israel’s war with Iran. Many Asian nations that supply fuel rely on Australia’s gas exports, so Albanese scuppered the idea. Related Article Analysis

World.title: Appetite for reflection
World.content:
Paul Taylor of Winston Hills doesn’t mind a bit of mobile fare when he says: “I’ve only just noticed that the badge on newer models of BYD appears as CYE when the car approaches in the rear-view mirror. I did wonder about any subliminal messaging but can only conclude that it may be a traditionally formatted attempt to cash in on the burgeoning fast food delivery car market. Perhaps it should be read as Express Yum Cha.”

“I can sympathise with Jack Dikian’s childhood recollections of watching Play School (C8) and his disappointment in choosing the incorrect window,” says Viv Munter of Tumbi Umbi. “During the ’70s, I recall watching Romper Room and waiting with bated breath for Miss Helena to acknowledge my name when she peered through the magic mirror. Disappointingly, she could never see me.”

“Hey, Jim Dewar. As one of your old fossils (C8), I’m sure that there must be someone, somewhere, that would complain about my demise,” hopes Robert Hosking of Paddington. “Meanwhile, I am seeking bids from cashed-up billionaires for the calcium components of my remains. Do I hear a starting bid of $1m?”

Jennifer Killen of St Peters has another regional first-time film (C8) experience: “My first visit to Leeton’s beautiful Roxy Theatre was a big adventure for a preschooler. I remember nothing of the movie which engrossed my mother and great-aunt, but the decades have not erased the memory of climbing up and over the seats behind, all the way until I reached the top. I then realised I could open the blinds and look out across the main street from above. Much more fun than watching the movie.”

“In the early ’50s, my parents, my brother and I went to the pictures every Saturday night in Marrickville,” recalls Dennis Fardy of Warriewood. “We had reserved seats and wore pyjamas and dressing gowns so we could go straight to bed on getting home. Ironically, the only movie I can remember from that time is The Robe.”

World.title: ‘Getting rid of a headache’: Secret tape exposes land-swap deal for ‘toxic’ waste
World.content:
NationalWACourts ‘Getting rid of a headache’: Secret tape exposes land-swap deal for ‘toxic’ waste Holly Thompson July 22, 2026 — 8:24pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A secret recording that triggered a seven-year defamation battle embroiling politicians including federal Liberal MP Andrew Hastie has finally been played in court, revealing a businessman coached a contact on how to engineer a land swap with the government that would see “toxic soil” dumped and buried. In the 2019 recording, prominent West Australian businessman Greg Poland coached landowner Aaron Grainger, on how to “solve a political headache” for the state government, by facilitating the removal of millions of tonnes of allegedly contaminated soil from an airport development. Greg Poland arriving at David Malcolm Justice Centre for his court case against WAtoday/Nine Publishing. Colin Murty Poland, who was recorded without his knowledge in the restaurant of the Subiaco Hotel in Perth, pushed the idea of a land swap, which would allow Grainger to take ownership of a valuable sand-mining site south of Perth in exchange for giving the government a place to dump the allegedly contaminated soil from the development. Poland encouraged Grainger to send him a letter setting out the plan, and said he would then use his influence as deputy chairman of the Peel Development Commission, to push the plan to then Transport Minister Rita Saffioti and then-regional development minister Allanah MacTiernan.



Grainger repeatedly expressed reservations about the idea. Related Article Courts Andrew Hastie in court as businessman sues over ‘toxic soil’ claims Poland, the chairman of Strzelecki Group and owner of multiple commercial and residential developments around WA, is suing this masthead and its former journalists over the publication of two stories based on that recording. Hastie and former WA Liberal Leader Zak Kirkup have also been drawn into the proceedings over their alleged roles in the dissemination of the recording. Poland’s lawyer Martin Bennett fought to stop the recording being reported on during Wednesday’s proceedings, questioning its authenticity by saying the format of the recording submitted for use in the trial was an MP4, not an MP3 like the original file was.



He also argued no publication of the recording should be allowed until the final judgment had been made, given one of the things the plaintiff sought was the deletion of the recording in all its formats should his case be successful. However, Nine’s lawyer Matthew Lewis, SC, argued it was odd that Poland would not want the recording published, given he had maintained throughout the proceedings it would “vindicate” his side of the story. Andrew Hastie arrives at court on Monday. Colin Murty Justice Matthew Howard considered several points, including that the recording was suggested to have been made illegally, but said no part of the plaintiff’s case argued that the recording contained any defamatory statements. It remains unclear whether the recording will be able to be submitted as evidence.



In the audio subsequently played in court, Poland can be heard giving advice to Grainger, who owns of a block of land in Waroona, about 100 kilometres south of Perth. Poland and Grainger discuss how to make a deal with the state government to relocate between two and eight million tonnes of “toxic sand” from a major infrastructure project in the city to Grainger’s land. “No way in the world they are going to allow that toxic sand to be spread … they’ve got to get rid of it,” Poland can be heard saying. He then tells Grainger that, “what we want to say to you is we’re not going to tell you what to do. But I could say in another way, if I was you, this is what I’d probably think”. In the audio, Poland suggested writing a letter to the state government offering a land-swap deal. If Grainger sold his land to the state government, they could then use it to dump the soil from the airport link development.



In return, Grainger would then own the sand, worth up to $600 million, to be used in construction. In the audio, Grainger stated he could take two million tonnes of the soil from the airport link project, but that he could take the full eight million tonnes if they allowed him to clear more of his land, and discusses mentioning that in the letter. Poland then recommended not asking for the permit to clear more land, and to instead offer to take the two million tonnes of soil to start, with the possibility of taking more down the track. “Keep it simple, they will come straight to you once you’ve done one favour,” Poland says in the audio. “Once you’ve done one favour, they’ll ring you and they’ll steamroll anything through.



“Rita [Saffioti] will just push it through. Alannah [MacTiernan] and Rita will just steamroll it. They’ll just steamroll it. “If we could pull this off, whatever you want, Rita would be your friend.” Related Article Courts Perth developer tells defamation trial WA government called on him to solve ‘headache’ Grainger, Poland and Lisa Taylor, who was the Peel Development Commission’s commercial manager at the time, then discuss the Waroona site as the ideal location to take the soil, because the area is “already contaminated”. “It’s all contaminated anyway … the advantages of my spot is, I’ve got the shire tip right next door and I’ve got another private tip on the other side of me, and I’ve got Alcoa,” Grainger can be heard saying.



Near the end of the meeting, Poland can be heard thanking Taylor for not taking notes, stating he was “unorthodox”. Lewis cross-examined Poland, both before and after the recording was played, homing in on his affidavit where the developer claimed the meeting which had been recorded had taken place in a “private lounge”. Poland has also claimed several times the meeting was at 11.30am, which he stood by when documents showed the meeting had been scheduled for 9.30am. “You were trying to convey you were in a secluded set-up,” Lewis said. “Well we were,” Poland replied, before later also stating: “You should be able to have a private conversation anywhere.”



Lewis said meeting in one of the main rooms at the Subiaco Hotel was not a private lounge, and suggested Poland had deliberately tried to make the meeting seem more secluded than it was to make a point about why it should not have been recorded. Poland denied that claim. After the recording was played, Poland was asked again whether he believed the meeting to be private, due to the audible background noise including children and chairs scraping. “You’re trying to con me, I won’t be conned,” he replied, claiming anything would sound louder if it was played at an increased volume. “I was there, you weren’t, sorry to be rude, there was one other customer there,” he said.



“There was obviously more than one,” Lewis replied, which Poland denied. He will return to the stand on Thursday morning. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Former Labor MP accuses Josh Burns of acting as ‘human shield for Penny Wong’
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalALP Former Labor MP accuses Josh Burns of acting as ‘human shield for Penny Wong’ Matthew Knott and Paul Sakkal Updated July 22, 2026 — 8:02pm ,first published 3:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The head of the nation’s peak Jewish body has condemned Labor for removing a call for listed terror group Hamas to disarm from its draft policy platform as tensions erupted between former close allies over the issue ahead of the party’s national conference. Labor planned to present a unified front on the contentious issue by having two MPs from Melbourne – Josh Burns, who is Jewish, and Basem Abdo, the son of Palestinian refugees – jointly present the section of the platform on Israel/Palestine in Adelaide on Saturday, the last day of the gathering. Executive Council of Australian Jewry co-chief executive Peter Wertheim said he was disappointed by the wording of the draft platform. Dominic Lorrimer But infighting over wording of the platform, which was recently amended to be tougher on Israel and less demanding of the Palestinian side, threatens to derail hopes for an uplifting moment. The dispute has sparked an incendiary attack on Burns by former Labor MP Michael Danby, who accused his successor and former chief of staff of acting as a “human shield” for Foreign Minister Penny Wong and demanded he withdraw his support for the platform unless it is rewritten.



Executive Council of Australian Jewry co-chief executive Peter Wertheim, a longtime confidant of Albanese, said the draft platform lacked balance and failed to reflect the government’s stated policy positions. “Instead of providing an honest assessment of the leadership on both sides of the conflict, the draft platform regurgitates the same old one-eyed obsession with blaming Israel,” Wertheim said in the Jewish peak body’s first comments on the draft platform. Related Article ALP Israel accused of ‘extraordinary’ intervention in Labor politics “It is a reasonable question to ask why the ALP national conference is not backing in the Albanese government in expressly recognising the government’s position on excluding Hamas and requiring the Palestinian Authority to honour the commitments for governance reform upon which the government’s recognition of a Palestinian state was explicitly based.” Wertheim said Albanese and Foreign Minister Penny Wong had repeatedly argued there must be no role for Hamas in Gaza, raising questions about why wording reflecting this stance had been expunged from the draft platform.



“Even Hamas itself has acknowledged it, by announcing a hand-over of its government functions to a US-backed technocratic committee,” Wertheim told this masthead. “But apparently the ALP National Conference cannot quite bring itself to acknowledge it. The best it can do is refer to Hamas, in passing, as a terrorist group.” Labor MP Josh Burns has been criticised by his predecessor Michael Danby. Sitthixay Ditthavong Wertheim said the platform also failed to reflect the government’s insistence that recognition of Palestinian statehood relied on commitments from the Palestinian Authority, which governs parts of the West Bank, to reform its governance, terminate payments to the families of Palestinian prisoners, institute schooling reform, and hold general elections. Wertheim and Albanese formed a bond two decades ago when Albanese opposed the boycott, divestment and sanctions movement against Israel. Albanese regularly consults Wertheim on matters related to the Jewish community.



Albanese told the United Nations General Assembly last September that “the terrorist organisation Hamas can have no role in Palestine’s future”, adding Australia’s recognition of a Palestinian state was predicated on commitments from the Palestinian Authority, including that “Hamas would hand over its weapons to Palestinian security forces – and never control Gaza again”. On the prospect of Burns co-sponsoring the motion on Israel and Palestine, Danby told this masthead: “I’ve never publicly criticised my successor, but I’m aghast that he is acting as a human shield for Foreign Minister Penny Wong. “He ought to withdraw his name if the original positions on Hamas and the Palestinian Authority, promised by Prime Minister Albanese, are not included in the final platform resolution.” Michael Danby during his final speech in parliament in 2019. Dominic Lorrimer Danby, a staunch supporter of Israel, held the seat of Melbourne Ports – now called Macnamara – from 1998 to 2019, before he retired and was replaced by Burns. His use of the phrase “human shield” is inflammatory given it is often used by Hamas’ critics to describe the way the group embeds itself within Gaza’s civilian population.



Burns worked in Danby’s office, including as his chief of staff, and praised his predecessor for his courage in his first speech to parliament. He declined to comment. The latest version of the draft platform condemns the use of violence, including by Hamas, but earlier versions included an explicit reference that “Hamas must disarm and can have no role in the State of Palestine”. An earlier draft also said that Labor “will continue to work with the international community to hold the Palestinian Authority to its commitments and to encourage normalised relations between Israel and its neighbours”. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict Israel blasts Labor’s ‘one-sided’ policy platform as Palestinian advocates push further When announcing $25 million in new aid funding for Palestine on Tuesday, Foreign Minister Penny Wong said: “Hamas can play no role in the State of Palestine.”



Wong, who is in the Philippines for a meeting of the Association of South-East Asian Nations (ASEAN), used a speech on Wednesday to again condemn China’s test-firing of a missile in the Pacific earlier this month, saying it came “with too little information and notification”. “It comes in the context of China’s rapid military build-up, including of its nuclear arsenal, without the transparency or reassurance the region expects, which is why Australia has described the test as provocative and destabilising,” she said. Several Labor sources said former cabinet minister Ed Husic, a fierce critic of Israel’s conduct in the war in Gaza, had been pushing internally for the platform to go further in its criticisms of Israel. Husic did not respond to requests for comment. The draft version calls out Israel for settler violence in the West Bank, condemns a controversial new death penalty law and backs two international courts considering genocide and war crimes charges against Israel. World.title: Clumsy video causes trouble for UK PM on his second day
World.content:
WorldEuropeUK politics Clumsy video causes trouble for UK PM on his second day David Crowe July 22, 2026 — 7:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: A clumsy joke has backfired on cabinet ministers soon after they were named to their posts by British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, just as he vowed to set a new tone and direction for the government upon taking power this week. The ministers were caught on video trading jokes about the early release of prisoners in a light-hearted conversation in London, but their banter provoked swift criticism when the video was leaked on social media. Loading Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood and Defence Secretary Wes Streeting apologised for the gaffes after their opponents accused them of making light of a prison scandal that has outraged critics who do not want criminals released early. It also cast a cloud over Burnham’s attempts to win support from voters in his first days in office, starting with decisions to cut taxes on household electricity bills and reduce bus fares.



Burnham has rewarded allies in a cabinet reshuffle that has removed some of the ministers who were closest to his predecessor, Keir Starmer, in moves that have cheered the new leader’s supporters on the progressive side of the Labour Party. The video appeared to be news footage taken from a distance, with audio from a boom microphone, while ministers spoke after they were confirmed in their posts, apparently unaware their words could be recorded. The gaffe by Andy Burnham’s senior ministers have cast a cloud over the UK prime minister’s first days in office. Bloomberg Streeting was speaking with Mahmood and the new Justice Secretary, Alex Norris, when he made a remark about prisoner release. Streeting suggested to Mahmood that Norris was “the enemy” and wanted to “let them all out” – an apparent reference to the Justice Secretary’s role in the early release of prisoners.



Related Article Opinion

Sleeping rough The new UK PM made a brave pledge. Our PM should follow suit Erin Longbottom Anti-homelessness advocate Mahmood replied: “No, he’s not.” The three laughed at the quip. While they did not make light of a serious case of early prisoner release, the social media video sparked criticism from Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch, who pointed to headlines on Wednesday about convicted killers being released early. “Yesterday Cabinet ministers were joking about letting criminals out of jail early,” she said on Wednesday morning (about 6.30pm, AEST). “Burnham has already said he doesn’t think rapists and paedophiles should be out early. I sincerely hope that extends to the killers of emergency workers.”



Badenoch cited the news that the two prisoners, who killed police constable Andrew Harper seven years ago, could be set free under the Labour early-release policy to ease overcrowding in prisons. Within hours, Burnham responded by asking the justice secretary to review the case and telling the media that the main perpetrator would not be subject to any early release. Streeting apologised on X for the remark and said he had been referring to a similar joke shared by Conservative ministers when former prime minister Theresa May talked about prison release with former minister Kenneth Clarke. View post on X “I hope everyone can see there was no ill intent behind this ribbing of the new Justice Secretary,” he said.



“But I appreciate these are very serious issues and am sorry for any offence inadvertently caused by this moment of levity.” Streeting posted a news story with the remark by May as prime minister in 2017 when she joked about Clarke in the House of Commons. “When I was Home Secretary and he was Justice Secretary, I used to say that I locked ’em up and he let ’em out,” she told the House. Ministers Shabana Mahmood, Wes Streeting Angela Eagle ahead of UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s first cabinet meeting in Downing Street. Bloomberg Mahmood also apologised and blamed the Conservatives for the challenges in the justice system. The video embarrassed the government just as ministers celebrated their appointments after Burnham sacked ministers loyal to Starmer, highlighting the personal divides within Labour.



Burnham removed David Lammy, who was justice secretary and deputy prime minister, and Rachel Reeves, who was chancellor of the exchequer. Promotions were awarded to those who helped bring Starmer down. The new chancellor of the exchequer, John Healey, quit as defence secretary on June 11 over a dispute about funding the military. This rocked the government one week before Burnham won a by-election that returned him to parliament and cleared the way for him to challenge Starmer. The new energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, quit the ministry on May 12 along with several others who wanted Starmer to step down. She entered parliament in 2024 and now has one of the most challenging portfolios in the government. Angela Rayner, the former deputy prime minister and housing minister, returns to her old portfolio, but not the deputy’s position. She stepped down last September due to criticism of her tax arrangements, creating a rift with Starmer that led her to support Burnham. In a key cabinet appointment, Louise Haigh becomes first secretary of state and the “enforcer” for Burnham’s policies. She was a member of Starmer’s first ministry but had to quit in November 2024 when the media reported a 2013 incident in which she wrongly claimed her phone had been stolen.



Streeting quit as health secretary on May 14, in one of the biggest moves to undermine confidence in Starmer and his administration. The new foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, was previously energy secretary and was reported to have clashed with Starmer in a cabinet debate over the Iran war. The Spectator reported in early March that Miliband was critical of letting US forces use UK bases. Burnham is also preparing to elevate Anas Sarwar, the head of the Labour Party in Scotland, to the House of Lords so he could take up a position in the national government. Sarwar called on Starmer to resign during a press conference widely televised on March 24, weeks out from elections for the Scottish parliament. Labour lost those elections to the Scottish National Party. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: We feel your pain: PM sets election battle lines with One Nation, pledges cost of living relief
World.content:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will set up his bid for a third term with a promise of further expensive cost of living measures to address financial stress fuelling One Nation’s ascension as he expands a program to pay health workers as they study. However, Labor ministers are downplaying the prospect of a tax on gas exports before a fight at its national conference on the popular proposal, signifying tension in Labor ranks over how aggressively Albanese is pursuing populist causes. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese addresses the national Labor conference in 2023. Alex Ellinghausen In a speech to Labor faithful on Thursday that Albanese will use to frame the election’s battle lines, the prime minister will invoke 135 years of Labor tradition on practical responses to boost workers’ living standards rather than “raging against a system … without a plan to fix it”. Albanese will say that “people have been given every reason to feel like the economy is simply not working for them” as he seeks to boost the government’s political fortunes and meet pessimistic voters where they are.



“That goes deeper than sentiment – it’s a reality people are up against,” he will say, according to an advance copy of his speech, noting he was riding “rough seas” after a series of economic shocks and an oil crisis sparked by the Middle East war. Related Article Political leadership Albanese once took on his own frontbench. Now he’s in charge, that would never happen “It’s how we prove that the status quo is not set in stone. How we demonstrate to Australians that their hard work will pay off, that their effort is worth it. That faults in the system can be fixed [and] that Labor is delivering the real change Australians deserve.” His emphasis on helping voters pay their bills, and stating this was a fundamental contrast with his opponents, suggests that Labor will test the fiscal boundaries and focus on cost of living relief in its next two pre-election budgets after spending political capital on revenue-raising tax concession changes this year. Albanese does not mention One Nation by name but his exhortations to reject populist politics underline the upended political dynamic two years out from the next election. Just over a year after his historic win, Albanese’s party has dropped 6.5 percentage points on first-preference vote, according to Poll Bludger’s average of major polls, and is only narrowly ahead of Pauline Hanson’s party, with the Coalition languishing in third.



Albanese will take a veiled swipe at Hanson’s recent controversies on race relations by suggesting the surging populist leader was “blaming people who cannot defend themselves” and championing a form of politics that “doesn’t build anything”. In the face of criticism from Opposition Leader Angus Taylor about an expanding and unproductive care sector, Albanese will on Thursday announce Labor is extending financial support to health students while they undertake training as part of their degrees. Labor did not provide the cost of the policy. Related Article University University in 2027: see how much your degree will cost This will offer a weekly stipend to thousands of students in physio and occupational therapy, clinical psychology, pharmacy and podiatry, speech pathology, audiology, radiography, rehab therapies and paramedics. The government first announced in its 2024 budget that it would give weekly payments to students undertaking practical placements for their teaching, nursing, midwifery and social work qualifications – one of its cost of living pitches to young Australians before the 2025 election. The indexed subsidy is almost $340 a week.



But allied health groups and young students in health professions wanted the prac payments extended to them. The issue has been taken up in parliament by independents Helen Haines and David Pocock. Photo: Matt Golding Parliamentary Budget Office modelling commissioned by Haines found that extending the payments to health and medical students – including psychologists, paramedics and physiotherapists – would cost $290.4 million through to the 2028-29 financial year, on top of $505.3 million budgeted for the current scheme over the same period. Albanese said the program had changed the lives of students who were struggling to make ends meet during university, moving in with their parents or juggling part-time work with their placements to pay rent. Causing headaches for Albanese has been a campaign from MPs including Labor’s Ed Husic, unions, the left-wing Australia Institute think tank, and online content creators to levy gas firms with a 25 per cent export tax.



The issue caught on in the public discourse right at the same time as Albanese was trying to secure fuel from Asian neighbours at the start of the US and Israel’s war with Iran. Many Asian nations that supply fuel rely on Australia’s gas exports, so Albanese scuppered the idea. Related Article Analysis

ALP Flying the flag for a fight nobody else wanted to have However, a section of the party’s draft platform states that Labor will ensure Australians “receive a fairer return from their natural resources”, opening the door to a tax later this term. Treasurer Jim Chalmers and others in the government have been open to a fresh revenue grab on resources firms. The renewed fighting in the Middle East means that the issue of fuel scarcity may again come to the fore, adding pressure on Albanese to downplay a new tax as he did on the weekend. Ministers have also tried to quash talk of a tax. “The position of the government has been that we haven’t supported a gas tax,” Environment Minister Murray Watt said on Nine’s Today program on Wednesday.

World.title: ‘Getting rid of a headache’: Secret tape exposes land-swap deal for ‘toxic’ waste
World.content:
NationalWACourts ‘Getting rid of a headache’: Secret tape exposes land-swap deal for ‘toxic’ waste Holly Thompson July 22, 2026 — 8:24pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A secret recording that triggered a seven-year defamation battle embroiling politicians including federal Liberal MP Andrew Hastie has finally been played in court, revealing a businessman coached a contact on how to engineer a land swap with the government that would see “toxic soil” dumped and buried. In the 2019 recording, prominent West Australian businessman Greg Poland coached landowner Aaron Grainger, on how to “solve a political headache” for the state government, by facilitating the removal of millions of tonnes of allegedly contaminated soil from an airport development.
