Greg Poland arriving at David Malcolm Justice Centre for his court case against WAtoday/Nine Publishing. Colin Murty Poland, who was recorded without his knowledge in the restaurant of the Subiaco Hotel in Perth, pushed the idea of a land swap, which would allow Grainger to take ownership of a valuable sand-mining site south of Perth in exchange for giving the government a place to dump the allegedly contaminated soil from the development. Poland encouraged Grainger to send him a letter setting out the plan, and said he would then use his influence as deputy chairman of the Peel Development Commission, to push the plan to then Transport Minister Rita Saffioti and then-regional development minister Allanah MacTiernan.



Grainger repeatedly expressed reservations about the idea. Related Article Courts Andrew Hastie in court as businessman sues over ‘toxic soil’ claims Poland, the chairman of Strzelecki Group and owner of multiple commercial and residential developments around WA, is suing this masthead and its former journalists over the publication of two stories based on that recording. Hastie and former WA Liberal Leader Zak Kirkup have also been drawn into the proceedings over their alleged roles in the dissemination of the recording. Poland’s lawyer Martin Bennett fought to stop the recording being reported on during Wednesday’s proceedings, questioning its authenticity by saying the format of the recording submitted for use in the trial was an MP4, not an MP3 like the original file was.



He also argued no publication of the recording should be allowed until the final judgment had been made, given one of the things the plaintiff sought was the deletion of the recording in all its formats should his case be successful. However, Nine’s lawyer Matthew Lewis, SC, argued it was odd that Poland would not want the recording published, given he had maintained throughout the proceedings it would “vindicate” his side of the story. Andrew Hastie arrives at court on Monday. Colin Murty Justice Matthew Howard considered several points, including that the recording was suggested to have been made illegally, but said no part of the plaintiff’s case argued that the recording contained any defamatory statements. It remains unclear whether the recording will be able to be submitted as evidence.



In the audio subsequently played in court, Poland can be heard giving advice to Grainger, who owns of a block of land in Waroona, about 100 kilometres south of Perth. Poland and Grainger discuss how to make a deal with the state government to relocate between two and eight million tonnes of “toxic sand” from a major infrastructure project in the city to Grainger’s land. “No way in the world they are going to allow that toxic sand to be spread … they’ve got to get rid of it,” Poland can be heard saying. He then tells Grainger that, “what we want to say to you is we’re not going to tell you what to do. But I could say in another way, if I was you, this is what I’d probably think”. In the audio, Poland suggested writing a letter to the state government offering a land-swap deal. If Grainger sold his land to the state government, they could then use it to dump the soil from the airport link development.



In return, Grainger would then own the sand, worth up to $600 million, to be used in construction. In the audio, Grainger stated he could take two million tonnes of the soil from the airport link project, but that he could take the full eight million tonnes if they allowed him to clear more of his land, and discusses mentioning that in the letter. Poland then recommended not asking for the permit to clear more land, and to instead offer to take the two million tonnes of soil to start, with the possibility of taking more down the track. “Keep it simple, they will come straight to you once you’ve done one favour,” Poland says in the audio. “Once you’ve done one favour, they’ll ring you and they’ll steamroll anything through.



“Rita [Saffioti] will just push it through. Alannah [MacTiernan] and Rita will just steamroll it. They’ll just steamroll it. “If we could pull this off, whatever you want, Rita would be your friend.” Related Article Courts Perth developer tells defamation trial WA government called on him to solve ‘headache’ Grainger, Poland and Lisa Taylor, who was the Peel Development Commission’s commercial manager at the time, then discuss the Waroona site as the ideal location to take the soil, because the area is “already contaminated”. “It’s all contaminated anyway … the advantages of my spot is, I’ve got the shire tip right next door and I’ve got another private tip on the other side of me, and I’ve got Alcoa,” Grainger can be heard saying.



Near the end of the meeting, Poland can be heard thanking Taylor for not taking notes, stating he was “unorthodox”. Lewis cross-examined Poland, both before and after the recording was played, homing in on his affidavit where the developer claimed the meeting which had been recorded had taken place in a “private lounge”. Poland has also claimed several times the meeting was at 11.30am, which he stood by when documents showed the meeting had been scheduled for 9.30am. “You were trying to convey you were in a secluded set-up,” Lewis said. “Well we were,” Poland replied, before later also stating: “You should be able to have a private conversation anywhere.”



Lewis said meeting in one of the main rooms at the Subiaco Hotel was not a private lounge, and suggested Poland had deliberately tried to make the meeting seem more secluded than it was to make a point about why it should not have been recorded. Poland denied that claim. After the recording was played, Poland was asked again whether he believed the meeting to be private, due to the audible background noise including children and chairs scraping. “You’re trying to con me, I won’t be conned,” he replied, claiming anything would sound louder if it was played at an increased volume. “I was there, you weren’t, sorry to be rude, there was one other customer there,” he said.



“There was obviously more than one,” Lewis replied, which Poland denied. He will return to the stand on Thursday morning. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Former Labor MP accuses Josh Burns of acting as ‘human shield for Penny Wong’
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalALP Former Labor MP accuses Josh Burns of acting as ‘human shield for Penny Wong’ Matthew Knott and Paul Sakkal Updated July 22, 2026 — 8:02pm ,first published 3:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The head of the nation’s peak Jewish body has condemned Labor for removing a call for listed terror group Hamas to disarm from its draft policy platform as tensions erupted between former close allies over the issue ahead of the party’s national conference. Labor planned to present a unified front on the contentious issue by having two MPs from Melbourne – Josh Burns, who is Jewish, and Basem Abdo, the son of Palestinian refugees – jointly present the section of the platform on Israel/Palestine in Adelaide on Saturday, the last day of the gathering. Executive Council of Australian Jewry co-chief executive Peter Wertheim said he was disappointed by the wording of the draft platform. Dominic Lorrimer But infighting over wording of the platform, which was recently amended to be tougher on Israel and less demanding of the Palestinian side, threatens to derail hopes for an uplifting moment. The dispute has sparked an incendiary attack on Burns by former Labor MP Michael Danby, who accused his successor and former chief of staff of acting as a “human shield” for Foreign Minister Penny Wong and demanded he withdraw his support for the platform unless it is rewritten.



Executive Council of Australian Jewry co-chief executive Peter Wertheim, a longtime confidant of Albanese, said the draft platform lacked balance and failed to reflect the government’s stated policy positions. “Instead of providing an honest assessment of the leadership on both sides of the conflict, the draft platform regurgitates the same old one-eyed obsession with blaming Israel,” Wertheim said in the Jewish peak body’s first comments on the draft platform. Related Article ALP Israel accused of ‘extraordinary’ intervention in Labor politics “It is a reasonable question to ask why the ALP national conference is not backing in the Albanese government in expressly recognising the government’s position on excluding Hamas and requiring the Palestinian Authority to honour the commitments for governance reform upon which the government’s recognition of a Palestinian state was explicitly based.” Wertheim said Albanese and Foreign Minister Penny Wong had repeatedly argued there must be no role for Hamas in Gaza, raising questions about why wording reflecting this stance had been expunged from the draft platform.



“Even Hamas itself has acknowledged it, by announcing a hand-over of its government functions to a US-backed technocratic committee,” Wertheim told this masthead. “But apparently the ALP National Conference cannot quite bring itself to acknowledge it. The best it can do is refer to Hamas, in passing, as a terrorist group.” Labor MP Josh Burns has been criticised by his predecessor Michael Danby. Sitthixay Ditthavong Wertheim said the platform also failed to reflect the government’s insistence that recognition of Palestinian statehood relied on commitments from the Palestinian Authority, which governs parts of the West Bank, to reform its governance, terminate payments to the families of Palestinian prisoners, institute schooling reform, and hold general elections. Wertheim and Albanese formed a bond two decades ago when Albanese opposed the boycott, divestment and sanctions movement against Israel. Albanese regularly consults Wertheim on matters related to the Jewish community.



Albanese told the United Nations General Assembly last September that “the terrorist organisation Hamas can have no role in Palestine’s future”, adding Australia’s recognition of a Palestinian state was predicated on commitments from the Palestinian Authority, including that “Hamas would hand over its weapons to Palestinian security forces – and never control Gaza again”. On the prospect of Burns co-sponsoring the motion on Israel and Palestine, Danby told this masthead: “I’ve never publicly criticised my successor, but I’m aghast that he is acting as a human shield for Foreign Minister Penny Wong. “He ought to withdraw his name if the original positions on Hamas and the Palestinian Authority, promised by Prime Minister Albanese, are not included in the final platform resolution.” Michael Danby during his final speech in parliament in 2019. Dominic Lorrimer Danby, a staunch supporter of Israel, held the seat of Melbourne Ports – now called Macnamara – from 1998 to 2019, before he retired and was replaced by Burns. His use of the phrase “human shield” is inflammatory given it is often used by Hamas’ critics to describe the way the group embeds itself within Gaza’s civilian population.



Burns worked in Danby’s office, including as his chief of staff, and praised his predecessor for his courage in his first speech to parliament. He declined to comment. The latest version of the draft platform condemns the use of violence, including by Hamas, but earlier versions included an explicit reference that “Hamas must disarm and can have no role in the State of Palestine”. An earlier draft also said that Labor “will continue to work with the international community to hold the Palestinian Authority to its commitments and to encourage normalised relations between Israel and its neighbours”. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict Israel blasts Labor’s ‘one-sided’ policy platform as Palestinian advocates push further When announcing $25 million in new aid funding for Palestine on Tuesday, Foreign Minister Penny Wong said: “Hamas can play no role in the State of Palestine.”



Wong, who is in the Philippines for a meeting of the Association of South-East Asian Nations (ASEAN), used a speech on Wednesday to again condemn China’s test-firing of a missile in the Pacific earlier this month, saying it came “with too little information and notification”. “It comes in the context of China’s rapid military build-up, including of its nuclear arsenal, without the transparency or reassurance the region expects, which is why Australia has described the test as provocative and destabilising,” she said. Several Labor sources said former cabinet minister Ed Husic, a fierce critic of Israel’s conduct in the war in Gaza, had been pushing internally for the platform to go further in its criticisms of Israel. Husic did not respond to requests for comment. The draft version calls out Israel for settler violence in the West Bank, condemns a controversial new death penalty law and backs two international courts considering genocide and war crimes charges against Israel. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Premier, it’s time to act on the Big Build
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Premier, it’s time to act on the Big Build July 22, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. The Age’s investigation into the Big Build continues to expose more situations where Premier Jacinta Allan hasn’t confronted them and ensured that they are properly investigated and, where appropriate, legal proceedings undertaken. As your correspondent (Letters, 22/7) says: ″⁣The refusal to call a royal commission into the Big Build – despite persistent concerns about governance and culture – is indefensible. The call for a royal commission will not go away.″⁣

In early June, the premier conceded the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission needed to be empowered to investigate the Big Build money trail with a broader remit to investigate corruption in state institutions. However, the increased powers would not be available until the end of 2027. If she acted now and brought forward the legislation for an additional remit for IBAC (with proper funding), it may prove to be an acceptable alternative to a royal commission. It would take months before IBAC concluded its investigation, during which there will be matters that emerge that may be embarrassing to government. However, it would show that she has begun a substantial process, and perhaps start to recover some validity before the November election.

Bill Pimm, Mentone Trying to defend the indefensible

As the chorus grows louder for a royal commission in Victoria on the Big Build, it has become an almost comic spectacle watching the premier basically trying to defend the indefensible, using any tactic she can find – verbalising when she shouldn’t, casting doubt on expert opinion and using evidence to support her claims without authority.

And we learnt that at a recent cabinet meeting to head off any concerns within her own party, she enlisted the support of three senior ministers to shut it down and “grind it out”.

Watching this unnerving experience leads any reasoned person to ask, what actually is the premier hoping to hide? Why do 70 per cent of Victorians, as quoted by The Age, feel the need for a royal commission but the premier constantly ignores this? Surely, this constant frowardness accounts for her unpopularity levels being off the Richter scale? Most Victorians, I think, feel it’s time to reveal all.

Tony Davidson, Glen Waverley A minister who can’t read the classroom

Victoria’s Education Minister Ben Carroll does not seem able to read the classroom. Three times now, rank-and-file teachers and support staff have rejected his department’s offers on pay and conditions. Carroll has had nearly three years to halt the rundown in Victorian public education resourcing and consequent escalation in teacher and education support staff stress and burn-out. The underfunding of public education is at the core of the problem, and with everything that’s going on, Carroll still cannot commit to bringing Victoria up to the same level of funding as other states.

Attempting ″⁣sweetheart″⁣ deals with the Australian Education Union leadership that in no way addressed the crisis was a big mistake. It demonstrated a complete lack of understanding of what is going on in his own department. Next, his attempt to go around the union with a direct offer to education workers failed when confronted with the organised opposition of union rank-and-file members.

Surely, it’s time to ″⁣talk turkey″⁣ and strike a deal that fundamentally addresses the funding shortfall, and improves teaching conditions and the quality of public education in Victoria.

Mike Naismith, Clifton Hill



Mixing demographics for housing needs

Thanks to your correspondent (Letters, 16/7) for calling out deliberate segregation of housing occupants based on affordable versus higher-value homes. This is an ugly and divisive feature of our competitive and aspirational society. Housing policy at all levels of government must ensure a more even demographic mix. And a chance to get along with others.

Nina Earl, Mordialloc THE FORUM Grandeur gone

Thank you, Rob Adams, for the article, “What makes Melbourne special is its unique CBD. One building could bring it all undone” (22/7). This part of the Metro train development makes my blood boil. When one stood in Federation Square and looked towards Flinders and Swanston streets, the city looked spectacular – St Paul’s Cathedral, Young & Jacksons, Flinders Street Station and Clements House. The train development should not have added anything above the height of the buildings they demolished. But instead of seeing a wonderful heritage-listed building, now we will have an ugly, 40-metre, imposing office building (of all things) by the corner.

Heaven forbid if they extend the height to 76 metres. This corner was one of Melbourne’s greatest assets. Who is responsible for destroying it?

Owen Jones, Williamstown A city’s human scale

The factors that influence urban growth change over time. Limitations may be imposed by climate, topography, geographical location and other “environmental” considerations. The pace of technological change is ensuring that cities can no longer evolve organically. Many traditional urban design strategies seem increasingly irrelevant in the light of changing communication, access and transport realities. Rob Adam’s’ plea for respect of human scale and the 1985 Melbourne Strategy Plan (Comment, 22/7) reads a trifle wistfully, 40 years on, but there may yet be hope.

Such factors as increased working from home, aided by revolutionised communications and powered by AI, may well result in the sort of decentralised development pattern that urban planners used to wish for.

Melbourne needs to take a longer view: human scale is vital for the city’s health, and developers need to look more creatively at the ways their current economic models may be influenced by the likely pace and direction of change.

Jenifer Nicholls, Windsor Just like firewood

I agree with the call to ban wood fires (Letters, 22/7) especially in urban areas. Even before the findings that the smoke increased risk of dementia I just cannot believe that it is reasonable for one household to inflict their smoke on neighbours. It stops me opening my windows in morning to air out house, or putting my washing on the line.

Helen Day, Torquay



Next, the flat Earth

I read with incredulity the article, ″⁣Early images of deaths during pandemic were staged″⁣ (22/7), in which One Nation senator Malcolm Roberts claimed that images of deaths in Italy and China in the early stages of the pandemic were fake. That a member of parliament indulges in such a ludicrous conspiracy theory is not just laughably ridiculous, but disrespectful to those people, and the millions of others around the world who died, to the families who grieved, and to the medical workers who in some cases also gave their lives to help the victims. It is gutter-level politics.

Do we need a person of this calibre to hold a position of responsibility in our parliament? I await his views on a flat Earth and faked moon landings.

Bruce McClure, Middle Park Joyce, we have a problem

Re Barnaby Joyce’s suggestion that illegal immigrants be targeted through doctors’ visits (″⁣Joyce goes from lighting the fires to carrying the bucket″⁣, 22/7): First problem is Medicare, which is available for refugees, humanitarian entrants and eligible asylum seekers, but not for illegal immigrants, so a government of any persuasion could not use Medicare to flag their attendance.

Second problem: Identification. GPs and hospitals see and treat many people without Medicare cards. Most are on visas, some are illegal entrants or overstayers (we don’t distinguish, or indeed ask, or need to know). Each is a patient with a health issue, some very serious or acute. We treat a medical problem, not a visa status.

Third problem: Confidentiality. If patients thought we were about to report them to authorities, they wouldn’t present. Doctors are bound by confidentiality unless someone is in danger. We look after people, we don’t demonise them.

Dr Will Twycross, Mansfield Barking up wrong tree

It’s a sad reflection on our political maturity when a command to stop a dog barking becomes the key talking point in the national political discourse. Surely, there are more important issues to yap about.

Martin Newington, Aspendale Premier, act for teachers

Teachers care for and educate our children. We cannot do without them. It’s shameful that they have to go on strike to secure better pay and working conditions. Jacinta Allan, if you want our respect and votes, respect our teachers. Speak to your people and make this happen. Make it so that teachers never again have to go on strike.

Merron Cullum, Cremorne Take independent path

Your correspondents are right to despair about the Victorian Big Build (Letters, 22/7). It sits alongside rising debt, rogue native forest logging, and continued support for duck shooting as some of the many concerns in our state. These are all issues that Jacinta Allan has struggled to address.

As one correspondent noted, however, under Labor, Victoria’s progress on a Treaty as well as the state’s commitment to renewable energy targets has been commendable. Jess Wilson’s Liberal Party has signalled it would drop both of these positives. One Nation candidates would almost certainly do the same. Come November, I hope many of us can support independent or minor party candidates. They might be able to hold onto the positives and confront the challenges with integrity and transparency.

Amy Hiller, Kew



AI’s opportunities

The first industrial robot, Unimate, began work at General Motors in the United States in 1961. Kawasaki licensed the technology, producing its own versions by 1969. By the mid 1970s, Europe had developed advanced industrial robots, but there was resistance to their adoption. Japan embraced them, especially in the car industry, helping its rise to global leadership in motor manufacturing. Today, all motor manufacturers have adopted robots to remain competitive.

AI is no different. It is another technology that will reduce the need for human labour in certain areas. We can choose to be dragged along, or to be at the forefront in adopting technology safely and to the benefit of all.

Automation is accelerating. We welcome it in our homes, yet often discuss its social impact only in terms of lost jobs.

The question is not simply, “How many jobs will disappear?” but, “How should life and work function in an automated society?“

The debate must be about how to reshape our social structures, the ownership and governance of key technologies and the means of production, and how to make sure everyone (not just the few billionaires that own these companies) benefit from technology.

Ravi Corea, Macleod Pause data centres

Residents at Plumpton, West Footscray, Geelong, Port Melbourne and elsewhere have every reason to be alarmed at Jacinta Allan’s determination to hasten and expand data centre construction in Victoria (″⁣PM right to pump brakes on data centres″⁣, 18/7). The reasons are well-documented – immense energy and water demands, land misallocation, incessant noise, fire risk, pollution and ugliness. These downsides are plain to see in Melbourne.

Away from the cities, plans are being hatched for data centres in remote country in the Northern Territory, using gas from the Beetaloo Basin for energy generation and water from the Great Artesian Basin for cooling.

Each of these proposals is deeply problematic. The use of gas exacerbates global heating and the extraction of vast quantities of water from the Basin is a reckless exploitation of one of Australia’s natural treasures. Until the pros and cons are clearly spelt out, the case for a moratorium on new centres is compelling.

Tom Knowles, Parkville Security of a home

What is a house worth? To those with one, everything. To those desperate to secure one, everything. So why does a government that promises everything put its funds, resources, time and effort into everything else?

Housing satisfies a basic need for people. Everyone should have the opportunity to own one if not rent one. Why is the government still saying that it’s OK to have many while some have none? They are still, despite the changes, funding people to build property portfolios rather than allocating that money for social housing for the neediest in the community.

A home provides safety and security in most cases. It is more than just a monetary asset. It tightens family and social bonds. It holds memories. For many people, it is something that they can pass onto the next generation.

We have forgotten that for most people, a house is a lifetime commitment not something used for a quick turnover. Governments are so keen to analyse the housing market in terms of financial implications. Perhaps it is time that they looked at them through a social lens and discovered what home ownership means to people.

Greg Tuck, Warragul The world game

There might have been more people at the Collingwood-Carlton game at the MCG last weekend compared with the World Cup final, but more then 2 billion fans watched the game on TV. AFL remains a national game while soccer is truly the world game.

Nick Toovey, Beaumaris Positively perplexing

When was the last time Pauline Hanson said something positive about anyone or anything? I’ve drawn a blank.

Peter Heffernan, Balaclava



Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING One Nation

Barnaby Joyce shows that if you want a friend (to shout at), get a dog.

Malcolm McDonald, Burwood I suggest those aligned to One Nation vote for the dog.

Margaret Skeen, Ocean Grove



I, for one, am more interested in what Barnaby Joyce’s dog has to say than what Barnaby has to say.

Paul Caine, Glen Huntly Should Barnaby Joyce post-politics consider starting a dog obedience school?

Paul Miller, Albury God help us all if Malcolm Roberts reaches a position of power. He’s even starting to look like RFK jnr.

Pauline Walden, Brighton The Coalition and Labor don’t seem to realise that Pauline Hanson, like Donald Trump, is too different from other politicians to be defeated by the usual rules.

Tony O’Brien, South Melbourne Your correspondent (Letters, 21/7) suggests One Nation change its name to White Nation as a better reflection of its values. How about One White Nation? No ambiguity there.

Patrick Alilovic, Pascoe Vale South



For Pauline Hanson to say Gina Rinehart had “done it tough” is somewhat exaggerated. Rinehart attended boarding school at St Hilda’s Anglican School for Girls, an elite private school in Perth.

Suzanne Palmer-Holton, Seaford Furthermore

I am having some difficulty following the logic of Donald Trump when he complains about the meddlesome and fraudulent voting system, under which he was elected twice.

Graeme Bott, Sandringham I have a suggestion for teachers of English at our schools. Have a class competition to see if any student can make a sentence without the word “like” in it.

Madelene Alford, Richmond Finally

I got so excited to see the words “hyperbolic paraboloid”, (Letters, 21/7), that I had to reach for a Pringle.

Graham Bridges, Wodonga

World.title: Stuart Nash resigns as NZ First candidate, Winston Peters announces
World.content:
Stuart Nash has resigned as a New Zealand First candidate, Winston Peters has announced.

In a brief statement posted on social media late on Wednesday, the party leader wrote: "Stuart Nash has offered his resignation as a candidate and we have accepted."

Earlier, the prime minister ruled out Nash from serving as a minister in a government he leads.

Christopher Luxon also took to social media late on Wednesday night, following speculation on Nash's resignation as a New Zealand First candidate.

"Whether reports of Stuart Nash's resignation as a NZ First candidate are true or not, I am making clear he will not serve as a minister in my government."

Nash was roundly condemned on Wednesday by MPs at Parliament for calling National's Napier MP lazy for taking nine months off work at full pay.

In reality, Katie Nimon took six months away from Parliament after having a baby.

Earlier on Wednesday, Luxon had called the comments "sexist", and said Nash was channeling the "manosphere".

National Party leader Christopher Luxon (L) and NZ First candidate Stuart Nash (R). RNZ / Nate McKinnon and Dom Thomas

Asked if he'd have Nash around the Cabinet table, he only encouraged people to party vote National to avoid "numpties" from other parties.

Later that evening, Luxon said on social media, "Whether reports of Stuart Nash's resignation as a NZ First candidate are true or not, I am making clear he will not serve as a minister in my government.

"After several instances of poor behaviour, some politicians will claim he has changed.

"His lack of contrition after comments about one of my MPs' maternity leave this evening shows he hasn't."

In response to the criticism of his comments, Nash said in a statement on Wednesday afternoon the campaign was about who "shows up and delivers" for Napier.

"I'm happy to be judged on my own track record, achievements and work ethic. That's the contest I want."

For what it's worth he said, "I've got real respect for any working parent raising a newborn alongside a demanding job - that was never in question."

Nash added that was why he was part of a government that supported the extending of paid parental leave - "The law change that the National Party voted against, twice."

World.title: Waikato hospitals revert to paperwork after major IT outage
World.content:
Hospitals in the Waikato district have had their IT systems restored following a major outage.

Health NZ's Waikato group director of operations Stephanie Doe said emergency departments remained open and patients were safely cared for throughout the outage, which began at 10.44am on Wednesday.

The agency was continuing to monitor the situation closely, she said.

"Any impact to clinical systems is treated with the greatest urgency. We reverted to manual processes for a number of areas such as patient information tracking and results reporting. Urgent care, including our Emergency Department, was prioritised with additional resource in place," Doe said.

"Unfortunately, the outage meant some planned appointments needed to be deferred and affected patients will be contacted directly. We will reschedule appointments as soon as possible."

Earlier, Doe said a "network connectivity issue" had cut access to a number of applications used in Waikato hospitals.

This included Waikato, Thames, Te Kūiti, Tokoroa and Taumarunui.

"Where clinical systems are impacted, hospitals are reverting to manual processes to support continuity of care."

She said hospitals were prioritising urgent care and impacted patients would be contacted directly. Patients who have not been contacted should attend their appointments as normal.

She said the health agency was working to resolve the issue as quickly as possible.

A New Zealand Nurses Organisation delegate said access to patient history is limited to paper reports and any recent AI transcribed reports are not accessible.

There is slowed laboratory processing using paper based systems.

Doctors needed to view X-rays are required to walk to the X-ray department.

The ED is still functioning, but there is slower to access information and results, so longer wait times are predicted.

There is a reliance on cell phones to communicate as paging systems are not working and some patient call bells are not working.

RNZ has also seen correspondence to staff which said paper-based request systems must be used in the radiology department.

Theatres will continue for urgent and prioritised care, while the laboratory will be prioritising critical tests. Most outpatient clinics have also been deferred with clinical oversight.

The correspondence said the impacts were varied across services, depending on whether applications were hosted on local servers.

It also said the timeline to resolve the issue was "unknown."

Further correspondence advised staff there was a district-wide issue affecting the integrated software used, which was being investigated.

While it was being looked into and resolved, staff were told to "maintain all clinical documentation using paper-based notes".

"Staff should also continue to record and manage all patient contacts in accordance with the current paper documentation processes."

A further update would be provided as soon as the issue was rectified and "normal system functionality has been restored."

In the meantime, they were asked to ensure all patient documentation is completed and maintained on paper; all relevant patient contacts and interventions are recorded through paper-based process; and any urgent concerns or issues are escalated through the usual channels.

Staff were thanked for their patience and cooperation while it was being resolved.

PSA national secretary Fleur Fitzsimons said the outage was a result of "irresponsible cuts made to data and digital roles at Health New Zealand".

Fitzsimons said the outages would "become commonplace" because the date and digital expertise had been lost as a result of cost savings at Health New Zealand.

After another IT outage to hospitals in the upper North Island earlier this year, Auckland University computer scientist Dr Ulrich Speidel told RNZ the country's health IT systems were vulnerable due to decades of neglect.

World.title: Travel alert 'strongly' advises New Zealanders to avoid Middle East
World.content:
New Zealand has updated travel advice for the Middle East, with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs warning the military conflict between Iran and the US could escalate further in coming days.

The ministry's Safe Travel site says the situation remains unpredictable with military strikes and reprisal attacks happening in a number of locations.

It says if the security situation deteriorates further there could be travel disruption and airspace closures.

The alert warned that New Zealanders travelling through the Middle East transit hubs could become stranded for extended periods.

It has now issued a Level 3 alert - advising against all non-essential travel to Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates.

It advised people to consult with their travel insurance providers to understand the policy's conditions, including if government travel advisories or war exceptions could potentially void their coverage.

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency has issued advice to air operators to avoid Gulf airspace until at least 29 July 2026.

It said people should check with their travel providers to confirm if their flights were affected.

New Zealanders who were in the locations where travel alerts had been issued should monitor media closely for reporting of potential targets in the region and warnings issued by local authorities.

"For those travelling, we strongly advise New Zealanders to avoid the Middle East and consider other travel routes. If you need to transit these locations, stay as short a time as possible and avoid unnecessary activities. Airspace may close at short notice. Flights can change or stop suddenly. Borders can close," the advisory said.

"US strikes had been reported in many locations across Iran, including in Buschehr, Bandar Abbas, Chabahar, Konarak, Kurdistan, Sirik, Tabriz and Hamadan," it said.

World.title: Auckland school forced to cancel school camp as families unable to afford it
World.content:
Papatoetoe Intermediate School has been forced to cancel its school camp this year because so few families could afford it.

Despite attempts to keep the price down, only 160 out of 750 students confirmed they could go.

As inflation hits its highest level in two years, at 4.1 percent, the cost of fuel, electricity, rates and groceries all continue to go up.

Checkpoint is also aware of another school that been fundraising so no student was left behind.

Intermediate school cancels camp as families can't afford the cost Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

Papatoetoe Intermediate School principal, Pauline Cornwell told Checkpoint it was clear the economic situation was having a major impact on the community.

"We provide camp every two years, so the last time we went to camp, it was around $240, and this year, it's over $350."

She said that parents simply could not afford the fee, and there was no way the school had enough to cover the gap.

Cornwell said there were many factors out of their control that were driving up the price of the camp.

"Petrol has increased and the price of transporting children to and from camp has increased dramatically.

"We also have camp costs, so the camp that we go to is a great camp, but their staffing and consumer costs have increased markedly, and then our costs here at school, the payment of support staff to go to camp and the costs of supporting the children to get there and make sure that they've got the things that they need to have, all of that stuff's increased."

Cornwell said it was incredibly important for the school to provide their students with the opportunity to go to camp, with many coming from low socioeconomic backgrounds or new immigrant families.

"A lot of our students wouldn't have this opportunity at all, so we believe it's important for them to have a chance to go away and participate in things like bush walks and sleeping over together and eating together, as well as doing some of those activities that you just can't do on site or in the city.

"For our students, it's a once in a lifetime experience for many of them."

She said the fact that there were unable to provide that opportunity was worrying.

"The fact that we can't provide the opportunity for our children, just simply can't afford to bridge the gap, is just devastating."

Cornwell said she had heard of other schools having to cut back on their own camps due to similar issues around costs.

"I've heard of schools that have reduced the length of stay, and I've heard of schools who've reduced the length of the variety of options for camp across the board, so it's not just in low socio-economic communities, it's across the board."

Auckland Primary Principals Association president Lucy Naylor said they were also hearing fewer schools were offering camps.

"It's definitely widespread, it's definitely got worse in the last couple of years and I think for a lot of schools it would be an easy thing to let go because a lot of schools would perhaps see it as an add-on."

The rising cost of living was clearly having an impact, she said.

"The cost of camps has been going up probably for three, four years now... the cost of living obviously impacts that."

Naylor said it was easy to see how the costs could quickly add up.

"If you had a child in year six and one in year five, you're paying for two school camps, plus the beginning of year stationery, plus the school donation, plus any equipment or bits and pieces you need for camp - so those costs would be huge."

While some schools may be forced to cancel camps, Naylor worried that there was also a cost to doing that.

World.title: Southland man's kidney cancer surgery delayed for weeks amid urologist staffing woes
World.content:
A Southland cancer patient who needs regular surgery to control the growth has faced weeks of delays after a cancellation.

David Evans is bracing for the possibility his kidney cancer has spread - or he will be unable to keep his kidney - when he eventually returns to the operating theatre on Thursday.

The Winton man was scheduled for surgery two months ago, but it was postponed and then later cancelled.

It follows the resignation of two urologists - which Health New Zealand first confirmed in March - followed by "additional unanticipated absences", leaving the region with no permanent full-time urologists.

Southland cancer patient left in the dark after operation cancelled Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Health New Zealand said patients were being seen by one primarily Southland-based urologist and one specialist who visited weekly, while permanent full-time replacements were sought.

Evans said he had undergone surgeries every three to four months since last year to cut away the cancer.

His most recent operation was in January at Southland Hospital and the next was scheduled for 14 May, he said.

"They came and saw me on the day, very apologetic, saying that because of theatre overrun they would rebook me for the following week - which they did. But I received a phone call on the Monday to tell me that all surgeries had been cancelled and there was no follow up at all," Evans said.

He called the hospital countless times to find out when he could be rescheduled, but each time he was transferred to a voicemail at the urology department, he said.

"I just couldn't believe the lack of follow-up... I hadn't received anything until last week when, thank God, they said we've got a surgery booked in for this coming Thursday."

Hospital staff did not tell him about the urologist resignations - instead he read about them in the news as he sought an explanation for the change in plans, he said.

"I need the three and four month operations... this is coming up to about seven months now. With time comes longer growth periods and I don't know how far the cancer has travelled," he said.

Evans said he had no criticism for the doctors and nurses he had dealt with, but high-level decision-makers needed to show greater transparency and accountability.

"People are being sent home and are slowly dying because they cannot get into the hospital and that's tragic. It really is."

Health New Zealand apologises

Health New Zealand declined RNZ's request for an interview but - in a statement - southern group director of operations Craig Ashton said the organisation sincerely apologised for the treatment delays experienced by Evans.

No procedures could go ahead on the day Evans' surgery was scheduled because of unexpected leave from the treating urologist, he said.

"We acknowledge that any delay for surgery can be distressing and patients can be assured that surgeries and procedures are prioritised based on patient acuity and only deferred where absolutely necessary and only if it is clinically safe to do so," Ashton said.

"The decision to defer or delay care is never taken lightly."

Health NZ confirmed two urology positions in Southland remained vacant.

"We are exploring all avenues to improve our capacity, including ongoing recruitment efforts, seeking support from locums and Health New Zealand staff from other areas, and outsourcing where possible - both locally and in other locations in the South Island," Ashton said.

Long-standing issues criticised

Trish Wright - coordinator of the Southland Support Group of the Prostate Cancer Foundation - said she was absolutely gutted to hear the two urologists had resigned earlier this year.

Prostate cancer patients typically needed treatment sooner rather than later and relied on timely access to urologists, she said.

"If they are eligible for surgery and if it's recommended, our two urologists would certainly have done it in a timely fashion in past. I can't imagine how long these guys are going to have to wait when there is no urologist down here or urology surgeon at least," Wright said.

"It's mind-boggling what has what has happened with both of them going."

It seemed Health NZ had not done enough succession planning to prepare for the staffing gap and that was disappointing, she said.

"We know how hard it is to get doctors down here anyway. Imagine how big the waiting list is going to be by the time they manage to get another urologist down here... things are just going to get worse."

Health NZ's latest quarterly report showed cancer patients in Southland had the second-longest wait times for treatment anywhere in the country, behind Canterbury.

As of March, 18.9 percent percent of the region's patients were waiting longer than 31 days for their treatment to start.

Southland Kidney Society president Nobby Clark said the region's residents had long suffered from a postcode lottery, where speed of access to specialists and surgery appeared to be dictated by geography.

"You don't have to go too far to find shortages in just about every area you want to go to and certainly Southland Hospital suffers from that," he said.

Cancer Society Southern chief executive Christine Prince said it was common for Southlanders to wait weeks or even months for treatment.

"There seems to be long, long, ongoing issues involved with resourcing and access of care for patients across Otago-Southland. This encompasses... bladder cancer, prostate, kidney cancer... it's quite significant," she said.

World.title: Union says north Waikato prison staff shortcutting puts 'public at risk'
World.content:
The union representing prison staff says staff shortcutting at a north Waikato prison is only putting the public at more risk.

Short-staffing, low staff morale, no onsite drug testing for years, contraband readily available, and filthy uninhabitable parts of the jail were just some of the serious concerns identified at the Spring Hill Correctional Facility.

A report by the inspectorate office also highlights issues with staff absences and inexperience, long lockdowns for inmates, inadequate meals, clothing and bedding.

The prison was over capacity for its original design as an end destination site for 650 prisoners. It had essentially became a remand site, Chief Inspector Janis Adair said, housing over 800 prisoners at the time of inspection. The report found this change in population proving a challenge for the site's infrastructure and staff alike.

The inspection found custodial staffing levels were at 94 percent, but that morale was low amongst custodial staff and unplanned absences, like sick leave, were common and left units short staffed.

"The lack of availability of custodial staff and the unsuitable infrastructure had significant impacts across the prison."

Corrections Association New Zealand president Floyd du Plessis said the report was not surprising.

"The component that is surprising to us is the statement from Corrections that these things have all been addressed and progressed. From what our members are saying on the floor, the people that work in that prison on the floor every day, they haven't seen an improvement. They're still seeing daily occurrences of short staffing, corners being cut and safety still a continual issue."

He said overall staffing numbers had increased, but due to financial restraints were still not covering shifts.

"Where staff are sick or short, they're not putting on additional shifts to replace those and so on a daily basis, they're actually still running short just for a different reason.

"The fact that prisoners aren't able to be brought out for programs, interviews, health checks, and that drives that tension and concern, and that's exactly the problem the report identified, but we're still seeing that same problem occurring now."

He said when a prison isn't staffed properly it just means rehabilitation programmes and interventions weren't able to happen, so prisoners were sitting there with no reintegration or offending needs addressed.

Then, they're being released, having not gone through all of those programmes to improve.

"That puts the community at an even greater risk than they already are," du Plessis said.

"We can't shortcut staffing in a place like a prison. The staffing's built to the minimum we possibly need to safely run and as soon as you do any reduction in that, things stop. And the first thing that stops is those programs, those interventions, those interviews that are needed to help identify chronogenic needs and all those interventions that are required to help change their way of thinking.

"A prison that's running badly puts the public at risk. It's not some hidden thing that sits in a corner.

"Unfortunately, it all comes down to fiscal. They see it as a financial line item, we see it as a safety thing... As much as people think it's forgotten, all of these people get released, all of them come back to the community. Unless we improve it, public and staff have been placed at risk."

He said staff felt extremely at risk.

"We have regular reports from staff that they're not feeling safe. They're cutting corners to just get through the day. Every time they cut a corner, they're putting themselves at risk and they're facing a lot of backlash.

"So when prisoners don't get out, when they don't get access to those different programs or nurses and the like. They lash out, they get frustrated, and they lash out at staff, and we're seeing that on a weekly basis."

That, he said ranges anywhere from ongoing threats of violence to actual violence on a daily basis.

"The more staff you have, the more you can do and that's the key. We keep trying to get more done with less stuff. And in an environment like ours with the risks and concerns we face, it's just impossible. It's either safety or it's not. And the reality is you can't do anything more unless you make it safe and the only way to make it safer is more staff.

"Nintety-nine per cent of corrections officers join the job because they want to make a difference. They want to work and get these things running right. But it's hard when you're short staff and you're just not able to."

Corrections custodial services commissioner Sean Mason said, in response to the report, it was positive to see many of the areas identified for improvement in the report aligned with work Corrections had already addressed or that was underway since the inspection was carried out more than a year ago.

"Many prisoners go to extreme lengths to get contraband into prisons and Corrections is constantly working to stay one step ahead in contraband prevention."

Drug testing was reintroduced in November 2025 after it was suspended during the Covid-19 pandemic, he said, when all non-essential prison activities were paused to reduce operational risks and support public health requirements and when staffing pressures were at their tightest.

Mason also said following an extensive nationwide recruitment drive, there was now an additional 45 custodial staff working at the site, and this had reduced the day-to-day impact on the prison when staff called in sick.

World.title: Public toilets in Mackenzie District to get $2.5 million investment
World.content:
The Mackenzie District mayor says a $2.5 million investment to improve public toilets is a "good start going forward".

"We've been banging on their door for for quite some time," Scott Aronsen says.

The money will come from the International Visitor Levy (IVL) and be used to introduce user-pays systems at some public toilet facilities in the district.

Some of the toilets could be "easily converted" he said, while others would be upgraded.

Aronsen said the investment was an important step towards creating a fairer and more sustainable way of funding public facilities.

He said the money would help "offset" some of the cleaning cost, which is about $800,000 a year.

"We need to try and regather some of that cost back because at the moment that's falling squarely on the ratepayer of the Mackenzie district."

The public toilet network in the district is used an estimated one million times each year, with the overwhelming majority of those users being visitors.

"They're heavily utilised, and it's a significant cost," Aronsen said.

He acknowledged not everyone would agree with it, and realised as a district "we're sort of sticking our neck out on the line a little bit," but it was a means of being able to gather some revenue outside the normal rates base to fund the facilities they "obviously" had to have.

The council will now begin planning for the programme including consultation.

The funding is part of a $3.8 million investment to improve public toilets in two of New Zealand's "busiest visitor destinations", according to Tourism and Hospitality Minister Louise Upston.

It would support upgrades and new facilities in the Mackenzie and Queenstown Lakes districts.

"Both districts welcome large numbers of visitors each year, placing significant pressure on infrastructure normally funded by ratepayers," Upston said.

World.title: Christopher Luxon calls out NZ First's Stuart Nash on 'sexist' comment
World.content:
The Prime Minister says comments by New Zealand First candidate Stuart Nash about a National MP's maternity leave are "sexist", and he along with his party are "channelling the manosphere".

"He's had a history of making very derogatory comments around women over many years," says Christopher Luxon.

"Every woman in the country would understand that those comments are sexist and they're grossly inappropriate."

The MP in question, Katie Nimon, has laughed off the comments saying she's achieved more with National for Hawke's Bay in three years "with a baby" than Nash has in nine years.

"You can be a mum, and work and achieve great things," she told the Debating chamber on Wednesday.

On the Cross Party Lines podcast, former National minister Chris Finlayson revealed Nash had sent him a text saying the MP for Napier, Katie Nimon, was the "laziest MP" he'd ever come across.

"Katie took nine months off on full pay, went back for a week, then took another month off.

"Laziest MP I've ever come across. Nice woman, but ill suited to the rigours of being an electorate MP," said Nash.

Nash has previously apologised for describing a woman as a "person with a p***y and a pair of t**s" last year, resulting in him resigning from his job at recruitment agency Robert Walters after a formal review was initiated by the company.

Katie Nimon told RNZ on Wednesday Nash was making his views on women "very clear," and confirmed she was back working in the electorate after around 10 weeks before coming back to Parliament after six months.

"I'll let my actions speak louder than his words."

She later told reporters she'd had to have "a little giggle" because the comments weren't true.

Nimon said she took her son everywhere, and would look back on his history as part of all the things she had achieved for Hawke's Bay.

"In fact, I've achieved more with National for Hawke's Bay in three years with a baby than he has in nine years."

Nash released a statement late this afternoon saying this campaign was about who "shows up and delivers" for Napier.

"I'm happy to be judged on my own track record, achievements and work ethic. That's the contest I want."

For what it is worth he said: "I've got real respect for any working parent raising a newborn alongside a demanding job - that was never in question."

That was why he was part of a government that supported the extending of paid parental leave - "The law change that the National Party voted against, twice," Nash added.

But Luxon, along with other MPs, lashed out at Nash's comments, saying Nash channels the "manosphere".

"Katie Nimon's an incredibly hard-working MP," he said, and a "real talent for this place".

Most importantly, she was someone who had taken parental leave "as you would reasonably expect, as I have encouraged her to do so".

Luxon called for people to party vote National so he wouldn't have to have "numpties from other parties" around the Cabinet table.

National Minister Chris Bishop echoed this, saying "you're joking" when the comments were put to him, "that's just disgusting".

"Stuart Nash needs to take that kind of misogynistic behaviour and stay in Napier."

Bishop said Nimon had taken parental leave "as she should", and she was "one of the hardest working MPs" he knew, describing her presence with her baby during her parental leave at a sod turning event in Hawke's Bay.

"If in the unlikely event he makes it back to Parliament, he will find that the world's actually moved on from those kind of 1950s attitudes."

Another National minister, Nicola Willis, was just as scathing, saying "raising children isn't a lazy job".

"It's a hard job and involves a lot of hard work," adding that parenthood "does not somehow exclude us from being able to take positions of public leadership."

Willis said if Nash thought women and men juggling children and work were lazy and don't deserve leadership roles, "you need to go back to the 1920s because they need their ignorant man back".

ACT leader David Seymour told RNZ it was unhelpful and offensive and "probably shows a little bit of an anti-woman bias that I don't think is going to help unlock New Zealand's potential.

"I was astonished the more I thought about it, young working mums are many things but they're certainly not lazy."

He said it was up to Winston Peters to explain why people in his party "seem to keep saying these kinds of things".

Labour leader Chris Hipkins told RNZ Nash was a "walking liability" for New Zealand First.

"His views do not reflect 21st Century New Zealand.

"Women are absolutely entitled to take parental leave, they should not be criticised for doing so."

Greens co-leader Marama Davidson said she was not surprised, that the comments were pretty vulgar and she did not want to give him any more airtime.

"This is not the conversation that we should be upholding as politicians, and the undermining again of women, surely Stuart Nash has had enough of undermining women for his lifetime."

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters is out of the country, but Deputy Leader Shane Jones wouldn't comment on the issue.

"I haven't heard them, and I won't be commenting on them," he said.

Asked again by reporters later, he said he wanted to understand the context the comments were made before commenting.

His New Zealand First colleague Casey Costello also said she hadn't heard the comments, but didn't think it was appropriate "to accuse any woman who takes maternity leave for having time off".

She did say she thought Nash was "genuinely a good guy".

World.title: Lewis breaks Australian 100m record, beats five-time Olympic champ
World.content:
Torrie Lewis has set a new Australian women's 100 metres record after breaking her own national record at a meet in Slovakia.

Lewis ran a time of 11.04 seconds, beating her previous record time of 11.08 as she beat out Jamaica's five-time Olympic champion Elaine Thompson-Herah, who finished in second.

The 21-year-old Lewis also competed in and won the 200m event, where she ran a 22.66.

It is the third separate time Lewis has broken the Australian 100m record, having previously done so as a 19-year-old in 2024 by running an 11.10 before lowering that mark to 11.08 at last year's World Championships.

Lewis beat out Jamaican sprint icon Elaine-Thompson Herah (pictured). (Getty: Al Bello)

Lewis made her Olympic debut in the 200m event in Paris two years ago and finished in the semifinals after running a then-personal-best time of 22.89. She also competed in the 4x100m event in Paris.

The women's 100m record is owned by late American sprint legend Florence Griffith-Joyner, who ran a 10.49 at the US Olympic trials in 1988. Thompson-Herah holds the second-fastest 100m mark of all time at 10.54.

Griffith-Joyner also holds the world record for the 200m, 21.34, a mark she set at the 1988 Olympics in Seoul.

Both records are among the longest-standing across all women's athletics.

The career-best 100m time comes at the perfect time for Lewis, who is poised to compete in the 100m, 200m and 4x100m relay events at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

World.title: Fox sisters combine in 'dream team' for gold medals at World Championships
World.content:
The gold rush at the world titles has continued for Jess Fox, with the canoe slalom legend spearheading the Australian women's kayak team to victory in Oklahoma.

A day after three-time Olympic champion Fox claimed gold in the kayak cross time trial event, the 32-year-old joined her younger sister Noemie Fox and Kate Eckhardt at the top of the podium.

The victory at Riversport Rapids on Tuesday (Wednesday AEST) continued Fox's successful return to competition since undergoing surgery to remove a tumour from a kidney last August.

Loading Instagram content

It is the second title for the trio after winning gold in London in 2023 in the same event, which is only contested at the world championships.

Competing on the same course that will host the canoe slalom at the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, the Australians used experience and expertise in their clinical run to put pressure on the final three teams.

In third place heading into the final third of the race, the trio lifted to complete a clean run through the gates and finish 0.64 seconds ahead of France and Slovakia.

"We're a bit of a dream team," Noemie said.

"We've been training so well and supporting each other. There was so much trust and support in the lead in, and we felt so good and wanted to do our best out there.

"To share these moments and be so proud of what we've done and to have those moments in an individual sport where we can collectively push each other and celebrate together is so special.

"It was just so much fun out there and to be rewarded with a gold medal is amazing, and I'm so proud of our double title now."

The golden girls also had success in the individual kayak race, with all qualifying for the top 30 semifinals.

Despite posting the fastest time of the day, Jess Fox, who is chasing a 16th world title, was docked for two gate touches and progressed in ninth place.

Jess Fox is chasing a 16th world title. (ABC News: Sean Tarek Goodwin)

"A bit of a shaky start with the two touches back-to-back, but overall it was then solid and I kept the boat speed on and I knew I would have to push to qualify because you never know — that top 30 can be really tight especially on a course like this," she said.

Eckhardt qualified in 11th position and Noemie was 25th.

In the men's kayak teams final, the Australian men had an unfortunate 50-second penalty in their run and finished 18th.

They had better luck in the individual kayak heats, with all six paddlers progressing through to the K1 semi-finals.

Olympian Tim Anderson was the best of the Aussies in eighth.

AAP

World.title: Former Socceroos captain Paul Wade reveals probable CTE diagnosis
World.content:
Former Socceroos captain Paul Wade has revealed he has been diagnosed with "probable" chronic traumatic encephalopathy, which has been linked to repeated head knocks and injuries.

In a statement put out by Professional Footballers Australia (PFA) on Wednesday, Wade said he was diagnosed in late 2024 with a suspected case of the disease after experiencing neurological symptoms.

He said this was upgraded after further assessments to probable in 2025.

The disease can only be confirmed after death.

"They did the tests … and [the neurologists] went, 'Oh, we've got a real problem here'," he told the ABC.

Symptoms of the disease can include depression, memory loss, tremors, poor impulse control and suicidal thoughts.

After scans showed it was probable CTE he said he just "stood there" and thought "am I going to die from this?"

Wade revealed a diagnosis of probable chronic traumatic encephalopathy. (7.30)

Wade's neurologist Rowena Mobbs made the "probable" diagnosis after two years of monitoring his symptoms and extensive testing.

Dr Mobbs said neurologists across Australia started using "probable" diagnoses to refer patients to the right treatment.

"It's not about fear, it's not about giving any definitive diagnosis, but it's about getting appropriate care and support to people," she said.

"I think Paul and his family want to see people in the community feeling confident that they can come forward for help and getting that right dementia care."

'He knew something was wrong'

Wade, who now lives on the Central Coast, north of Sydney, said receiving the diagnosis was "difficult" but wanted to share his experience to raise awareness of concussion and brain health across all levels of football.

"Football gave me so much. It gave me a life, a career, incredible experiences and the privilege of representing Australia," he said.

" But I also must be honest about the challenges I now face and the uncertainty that comes with living with a neurodegenerative condition. "

Asked whether the probable diagnosis was linked to his time playing, he said "it must have had something to do with it".

"I think about the number of times at a training session I headed a ball."

Dr Mobbs said Wade expressed a level of "validation" when he received the "probable" diagnosis.

"He knew it in himself… He knew something was wrong, he knew it felt different," she said.

Head of neuropathology at Sydney's Royal Prince Alfred Hospital, Michael Buckland, said a "probable" CTE diagnosis should be used for research purposes rather than in a clinical context.

"We have no idea how accurate that [diagnosis] is, it's still being tested," he said.

"The authors of the paper, that defined what probable CTE is, strongly cautioned against using it in a clinical setting, and they and others recognise the real risk of harm in giving someone a diagnosis that you can't really be confident about."

However, Dr Buckland commended Wade for raising awareness of the condition.

"I think he's done a very generous and courageous thing by speaking publicly," Dr Buckland said.

Doctor urges ban to headers by children

Rowena Mobbs said Wade's diagnosis came after "extensive testing". (ABC News: Michael Nudl)

After 30 years of exposure to head knocks in soccer, including headers, Dr Mobbs said repetitive traumatic brain injury was the "main burden" for Wade.

Dr Mobbs urged Football Australia to ban headers for children playing soccer under the age of 12.

"We must hold onto our activity and sport in life, for our kids especially, but we need to lower the repetitive head injury burden," she said.

"That's where we need good care in the community, with our excellent health systems, the government to step in and provide funding for research, and for us all to be aware of our lifetime burden of head injury and try and prevent it where possible."

Sixty-four-year-old Wade, who led the national team for six years in the 1990s, said more understanding was needed about the long-term effects of repeated head impacts to "protect future generations".

"If sharing my experience can help someone seek support, create better education and prevention, or help the game take brain health more seriously, then it is worth doing," Wade, who also lives with epilepsy, said.

'Advancement of the game'

Wade's announcement comes less than a month after Four Corner's revealed 33 Australian Rules players had been diagnosed with CTE.

Wade (left) leading out the Socceroos for the 1993 Australia v Argentina FIFA World Cup play-off match. (Getty Images: Joe Mann/Offside)

He said people concerned should not stop playing contact sports "because if you do we're going to have an even bigger problem with mental health and wellbeing".

"To the people actually making the rules we've got to come up with ways we can make it safer," Wade said.

"If I could say to Football Australia, or even FIFA, if you're listening, let's put some protocols in there because you've got everything about concussion.

"[But] you don't talk about CTE and how we can change the game and change the training and change the age so that it's minimalised, so we're not exposing kids to CTE."

He asked who was going to "stand up and be brave and say no", and assert boundaries.

"Someone's got to say no. Kids are … heading a ball 12 years or under. Make it 14, I don't care," he said.

PFC Chair Francis Awaritefe urged sporting organisations to ban heading for young players, particularly until children learn the "proper technique".

"We shouldn't even be waiting, I think we should be doing it now," Mr Awaritefe said.

PFA chief executive Beau Busch said Wade's decision to open up about his diagnosis was an "important act of leadership".

"In sharing his story Paul has once again illustrated his truly remarkable commitment to the advancement of the game," Mr Busch said.

"He is doing so not only for himself but for the players and families who are facing, or may one day face, similar questions about brain health."

Mr Busch said Australian football must be proactive in tackling brain injuries "through better policies, research, education and support for former players".

A decorated career

Wade, who was born in England in 1962, came to Australia at 11 years of age with a passion for football, moving his way up to senior positions within Victorian clubs including Croydon, Green Gully, Brunswick and South Melbourne.

In 1985 he claimed a spot in the Australian team, playing his first full international against Czechoslovakia the following year.

He then captained the Australian soccer side from 1990 to 1996.

Wade was captain of the Socceroos for six years. (News Video)

On Football Australia's website Wade is credited with 345 national league appearances, 119 matches played for Australia, and 84 full internationals.

Wade also played in the 1988 Olympic Games and two World Cup qualifying campaigns.

After he retired as a player he became involved with TV commentary and coaching clinics for kids.

His career and the impacts of his neurodegenerative condition will be explored in an upcoming mini documentary being produced by PFA.

World.title: Spanish chief accuses FIFA boss of 'destroying the football industry'
World.content:
Gianni Infantino should resign as head of FIFA for "destroying the football industry" by expanding international competitions, according to Javier Tebas, the president of Spain's football league La Liga

It is not the first time he has lashed out at Infantino over fixture congestion and for considering a proposal to expand the 2030 men's World Cup from 48 teams to 64.

"Increasing the number of national teams makes no sense. The football industry isn't just the World Cup, which is the most important event. But not everything can revolve around the World Cup," Tebas told La Gazzetta dello Sport.

Players and fans made the World Cup a success, but the politics shouldn't be forgotten The biggest ever World Cup brought diverse communities together and galvanised its non-traditional footballing co-hosts, but the concerns raised from the start have not disappeared in the positive afterglow.

"In my opinion, yes, I think his time is up," he said of Infantino. "However, he has the support of the system and the federations, so there's not much more to add, is there? There's no opposition candidate, nobody wants to stand just to lose. This is the system and it's rotten at its core.

"He shouldn't stay, but he won't leave. I've heard many people who are against Infantino. They say it, but then they do nothing. I don't know what's worse, the silence or the complicity, because those who stay silent are perfectly aware of the damage football is suffering."

South American soccer's ruling body CONMEBOL has made an official proposal to expand the 2030 World Cup to 64 teams. The competition is already set to be the most sprawling edition, with six host nations spread across three continents.

"It's national competition that sustains this sport," Tebas added. "They are destroying the football industry, which generates tens of thousands of jobs, for an event that lasts 40 days and involves a minority of players."

The World Cup final had a 27-minute half-time interval thanks to a half-time show featuring artists such as Justin Bieber (pictured). (Reuters: Amanda Perobelli)

He also criticised world football's governing body FIFA over the new hydration breaks implemented at the World Cup, which ended on Sunday, as well as the extended 27-minute half-time interval — rather than the standard 15 — during the final, in which Spain defeated Argentina 1-0.

The hydration breaks midway through each half were introduced to help players deal with the summer heat in the United States, Canada and Mexico. But critics say they had unintended consequences, ruining the flow of the game and giving coaches a chance to tactically shift momentum in their team's favour.

"FIFA arranges things as it pleases, for what it wants, for its own interests, certainly not for football," Tebas said. "Hydration breaks are a lie. We have them in La Liga, but only when it's genuinely hot. Here, the pitches in Dallas, Los Angeles, and Atlanta had air conditioning. It was a lie and just a break for advertising."

Infantino announced in April that he would run for re-election for a fourth term as president. The vote for the 2027–2031 period is scheduled for March 18 in Morocco.

La Liga boss Javier Tebas has not been shy about attacking Infantino in the past. (Getty Images: Oscar J. Barroso/Europa Press)

The Football Supporters Europe (FSE) group also called on the wider soccer community to hold FIFA to account.

In a statement on its website headlined "A World Cup that failed supporters", the FSE demanded "structural governance reforms to hand decision-making power back to the FIFA Council and Congress and ensure full consultation with clubs, leagues, players and supporters".

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

It added: "The 2026 World Cup should have been a celebration of the game and the supporters who give it life. Instead, it has too often become a case study in what is so deeply wrong with football today.

"From the outset, supporters were asked to place their trust in FIFA and "chill", but it prioritised spectacle and commercialisation over the match-going experience with key elements of football's identity being messed with. Over the last month, we've seen football contorted to the whim of Gianni Infantino and the Trump administration."

The FSE, accepted by European soccer's governing body UEFA as the recognised group representing fans in the region, then went on to attack "historically high ticket prices" and "skyrocketing transportation costs, bending of rules and procedures, exclusion of swathes of the global population and a lack of transparent communication".

"All this created an environment of confusion and distrust that has severely damaged the reputation of FIFA, the World Cup, and the integrity of football itself," its statement said.

"The lessons from this World Cup are clear: FIFA is unfit to govern global football. The future of the game cannot rest in the hands of a man who has proven yet again that he puts financial and political interests ahead of the future of our game."

AP

World.title: Cameron McEvoy has lived a life between trips to Glasgow
World.content:
When Cameron McEvoy travelled to Glasgow in 2014, he was a 19-year-old "kid".

Twelve years later, he returns to the site of his Commonwealth Games debut as a completely different man with a completely different outlook on a sport that is almost unrecognisable.

McEvoy emerged as part of the ill-fated batch of sprint stars at the 2012 Olympics — the so-called "weapons of mass destruction" who returned from London without a gold medal from any male swimmer.

Two years later, McEvoy won six medals, including two relay golds, at the Commonwealth Games despite still trying to find his place in the squad.

"I still felt like a new person on the team back in 2014," he told reporters at Glasgow airport on Wednesday morning (AEST).

Cam McEvoy says his 50m freestyle world record is just the beginning When Cameron McEvoy broke the long-standing 50m freestyle world record in March, he was at great pains to note that he believes he can go even faster.

"I was super shy; I wasn't really outspoken. I'm in the same sport but the way I'm conducting training on a day-to-day basis, the way being on the team feels now compared to as a rookie, almost feels like it's a new sport.

"It's going to be almost nostalgic being back at the Tollcross pool, seeing the set-up and going through the same thing I did as a teenager."

As he and the Dolphins touched down in the Scottish capital once again, McEvoy is a brand new man and one of only two Australian swimmers, along with Lakeisha Patterson, back for another go.

"A lot has changed," he said.

"I was basically a kid [in 2014], and now I've got my own kid. Things are very different now.

A baby-faced McEvoy won three individual silvers as part of a six-medal haul in Glasgow 12 years ago. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

"There's actually a member on the swim team who's 14 [Mia Hogan], so she was only two when I was back here competing last time.

"A lot has happened; basically, my entire international career has unfolded."

Do you know an athlete competing at the Commonwealth Games? Share with us Whether you are you a family member, a friend, a colleague or a coach, share your connection with us and how you will be supporting them.

McEvoy missed out on individual medals at his first three Olympic Games and is surprisingly still hunting his first individual Commonwealth gold.

At Glasgow 2014 he finished second in the 50m, 100m and 200m. At his home Games on the Gold Coast in 2018, the pain was amplified when he picked up bronze in the 50m but missed the medals in the 100m despite entering as the Commonwealth record holder and fastest qualifier for the final.

McEvoy struggled to bounce back from those setbacks, particularly at Rio 2016 and Gold Coast 2018, to the point that when the last Commonwealth Games were on, he was at home considering his future in the sport.

He said he was "in the wilderness", unsure if he wanted to continue swimming after so many painful disappointments, but teammate Elijah Winnington's mental resilience got him back in the pool.

"Elijah had just won the 400m freestyle world title on the back of falling short in Tokyo [2021 Olympics]. For me, I saw that as a massive inspiration," he said.
